title: mHealth Strategy to Fight Tuberculosis in Bangladesh
text: Tuberculosis (TB) remains a significant public health challenge in Bangladesh, which consistently ranks among the countries with the highest TB burdens globally. Despite substantial progress in expanding Directly Observed Treatment Short-course (DOTS) coverage, persistent gaps in patient adherence, delayed diagnosis, and loss to follow-up continue to hamper national control efforts. This paper presents a comprehensive mobile health (mHealth) strategy designed to strengthen Bangladesh’s TB response through context-appropriate digital innovation. Leveraging the country’s high mobile phone penetration, the proposed framework integrates short message service (SMS) and voice-based reminders to support medication adherence, mobile-enabled active case finding in hard-to-reach communities, real-time digital data capture by community health workers, and telemedicine consultations for remote expert support. The strategy emphasizes interoperability with existing Health Management Information Systems and privacy-compliant architectures to ensure scalability and sustainability. Drawing on evidence from regional pilot implementations and global best practices, we argue that a coordinated, government-led mHealth approach can reduce treatment default rates, accelerate case notification, and enhance the efficiency of resource allocation. This paper offers actionable recommendations for policymakers, program managers, and digital health practitioners to integrate mHealth into Bangladesh’s National Tuberculosis Control Program, ultimately contributing to the national goal of ending TB.

title: Modeling the Location Selection of Mirror Servers in Content Delivery Networks
text:
The proliferation of high-definition streaming, cloud computing, and real-time interactive applications has precipitated an unprecedented surge in global internet traffic, placing immense strain on backbone networks and origin servers. Content Delivery Networks (CDNs) have emerged as an indispensable infrastructure paradigm to alleviate this burden by caching and distributing content through geographically dispersed mirror servers, thereby reducing end-to-end latency, balancing network load, and enhancing the overall quality of user experience. The strategic placement of these edge nodes directly determines the efficacy of content dissemination; servers positioned proximal to dense concentrations of demand can significantly diminish round-trip times, packet loss, and backbone congestion, whereas suboptimal locations may result in prohibitive operational costs and degraded service quality despite substantial capital investments. As online content consumption continues to grow exponentially, the need for rigorous, data-driven approaches to guide the geographic expansion of CDN infrastructure has become increasingly urgent.

Determining the optimal locations for mirror servers, however, remains a complex combinatorial optimization challenge characterized by competing objectives and multifaceted operational constraints. Decision-makers must reconcile the inherent tension between minimizing deployment, maintenance, and bandwidth expenditures and ensuring stringent Quality-of-Service requirements, such as bounded latency, high availability, fault tolerance, and sufficient throughput capacity. Furthermore, the problem is complicated by spatial heterogeneity in user demand, temporal traffic fluctuations, peering agreements between autonomous systems, and the intricate topological structure of underlying networks. Existing studies have approached server placement through various heuristic, exact, and metaheuristic methods, yet many models either oversimplify real-world network dynamics, ignore the economies of scale associated with consolidated facilities, or fail to integrate cost-performance trade-offs within a unified analytical framework. Consequently, there exists a pronounced gap between theoretical optimization models and the practical realities confronting CDN operators.

This paper addresses these limitations by presenting a comprehensive mathematical model for the location selection of mirror servers in large-scale CDN architectures. By formalizing the interplay between infrastructure costs, latency constraints, spatial demand distributions, and server capacity limits, the proposed model identifies Pareto-optimal server placements that maximize end-user satisfaction while respecting budgetary and operational boundaries. The remainder of this article details the model formulation, develops an efficient solution methodology capable of handling realistically sized instances, and presents extensive computational experiments conducted on representative network topologies to validate the practical efficacy and scalability of the proposed approach.

title: Capturing Model Risk and Rating Momentum in the Estimation of Probabilities of Default and Credit Rating Migrations
text: Our estimation framework reveals that incorporating model risk increases one-year PD estimates by 35–60 basis points for speculative-grade issuers, while investment-grade PDs rise by 8–12 basis points relative to baseline cohort methods. Rating momentum contributes an additional 15–22% uplift in downgrade intensities for firms recently downgraded, compared to time-homogeneous Markov models. Specifically, the adjusted one-year migration matrix assigns a 3.2% default probability to BB-rated entities with two consecutive downgrades, versus 2.1% for static ratings. Model uncertainty accounts for roughly 18% of total predictive variance, with parameter instability during recessionary subperiods doubling the dispersion of PD forecasts. These results indicate that neglecting model risk and momentum dynamics systematically understates tail credit risk, particularly for issuers in intermediate rating categories. The integrated approach improves the Brier score by 0.04 and reduces out-of-sample forecast errors by 11% relative to the benchmark.

title: Input-to-state stability and Lyapunov functions with explicit domains for SIR model of infectious diseases
text: In this paper, we have established an input-to-state stability framework for the classical SIR model of infectious diseases by constructing Lyapunov functions with explicitly characterized domains. By rigorously defining the region of attraction and ensuring strict positivity of the domain, we have shown that the disease-free equilibrium remains asymptotically stable in the presence of bounded exogenous inputs, which may represent external perturbations such as immigration of infected individuals or time-varying transmission rates. The explicit construction of the Lyapunov function provides not only verifiable sufficient conditions for stability but also quantifiable bounds on the transient behavior of the susceptible, infected, and recovered populations. Our results extend the classical stability analysis of epidemic models by incorporating input-to-state stability properties, thereby offering rigorous robustness guarantees against disturbances. The characterization of explicit domains ensures that the biological relevance of the model is preserved, confining the analysis to the epidemiologically meaningful state space where all compartments remain nonnegative and biologically feasible. These findings contribute to the theoretical foundation of mathematical epidemiology by bridging nonlinear systems theory with disease dynamics, and provide tools for estimating the basin of attraction under uncertain forcing. Future research directions include extending the proposed ISS framework to more complex compartmental models, such as SEIR and networked metapopulation models, as well as exploring time-delay and switched systems to capture seasonality and intervention measures. The Lyapunov-based methodology developed herein may also serve as a theoretical basis for designing robust control strategies, such as feedback vaccination policies, that maintain stability despite persistent uncertain external inputs.

title: Mass-Matrix Differential-Algebraic Equation Formulation for Transient Stability Simulation
text: Transient stability simulation is fundamental to power system security assessment, yet conventional explicit or semi-implicit differential-algebraic equation (DAE) formulations often encounter numerical stiffness and modeling inflexibility when integrating high-penetration inverter-based resources and complex load dynamics. This paper proposes a comprehensive mass-matrix DAE formulation that unifies the differential and algebraic equations into a single cohesive framework, represented compactly as Eẋ = f(x), where the singular mass matrix E naturally distinguishes dynamic states from algebraic constraints without auxiliary interfacing logic. By assembling network, synchronous machine, and converter-interfaced generation models into a consistent sparse mass-matrix structure, the proposed approach eliminates the need for ad hoc interface treatments between differential and algebraic variables while enabling a simultaneous solution strategy. The resulting formulation is inherently compatible with general-purpose fully implicit DAE solvers, such as those based on backward differentiation formulas or implicit Runge-Kutta schemes, delivering superior numerical stability and larger step sizes under stiff conditions compared to traditional partitioned or semi-implicit methods. Furthermore, the mass-matrix paradigm facilitates modular model development, preserves the natural sparsity pattern of the power network Jacobian, and allows advanced sparse direct or iterative linear solvers to be exploited efficiently within each Newton iteration. Case studies on the IEEE 39-bus and 145-bus systems, along with a realistic 3,000-bus regional grid, demonstrate that the proposed method achieves comparable accuracy to established solvers while exhibiting improved computational robustness and efficiency during severe disturbances. The results indicate that the mass-matrix DAE formulation provides a scalable, flexible, and numerically robust foundation for next-generation transient stability simulation tools.

title: A novel hand-held interface supporting the self-management of Type 1 diabetes
text: Type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) necessitates rigorous daily self-management, encompassing frequent blood glucose monitoring, precise insulin dosing, carbohydrate counting, and exercise planning. The perpetual cognitive burden associated with these tasks frequently leads to self-management fatigue, diminished treatment adherence, and suboptimal glycemic outcomes, particularly among adolescents and young adults navigating complex social and academic environments. While continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) devices and smartphone applications have improved physiological data accessibility, existing digital tools often suffer from fragmented information architecture, limited interoperability, and poor contextual adaptation. Many interfaces prioritize passive clinical visualization over actionable, user-centered guidance, failing to deliver coherent decision support during time-sensitive daily scenarios such as mealtime insulin bolusing or hypoglycemia recovery. To address these critical limitations, this study presents a novel hand-held interface specifically engineered to facilitate comprehensive, integrated T1DM self-management. Unlike conventional applications that merely aggregate disparate data streams, our system unifies real-time glucose telemetry, predictive trend analysis, and personalized behavioral coaching within a cohesive, portable platform developed through iterative user-centered design. By incorporating context-aware notifications and streamlined interaction paradigms, the interface aims to reduce cognitive load and enhance situational decision-making. This paper details the design rationale, technical architecture, and preliminary evaluation results, demonstrating significant improvements in usability, user engagement, and perceived self-efficacy. These contributions advance the theoretical and practical foundations of mobile health (mHealth) interfaces for chronic disease management, offering actionable insights for the next generation of patient-centered diabetes technologies.

title: Functional clustering methods for resistance spot welding process data in the automotive industry
text: Resistance spot welding (RSW) is a dominant joining process in automotive manufacturing, generating high-resolution functional data through in-process monitoring of dynamic signals such as welding current, voltage, and electrode force. Conventional quality control relies on scalar summary statistics, often neglecting the rich temporal structure inherent in these curves and obscuring distinct process regimes. This paper proposes a functional clustering framework for RSW process data to identify homogeneous groups of welds based on the shapes of their functional profiles. By integrating functional principal component analysis with model-based clustering algorithms, the method reduces dimensionality while preserving critical dynamic features. Applied to industrial datasets from automotive body-in-white production, the approach successfully distinguishes between normal, expulsion, and cold-welding conditions, and reveals previously uncharacterized process variations. Results demonstrate that functional clustering outperforms traditional multivariate methods in both interpretability and anomaly detection accuracy, offering a scalable tool for in-line weld quality monitoring and process optimization.

title: Machine Learning Algorithm for NLOS Millimeter Wave in 5G V2X Communication
text:
The rapid proliferation of connected vehicles and intelligent transportation systems has propelled fifth-generation (5G) vehicle-to-everything (V2X) communication to the forefront of automotive innovation. By enabling ultra-reliable low-latency connectivity between vehicles, infrastructure, pedestrians, and networks, 5G V2X promises to revolutionize road safety, traffic efficiency, and autonomous driving. Central to achieving the stringent throughput and latency requirements of these applications is the utilization of millimeter-wave (mmWave) spectrum, which offers expansive bandwidth and supports multi-gigabit data rates. However, mmWave signals are inherently susceptible to severe path loss, atmospheric absorption, and penetration losses, rendering them predominantly viable only under line-of-sight conditions. In complex urban environments where buildings, foliage, and other vehicles frequently obstruct direct propagation paths, non-line-of-sight (NLOS) scenarios dominate, posing significant challenges to link maintenance, beam alignment, and reliable communication.

Traditional NLOS mitigation techniques, such as geometric relay selection, statistical channel modeling, and exhaustive beam sweeping, often struggle to adapt to the high mobility and dynamic topology characteristic of vehicular networks. These conventional approaches typically rely on simplified propagation assumptions or incur prohibitive overhead, making them inadequate for real-time 5G V2X systems where channel conditions evolve rapidly. Consequently, there is an urgent need for intelligent, data-driven methodologies capable of learning complex environmental features and predicting channel behavior without requiring exhaustive pilot transmissions or precise geometric knowledge.

To address these limitations, this paper investigates the application of machine learning algorithms to enhance mmWave V2X communication in NLOS environments. By leveraging historical channel state information, environmental maps, and vehicle kinematics, machine learning models can predict blockage events, optimize beam selection, and facilitate proactive handover decisions with minimal latency. Specifically, we propose a learning framework that intelligently predicts NLOS link quality and adapts transmission strategies accordingly, thereby improving communication robustness and spectral efficiency. The proposed approach aims to bridge the gap between the theoretical capacity of mmWave bands and the practical demands of reliable vehicular connectivity in obstructed scenarios.

title: A Novel Ensemble Deep Learning Model for Stock Prediction Based on Stock Prices and News
text:
This study proposed a novel ensemble deep learning framework that integrates quantitative historical stock price data with qualitative financial news to enhance stock movement prediction accuracy. By leveraging recurrent and attention-based neural networks to capture temporal dependencies in price sequences alongside transformer-based natural language processing models to extract sentiment and semantic features from news articles, the proposed architecture effectively synthesizes multimodal market information. Experimental results across multiple benchmark datasets demonstrated that the ensemble model consistently outperforms single-modality deep learning baselines and traditional statistical methods, thereby validating the hypothesis that textual and numerical data provide complementary predictive signals for financial forecasting.

The findings underscore that combining disparate information sources within a unified ensemble framework can mitigate the noise and volatility inherent in individual data modalities, yielding more robust and generalizable forecasts. This multimodal approach offers significant practical value for investors and risk managers seeking data-driven decision support tools in increasingly complex and information-rich financial markets.

Nevertheless, certain limitations warrant acknowledgment. The model's dependence on accurately timestamped, high-quality news annotations and its substantial computational requirements may constrain deployment in latency-sensitive, high-frequency trading contexts. Furthermore, the empirical evaluation focused on specific markets and time periods, potentially limiting generalizability across diverse geopolitical regions or alternative asset classes.

Future research directions include investigating adaptive attention mechanisms for dynamic feature fusion, optimizing architectures for real-time streaming data, and incorporating supplementary alternative data such as social media sentiment, earnings reports, and macroeconomic indicators. Extending the framework to portfolio optimization and multi-horizon risk assessment also represents a valuable avenue. Overall, this work contributes a scalable and effective multimodal deep learning paradigm that meaningfully advances the integration of textual analytics and quantitative financial modeling for stock prediction.

title: Medical device surveillance with electronic health records
text: Post-market surveillance of medical devices traditionally relies on voluntary reporting systems, which suffer from underreporting, delays, and incomplete data. Electronic health records (EHRs) offer unprecedented opportunities to transform passive monitoring into active surveillance by leveraging real-world clinical data at scale. This study examines the integration of EHR data for device safety monitoring through natural language processing and machine learning algorithms applied to structured and unstructured clinical narratives. By systematically extracting device-related adverse events, performance trends, and patient outcomes from large-scale repositories, our approach detects safety signals more rapidly than conventional pharmacovigilance frameworks. We demonstrate that EHR-based surveillance improves signal detection sensitivity, supports longitudinal device performance assessment, and enables population-level safety monitoring. Nevertheless, significant challenges persist regarding data standardization, interoperability, privacy protection, and algorithmic validation. These findings highlight the transformative potential of EHRs to complement existing surveillance infrastructures, enhance post-market vigilance, and inform evidence-based regulatory decisions, ultimately advancing patient safety in medical device utilization.

title: Cumulant methods in the estimation of response functions in time-invariant linear systems
text:
The estimation of response functions in linear time-invariant (LTI) systems constitutes a fundamental problem in system identification, signal processing, and control engineering. Accurate characterization of impulse or frequency response functions is essential for robust system analysis, controller design, and signal reconstruction. Conventional estimation approaches predominantly rely on second-order statistical measures, such as correlation functions and power spectral densities. While these methods perform adequately under ideal Gaussian assumptions and minimum-phase conditions, they encounter significant limitations when systems are driven by non-Gaussian inputs, contaminated by additive Gaussian noise, or exhibit non-minimum-phase characteristics. Notably, second-order statistics are phase-blind and provide no discrimination against Gaussian disturbances, thereby compromising estimation consistency in practical scenarios where noise statistics remain unknown or time-varying.

Higher-order cumulants, and their Fourier counterparts known as polyspectra, offer a compelling alternative for response function estimation in LTI systems. A distinctive advantage of cumulant-based methods lies in their inherent insensitivity to additive Gaussian noise of unknown covariance, as cumulants of order greater than two vanish for Gaussian processes. Furthermore, higher-order statistics preserve phase information and facilitate the identification of non-minimum-phase systems, which are ubiquitous in diverse applications ranging from telecommunications and seismic exploration to structural health monitoring. Although cumulant techniques have been extensively studied in the context of blind system identification, their systematic deployment for direct response function estimation in general time-invariant linear frameworks warrants further theoretical refinement and algorithmic development.

This paper presents a comprehensive study of cumulant methods for estimating response functions in time-invariant linear systems. We establish a rigorous theoretical framework connecting higher-order output cumulants to the system impulse response through multilinear convolutional relationships. Building upon this foundation, we derive computationally efficient estimators and analyze their statistical consistency, variance properties, and asymptotic performance under non-Gaussian excitation and colored Gaussian noise. Our theoretical findings are supported by numerical simulations, which demonstrate that the proposed cumulant-based approaches achieve superior accuracy and robustness compared with conventional second-order methods, particularly in challenging identification scenarios involving low signal-to-noise ratios, non-minimum-phase dynamics, or correlated measurement noise.

title: Noise induces continuous and noncontinuous transitions in neuronal interspike intervals range
text: In conclusion, we have demonstrated that noise can drive both continuous and noncontinuous transitions in the range of neuronal interspike intervals. Our results reveal that as noise intensity varies, the ISI range does not always change gradually but can undergo abrupt jumps, indicating the coexistence of distinct firing regimes. These findings highlight that stochastic inputs play a constructive role in shaping neuronal variability and temporal precision beyond mere perturbation. The identification of noncontinuous transitions suggests that small changes in synaptic noise or channel fluctuations may trigger sudden shifts in firing patterns, with potential implications for neural coding and network dynamics. This work provides a framework for understanding how intrinsic and extrinsic noise modulate spike-time variability across different neuronal models. Future studies may extend these results to coupled networks and more complex stimulus conditions to assess the robustness of these noise-induced transitions in vivo.

title: Biophysically grounded mean-field models of neural populations under electrical stimulation
text: External electrical stimulation is widely used in therapeutic and experimental neuroscience, yet predicting population-level responses remains challenging due to cellular heterogeneity and complex network dynamics. Here we develop biophysically grounded mean-field models that bridge single-neuron biophysics with macroscopic population activity under extracellular electrical stimulation. By systematically averaging conductance-based neuron models subject to applied electric fields, we derive low-dimensional dynamical systems describing the evolution of mean membrane voltage, firing rate, and synaptic activity across homogeneous and heterogeneous populations. The models capture salient phenomena observed in stimulated neural circuits, including frequency-dependent entrainment, resonance effects, and state-dependent shifts between excitation and inhibition. Comparison with large-scale network simulations demonstrates that the mean-field reduction accurately predicts population responses while drastically reducing computational cost. These results establish a principled, efficient framework for optimizing stimulation parameters and designing closed-loop neuromodulation strategies in clinical applications such as deep brain stimulation.

title: Augment Yourself: Mixed Reality Self-Augmentation Using Optical See-through Head-mounted Displays and Physical Mirrors
text: The ability to augment one's own appearance holds significant promise for applications ranging from education and healthcare to entertainment and personal expression. While mixed reality (MR) has enabled compelling virtual self-transformations, most existing approaches rely on video-see-through displays or virtual avatars, creating a mediated representation that inherently disconnects users from their physical selves. Physical mirrors, conversely, offer an authentic and intuitive channel for self-perception, yet they remain largely unexplored as a medium for digital augmentation when combined with optical-see-through head-mounted displays (OST-HMDs). In this paper, we present a novel system that bridges this gap by leveraging OST-HMDs and physical mirrors to enable real-time self-augmentation. Unlike conventional methods that replace the user's reflection with a fully rendered copy, our approach overlays digital content directly onto the user's genuine mirror image, preserving spatiotemporal fidelity while enriching self-perception with contextual virtual elements. We demonstrate the technical feasibility of geometric calibration and occlusion-aware rendering in this unique setup, and discuss implications for embodied interaction, behavioral intervention, and the future of MR interfaces.

title: A Novel Ramp Metering Approach Based on Machine Learning and Historical Data
text: Ramp metering is a widely adopted freeway management strategy to regulate on-ramp flow and mitigate recurrent bottleneck congestion. Conventional traffic-responsive algorithms, such as ALINEA and its coordinated variants, primarily rely on instantaneous detector measurements and often react to congestion after it forms, limiting their effectiveness under highly variable and predictable demand patterns. This paper proposes a novel ramp metering approach that systematically integrates machine learning with extensive historical traffic data to proactively optimize metering rates before breakdown occurs. Leveraging multi-year high-resolution observations—including mainline occupancy, speeds, ramp queue lengths, and time-of-day demand profiles—a gradient boosting ensemble is trained to capture complex nonlinear spatiotemporal relationships and predict near-future traffic states and optimal release rates. These predictions are embedded within a rolling-horizon optimization framework that explicitly balances mainline throughput, ramp queue storage constraints, and equity of access across multiple on-ramps. The proposed methodology was evaluated using empirical detector data from a heavily congested urban freeway corridor implemented within a microscopic simulation environment. Comparative experiments against the local ALINEA and coordinated zone algorithms demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves a 14% reduction in total system travel time, an 18% decrease in average delay, and a notable improvement in bottleneck throughput during peak periods. Sensitivity analyses further confirm that the model maintains robust performance under demand perturbations and incident scenarios not explicitly represented in the training data. These results suggest that exploiting historical traffic patterns through advanced machine learning provides a scalable and effective pathway for transitioning from reactive to proactive freeway traffic control.

title: Learning Heat Diffusion for Network Alignment
text:
Network alignment—the task of establishing node correspondences across multiple graphs—lies at the heart of cross-network analysis, with critical applications ranging from protein-protein interaction matching and social network reconciliation to knowledge graph fusion. Despite decades of research, aligning heterogeneous networks remains fundamentally challenging due to variations in scale, density, and topological structure, compounded by noisy or missing links that distort apparent similarities. Consequently, effective alignment requires principles that can robustly capture multi-scale structural patterns while remaining adaptable to domain-specific network characteristics.

Classical alignment methods typically rely on handcrafted topological features or rigid spectral criteria, which struggle to generalize across structurally divergent graphs. While recent embedding-based and graph neural network approaches have improved flexibility, they often fix the receptive field or aggregation strategy, limiting their sensitivity to both local neighborhoods and global architecture. Heat diffusion processes offer a principled alternative by modeling how information propagates through a network, naturally encoding geometric properties at multiple scales via the heat kernel. Nevertheless, existing heat-kernel-based methods usually presuppose a fixed diffusion rate and rely on analytical solutions, preventing the diffusion dynamics from adapting to the unique structural signatures of the networks being aligned.

To address these limitations, we propose a framework that learns the heat diffusion process specifically for network alignment. By parameterizing and optimizing diffusion dynamics directly from data, our method adaptively discovers the temporal and spectral scales that best reveal cross-network correspondences. This learned diffusion not only captures nuanced topological similarities robust to noise and structural heterogeneity but also provides an interpretable mechanism for understanding alignment decisions through the lens of continuous-time random walks on graphs. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that learning diffusion yields substantial improvements over both classical and contemporary learned baselines.

title: Fairness, Welfare, and Equity in Personalized Pricing
text: This paper has examined the multifaceted tensions among fairness, welfare, and equity that arise when firms deploy personalized pricing strategies at scale. Our analysis demonstrates that while personalized pricing can enhance allocative efficiency, expand market access, and increase total surplus, these gains often come at the cost of distributional concerns, perceived unfairness, and potential harms to vulnerable groups. We have shown that welfare effects depend critically on market structure, consumer heterogeneity, and the information environment, while equity implications are shaped by whether price discrimination amplifies or mitigates existing socioeconomic disparities. These findings suggest that a binary assessment of personalized pricing as either beneficial or harmful is insufficient; rather, policymakers, managers, and platforms must evaluate specific institutional contexts to design pricing mechanisms, transparency requirements, and safeguards that balance efficiency gains with distributive justice. Looking ahead, future research should explore dynamic fairness perceptions, the role of algorithmic transparency, consumer consent frameworks, and targeted regulatory interventions that preserve welfare while protecting disadvantaged consumers. Ultimately, the central challenge lies not in whether to personalize prices, but in ensuring that the fruits of data-driven markets are shared broadly and in ways that society deems acceptably equitable.

title: Superlinear Precision and Memory in Simple Population Codes
text:
Neural populations encode sensory, motor, and cognitive variables through coordinated firing patterns, yet the fundamental limits of such representations remain actively debated. Classical population coding theory establishes that, for independent neurons with overlapping tuning curves, Fisher information scales linearly with ensemble size N, yielding estimation precision that improves only as the square root of the population. This bound has profoundly shaped our understanding of neural computation, suggesting that achieving high fidelity necessarily requires vast neuronal resources or sophisticated circuit motifs.

Conventional wisdom holds that superlinear precision—where error decreases faster than 1/√N—requires mechanisms such as downstream optimized decoding, negative noise correlations, or elaborate recurrent dynamics that extend beyond simple feedforward architectures. Consequently, minimal population codes characterized by fixed tuning curves and independent Poisson-like variability have been largely excluded from theoretical accounts of enhanced scaling. Equally importantly, existing frameworks typically segregate encoding from memory: population activity is analyzed at a single moment, whereas mnemonic processes are treated as subsequent maintenance operations that preserve, but do not amplify, the initially encoded information. Whether temporal integration can fundamentally augment the precision of spatial population codes remains unexplored.

Here, we demonstrate that simple population codes can achieve superlinear precision when coupled with a basic memory mechanism that accumulates evidence over time. By deriving closed-form expressions for the Fisher information of feedforward populations with integrated spike counts, we show that a finite memory window transforms the scaling of estimation error from 1/√N to 1/N under biologically plausible conditions. This improvement does not require structured noise correlations, tuned recurrent connectivity, or complex decoding algorithms; instead, it emerges generically from the interaction between spatial tuning diversity and temporal accumulation. Our findings bridge population coding and sequential computation, reconceptualizing memory not merely as passive storage but as an active computational resource that amplifies the representational capacity of simple neural ensembles.

title: Value of agreement in decision analysis: Concept, measures and application
text: Decision analysis often relies on aggregating multiple perspectives, yet the formal treatment of agreement among decision makers, experts, or models remains underdeveloped. While disagreement is routinely analyzed as a source of uncertainty, the intrinsic value of agreement—specifically, its potential to reduce conflict costs, enhance implementation legitimacy, and improve predictive accuracy—has received limited analytical attention. This paper introduces a structured conceptual framework for the "value of agreement" (VoA) in decision analysis, distinguishing between epistemic agreement (convergence of beliefs), preferential agreement (alignment of values), and procedural agreement (consensus on process). We propose a family of quantitative measures that extend traditional reliability metrics by incorporating the decision consequences of consensus and dissent. These measures include a kappa-type coefficient weighted by outcome severity, an information-theoretic divergence measure capturing the cost of disagreement in expected utility terms, and a process-oriented index linking procedural consensus to implementation probability. Drawing on multi-attribute utility theory, we define VoA as the incremental expected value achievable when agreement is cultivated, measured against a baseline of independent evaluation. The measures are validated through an application in healthcare resource allocation, where multiple stakeholder panels evaluated priority-setting criteria under varying deliberation protocols. Results demonstrate that epistemic agreement yields the highest value in low-evidence environments, whereas procedural agreement dominates when implementation barriers are substantial. Preferential agreement exhibits context-dependent value, particularly when equity constraints are binding. The analysis further reveals that the marginal value of agreement is non-linear, exhibiting diminishing returns beyond moderate consensus levels. Sensitivity analyses show that the ranking of agreement types depends on the relative weight assigned to process versus outcome legitimacy. By operationalizing agreement as a decision-relevant resource rather than merely a statistical artifact, this work provides analysts with tools to assess whether investments in deliberation, facilitation, or structured elicitation justify their costs. The framework bridges normative decision theory and descriptive group behavior research, offering practical guidance for expert elicitation, participatory policy making, and multi-model ensemble forecasting.

title: Fairness, Welfare, and Equity in Personalized Pricing
text:
The proliferation of big data and algorithmic decision-making has enabled firms to move beyond uniform pricing toward granular, individualized pricing strategies. By leveraging detailed consumer profiles, browsing histories, and predicted willingness-to-pay, sellers can now tailor prices to specific individuals in real time. This transformation promises enhanced firm profitability and, under certain conditions, improved allocative efficiency by enabling transactions that might otherwise fail to occur in markets with diverse consumer valuations.

Yet the shift toward personalized pricing raises profound concerns about fairness, welfare, and equity. While traditional uniform pricing embodies a principle of equal treatment, algorithmic personalization may systematically disadvantage vulnerable populations, erode aggregate consumer surplus, and undermine trust in market institutions. The distributional consequences are particularly salient when price discrimination correlates with income, race, or other protected characteristics, exacerbating existing socioeconomic inequalities and complicating the standard economic calculus that privileges efficiency over equity.

This paper examines the intersection of personalized pricing with normative and positive economic analysis. We investigate how fairness perceptions and distributional preferences constrain optimal pricing strategies, evaluate the net welfare effects of personalization across heterogeneous consumer groups, and assess policy interventions designed to promote equitable outcomes. By integrating theoretical insights with equity considerations, we aim to provide a coherent framework for understanding when personalized pricing serves broader social objectives and when regulatory safeguards become economically and ethically warranted.

title: Variable Neighborhood Search for the Bin Packing Problem with Compatible Categories
text:
The computational experiments were conducted on 120 benchmark instances with item categories ranging from 3 to 15 and bin capacities of 100 and 150. The proposed Variable Neighborhood Search (VNS) was compared against CPLEX 12.10 and the best-fit decreasing heuristic (BFD). VNS attained the optimal solution in 94 of the 120 instances, yielding an average percentage deviation from the lower bound of merely 1.18%. CPLEX solved only 58 instances to optimality within the 3600-second limit, while VNS required an average runtime of 14.2 seconds. On the large-scale set with 500 items, VNS consumed 38.5 seconds on average and utilized 82.6 bins, whereas BFD required 96.4 bins and CPLEX failed to find a feasible integer solution within the time limit for 18 cases.

The analysis reveals that the structured shaking mechanism effectively escapes local optima induced by category compatibility constraints. Additionally, the category-aware local search reduced the bin count by an average of 9.3% compared to standard neighborhood structures that ignore compatibility. Sensitivity analysis shows that increasing the number of compatible categories from 3 to 12 raises the average runtime by only 22%, while solution quality degrades by less than 2%. These results demonstrate that VNS scales robustly, delivering high-quality solutions with substantially lower computational effort than exact methods.

title: Are temporary value-added tax reductions passed on to consumers? Evidence from Germany's stimulus
text: This paper assesses the pass-through of Germany’s temporary 2020 VAT cut to consumer prices. Using high-frequency micro data, we find that the reduction was only partially transmitted to final prices, with substantial heterogeneity across sectors. Pass-through was more complete in competitive retail markets characterized by flexible price-setting, whereas it remained constrained in service industries marked by menu costs and long-term contracts. The temporary nature of the policy likely weakened firms’ incentives to adjust prices, as the anticipated reversal diluted the expected gains from repricing. Consequently, a significant portion of the tax relief accrued to firms rather than to household purchasing power. These results indicate that temporary VAT reductions are a relatively blunt instrument for stimulating consumption. When designing fiscal stimulus, policymakers should weigh the structural rigidities of price adjustment and the limited credibility of temporary measures. In many circumstances, direct transfers to households may offer a more effective and equitable channel for supporting aggregate demand.

title: City size and the spreading of COVID-19 in Brazil
text: This study investigates the relationship between city size and the spatiotemporal dynamics of COVID-19 spread across Brazilian municipalities. Brazil’s pronounced urban hierarchy, characterized by vast socioeconomic disparities and highly heterogeneous population concentrations, offers a distinctive empirical context for examining how demographic scale, residential density, and interurban connectivity jointly shape epidemic trajectories in developing economies. Using comprehensive municipal-level data covering the period from March 2020 to December 2021, we integrate fixed-effects panel regressions with gravity-style mobility models to systematically evaluate the distinct and interactive effects of population size, urban density, and transport-network centrality on the velocity of initial outbreak onset, the magnitude of peak incidence, and cumulative mortality burden. Our empirical results uncover a nuanced and fundamentally non-linear association between urban scale and viral transmission. Major metropolitan regions and state capitals consistently recorded earlier first-case arrivals and markedly steeper initial growth curves, patterns largely attributable to elevated international and domestic connectivity, high volumes of commuter and long-distance mobility, and dense intra-urban socioeconomic interaction networks. Nevertheless, after carefully controlling for differential testing capacity, healthcare infrastructure quality, age structure, and the timing of non-pharmaceutical interventions, medium-sized and smaller municipalities demonstrated proportionally comparable—or in certain pandemic waves, substantially higher—age-adjusted incidence and mortality rates, indicating a marked spatial convergence in epidemiological vulnerability as the pathogen permeated the national urban system. We additionally demonstrate that raw population density is a considerably weaker predictor of outbreak severity than the structural topology of intercity mobility flows, particularly the betweenness and degree centrality of cities within Brazil’s highway and domestic air-transport networks. These findings challenge the prevailing narrative that pandemic risk is disproportionately concentrated in megacities and underscore the necessity of geographically decentralized public health surveillance, adaptive resource allocation, and spatially differentiated mitigation strategies tailored to municipalities across the entire urban size spectrum. This research contributes to urban epidemiology and health geography by elucidating the mechanisms through which hierarchical urban systems modulate infectious disease diffusion in large middle-income countries.

title: Differentially Private Secure Multi-Party Computation for Federated Learning in Financial Applications
text: Federated learning (FL) has emerged as a promising paradigm enabling collaborative model training across decentralized financial institutions without exposing raw data. However, the increasing stringency of financial regulations and the sensitivity of proprietary transaction records demand privacy guarantees that standard FL protocols alone cannot adequately provide. Although FL avoids direct data sharing, recent studies have demonstrated that gradient inversion, membership inference, and attribute inference attacks can still compromise client privacy during collaborative training. Existing privacy-preserving approaches, such as standalone differential privacy (DP) or secure multi-party computation (SMC), often suffer from either excessive noise-induced utility degradation or prohibitive communication and computational overhead, rendering them inadequate for high-frequency financial applications. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a unified framework that tightly integrates differential privacy with lightweight secure multi-party computation specifically tailored for federated learning in financial contexts. Our approach simultaneously ensures rigorous privacy bounds through formal DP guarantees and protects intermediate model updates via efficient SMC protocols, thereby achieving a pragmatic balance among confidentiality, computational efficiency, and model utility. Extensive experiments on real-world financial datasets demonstrate that the proposed framework effectively mitigates privacy risks without significantly compromising predictive accuracy or convergence speed, offering a practical and regulatory-compliant solution for cross-institutional collaborative finance.

title: Copula-Based Factor Model for Credit Risk Analysis
text: This paper proposes a copula-based factor model for analyzing portfolio credit risk, addressing the well-documented limitations of standard Gaussian copula frameworks in capturing complex dependence structures and tail co-movements among default events. By linking latent systematic factors through flexible Archimedean and elliptical copula specifications, the model accommodates asymmetric correlations, non-linear dependencies, and heavy-tailed risk factor distributions inherent in credit markets. We derive the joint default probability distribution conditional on macroeconomic states and outline an efficient simulation algorithm for estimating portfolio loss distributions. An empirical application to a large portfolio of corporate exposures demonstrates that the proposed framework yields significantly more accurate Value-at-Risk and Expected Shortfall estimates compared to traditional linear factor models, particularly during periods of systemic distress. Our findings underscore the importance of explicitly modeling copula dependence in credit risk assessment and provide a robust, computationally tractable tool for regulatory capital allocation and active risk management.

title: ConvGRU in Fine-grained Pitching Action Recognition for Action Outcome Prediction
text:
We evaluate the proposed ConvGRU framework on a dataset of 4,800 annotated pitching videos spanning six pitch types and four outcome classes. For fine-grained action recognition, our model achieves a top-1 accuracy of 89.2% and a mean Average Precision (mAP) of 87.5%, outperforming the CNN baseline (72.1% accuracy), vanilla LSTM (76.3%), Two-Stream network (80.5%), 3D ResNet (83.7%), and I3D (85.1%). The ConvGRU architecture attains a macro-averaged F1-score of 0.841 across all pitch categories, with particularly strong performance on fastball (91.2% accuracy) and changeup (88.4%) classes, while curveball remains the most challenging at 84.6% due to deceptive arm motion similarity with the slider class (86.3%). Per-frame analysis reveals that classification confidence surpasses 80% at 120 milliseconds before ball release.

For action outcome prediction, the model forecasts pitch results (ball, called strike, swinging strike, or hit in play) with an overall accuracy of 82.4%. This exceeds the logistic regression baseline (68.2%), frame-averaged CNN (71.5%), and standard GRU (74.5%). Integrating spatial convolution within the recurrent unit improves outcome prediction by 7.9 percentage points over the standard GRU, demonstrating that jointly modeling local limb dynamics and global temporal evolution is critical for anticipating results from incomplete pre-release kinematic sequences. Specifically, early prediction at 60% sequence length yields 78.9% accuracy, suggesting that outcome is largely determined by leg drive and torso rotation rather than late wrist action.

Ablation studies further validate each architectural choice. Removing the convolutional operator from the reset gate drops recognition accuracy to 84.3%, while replacing the ConvGRU with a ConvLSTM reduces outcome prediction accuracy to 79.8% and increases parameter count to 5.8M. The final model operates at 42 fps during inference with 4.2M parameters, confirming suitability for real-time coaching applications. Furthermore, gradient-weighted class activation mapping highlights that the ConvGRU consistently attends to the pitching arm and lead knee during the stride phase, whereas LSTM-based alternatives exhibit diffuse attention across the background. These results indicate that ConvGRU effectively captures fine-grained spatiotemporal dependencies in pitching mechanics, translating subtle pre-release cues into robust, generalizable outcome predictions.

title: Heavy tailed distributions in closing auctions
text:
This paper has provided robust empirical evidence that closing auction outcomes—both price changes and participation volumes—are characterized by heavy-tailed distributions that depart markedly from normality. By applying extreme value theory and power-law estimation to closing auction data, we have shown that the tails of return distributions decay substantially more slowly than during continuous trading sessions. These results indicate that standard Gaussian frameworks systematically underestimate the likelihood of extreme price movements in closing auctions, with material consequences for risk measurement and regulatory design.

Our findings carry direct implications for market participants and regulators. Risk managers should incorporate heavy-tailed specifications when calculating value-at-risk or setting intraday margin requirements specifically for auction periods. Likewise, exchange operators may need to calibrate price limits and circuit breakers to account for the elevated tail risk that arises when liquidity concentrates at the close. Recognizing the closing auction as a distinct microstructural regime—rather than a simple extension of continuous trading—is essential for accurate tail risk assessment.

Several directions warrant further investigation. Future work could examine the microstructural mechanisms driving these tails, including order imbalances, exchange-specific matching algorithms, and the interaction between cash and derivatives markets at expiration. Cross-market comparisons across jurisdictions and asset classes would also clarify whether heavy tails are a universal feature of closing auctions or specific to particular liquidity environments. Finally, developing forecasting models that explicitly exploit these distributional properties could enhance end-of-day risk allocation strategies.

In summary, the heavy-tailed nature of closing auctions demands specialized statistical treatment. Acknowledging these properties is a necessary step toward building more resilient trading systems and protecting market stability during periods of concentrated liquidity.

title: Investor Reaction to Financial Disclosures Across Topics: An Application of Latent Dirichlet Allocation
text: This study examines how investors react to distinct topics embedded in corporate financial disclosures. While prior literature has extensively documented market responses to aggregate disclosure events, limited attention has been paid to the heterogeneity in investor reactions across thematic contents. We apply Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA), a machine learning topic modeling technique, to extract latent topics from a large corpus of financial disclosures, including 10-K filings and earnings announcements. By mapping these topics onto subsequent market metrics—including abnormal returns, trading volume, and return volatility—we investigate whether and how the thematic composition of disclosures influences investor behavior. Our findings reveal significant cross-topic variation in market reactions: disclosures related to litigation risk, regulatory changes, and innovation tend to elicit stronger and more immediate investor responses, whereas routine operational discussions generate relatively muted reactions. We further show that these differential reactions are more pronounced among firms with higher information asymmetry and greater uncertainty. This study contributes to the literature by bridging textual analysis with capital market research, offering granular evidence that the thematic content of disclosures matters beyond its mere existence, with important implications for corporate disclosure policy, regulatory oversight, and market efficiency.

title: A Fully Integrated Sensor-Brain-Machine Interface System for Restoring Somatosensation
text: Brain-machine interfaces (BMIs) have achieved remarkable success in restoring motor function for patients with neurological disorders. However, most current neuroprostheses operate in an open-loop configuration, lacking somatosensory feedback that is essential for naturalistic motor control and environmental interaction. The restoration of tactile and proprioceptive sensations remains a significant challenge, as these modalities are critical for closed-loop sensorimotor integration. While recent advances in artificial sensors and intracortical microstimulation have separately demonstrated the feasibility of artificial sensory input, a fully integrated system that directly bridges external sensing with cortical perception has yet to be realized. Here, we present a fully integrated sensor-brain-machine interface system designed to restore somatosensation. By combining high-resolution flexible sensor arrays with real-time neural decoding and targeted intracortical microstimulation, our approach establishes a complete closed-loop pathway from physical interaction to perceptual restoration. This work provides a scalable framework for bidirectional BMIs and offers promising strategies for addressing sensory deficits in patients with nervous system injuries.

title: The effect of nudging personal and injunctive norms on the trade-off between objective equality and efficiency
text: Decisions involving resource allocation frequently require trading off objective equality against efficiency. Although traditional economic models treat this trade-off as a stable preference, emerging evidence indicates that social norms can systematically shift allocative choices. This paper examines whether light-touch nudges targeting personal and injunctive norms influence individuals' willingness to sacrifice efficiency to achieve more objectively equal distributions. Across incentivized between-subjects experiments, participants made distribution choices after receiving normative prompts emphasizing either personal moral standards or perceived social expectations. Results demonstrate that injunctive norm nudges significantly increase the likelihood of choosing objective equality over efficiency relative to a control condition, whereas personal norm nudges yield weaker, statistically non-significant effects. Mediation analysis further suggests that anticipated social approval drives the effect of injunctive norms. These findings imply that leveraging perceived social expectations is more effective than appealing to internal standards when encouraging equitable allocations, providing actionable guidance for policymakers aiming to promote distributive justice through choice architecture.

title: Hybrid Machine Learning Forecasts for the FIFA Women's World Cup 2019
text:
The FIFA Women’s World Cup has evolved into one of the most prominent international sporting events, with the 2019 tournament in France representing a pivotal moment for the women’s game in terms of global viewership, professional investment, and competitive parity. Accurately forecasting match outcomes and tournament progression, however, remains a formidable statistical challenge. Knockout-stage volatility, sparse head-to-head records between confederations, and rapidly shifting team strengths introduce layers of uncertainty that conventional statistical models often fail to capture fully.

While predictive analytics have been extensively applied to men’s football, the women’s game has received comparatively less scholarly attention, leaving an unresolved question regarding the efficacy of modern machine learning techniques within this distinct competitive environment. Single-model approaches, moreover, frequently overfit to idiosyncratic historical patterns or struggle to generalize across the structurally diverse landscape of international women’s football, where talent pools are deepening and competitive schedules remain uneven.

This study addresses these limitations by developing a hybrid machine learning framework specifically designed to forecast the FIFA Women’s World Cup 2019. By integrating diverse methodologies—including ensemble methods and feature-rich match predictors—we generate robust probabilistic forecasts for individual matches and overall tournament advancement. The hybrid architecture combines complementary algorithms trained on distinct data representations to reduce model-specific biases while accommodating the unique dynamics of the women’s international game. The remainder of this paper outlines the data architecture, model specification, and ensemble strategies, demonstrating that a carefully constructed hybrid system can substantially enhance predictive accuracy and provide a replicable foundation for forecasting future women’s tournaments.

title: Intervention Threshold for Epidemic Control in Susceptible-Infected-Recovered Metapopulation Models
text:
We derived the critical intervention threshold by analyzing the spectral radius of the next-generation matrix across a metapopulation of twenty patches with heterogeneous degree distributions. In the uncontrolled baseline, the global basic reproduction number was R0 = 2.8, inter-patch mobility coupling was χ = 0.15 per day, and patch-specific transmission rates ranged from β = 0.35 to 0.65 day⁻¹. Numerical integration showed that, without intervention, the epidemic reached a cumulative attack rate of 64% across the network and a peak prevalence of 8.2% at day 47, with high-connectivity patches peaking three days earlier and driving spatial synchronization.

Reducing mobility to χ ≤ 0.04 day⁻¹ alone proved insufficient to prevent a network-wide outbreak; however, combining mobility reduction with local transmission control revealed a sharp threshold. When patch-level interventions reduced local transmission by at least 62% (yielding an effective patch reproduction number R_p = 1.06) and inter-patch mobility was restricted to χ = 0.06 day⁻¹, the network-wide effective reproduction number dropped below unity (R_eff = 0.98). At this threshold, the cumulative attack rate fell to 4.1% and peak prevalence to 0.3%, effectively eliminating the epidemic within 90 days. Sensitivity analysis indicated that the threshold was driven primarily by the second largest eigenvalue of the coupling matrix; patches with connectivity in the top quartile required 5–7% stronger local suppression (67–69% reduction) to maintain control, whereas isolated patches remained subcritical under weaker intervention. These results demonstrate that epidemic containment in metapopulations depends on a nonlinear interaction between local suppression and mobility restriction, with a concrete bifurcation point separating large-scale synchronized outbreaks from rapid patch-level extinction.

title: Atomic iron and titanium in the atmosphere of the exoplanet KELT-9b
text: We present the detection of neutral iron and titanium atoms in the atmosphere of KELT-9b via high-resolution transmission spectroscopy. The presence of these refractory species in atomic form indicates that the dayside atmosphere reaches temperatures exceeding ~4000 K, thermally dissociating molecular compounds and preventing the condensation of rock-forming elements. Our results demonstrate that KELT-9b harbors an atmosphere dominated by atomic chemistry rather than molecular processes, consistent with predictions for the most intensely irradiated gas giants. The observed line profiles further suggest a thermal structure characterized by a steep dayside temperature gradient and limited day-night heat redistribution. These findings establish KELT-9b as a critical benchmark for atmospheric models of ultra-hot Jupiters and highlight the utility of high-resolution spectroscopy in probing heavy-element chemistry in exoplanetary atmospheres. Future observations at improved signal-to-noise ratios will enable precise abundance determinations and atmospheric dynamics studies, refining our understanding of chemistry and heat transport on these extreme worlds.

title: What is Wrong with Net Promoter Score
text: Despite its widespread adoption as a customer loyalty metric, Net Promoter Score (NPS) has attracted substantial methodological criticism that challenges its claimed predictive validity and managerial utility. This paper systematically examines the statistical and conceptual deficiencies underlying the NPS framework, arguing that its categorical simplification of an 11-point scale into Promoters, Passives, and Detractors discards valuable variance and introduces arbitrary cutoffs lacking empirical justification across diverse industries. We demonstrate that the "top-box" dichotomization substantially reduces measurement reliability and that the proposed single-question format often underperforms validated multi-item satisfaction scales in predicting actual customer behavior, retention rates, and revenue growth. Furthermore, the assumption that Detractors necessarily damage growth while Promoters drive it oversimplifies complex market dynamics and fails to account for significant cross-cultural response biases. Through comparative statistical analysis and a review of longitudinal studies, we show that mean-based or regression-based approaches frequently yield stronger predictive power and more granular, actionable diagnostic insights than the NPS calculation. The findings suggest that managers should move beyond this overly simplistic loyalty metric toward more nuanced measurement systems that capture the multidimensional nature of customer relationships. This study contributes to the marketing metrics literature by providing a rigorous empirical critique of NPS and offering evidence-based recommendations for customer feedback instrumentation.

title: A Bayesian cognition approach for belief updating of correlation judgement through uncertainty visualizations
text: Judging correlation from visualizations is a fundamental task in data-driven decision-making, yet human perception of correlation is systematically biased. While uncertainty visualizations have emerged as a promising tool to support more accurate statistical reasoning, how observers update their beliefs about correlation in response to visual uncertainty remains poorly understood. This study proposes a Bayesian cognition framework to model the belief updating process in correlation judgment through uncertainty visualizations. Grounded in the principle that human cognition approximates Bayesian inference, we formalize how prior beliefs about correlations are revised when observers are presented with visual representations of data uncertainty. Our approach quantifies the interplay between visual encoding of uncertainty and subjective probability updating, offering a computational account of how people integrate uncertain information. This work contributes to both visualization design theory and cognitive science by bridging the gap between visual uncertainty communication and human belief formation in analytical tasks.

title: General Domain Adaptation Through Proportional Progressive Pseudo Labeling
text: Unsupervised domain adaptation seeks to transfer knowledge from a labeled source domain to an unlabeled target domain amid distribution shifts. Despite recent advances, prevailing pseudo-labeling methods typically employ static confidence thresholds and uniform sampling strategies, which exacerbate error propagation and fail to account for class imbalance, thereby restricting their efficacy across heterogeneous adaptation scenarios. To address these limitations, we introduce Proportional Progressive Pseudo Labeling (PPPL), a unified framework for general domain adaptation that adaptively selects pseudo-labeled target instances based on evolving model confidence and dynamically estimated class proportions. Rather than fixing a global threshold, PPPL progressively increases the ratio of pseudo-labeled samples across training epochs, prioritizing reliable high-confidence predictions while enforcing class-wise balance through a proportional allocation mechanism derived from source statistics and target predictions. Complementing this label selection strategy, we integrate feature alignment to jointly optimize domain-invariant representations and semantically coherent target clusters in a unified pipeline without requiring scenario-specific architectural modifications. Comprehensive evaluations on standard visual benchmarks—including Office-31, Office-Home, VisDA-2017, and DomainNet—demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches under closed-set, partial-set, and open-set domain adaptation settings. These results confirm that proportional progressive selection effectively mitigates pseudo-label noise and fosters robust cross-domain generalization.

title: Assessing Viewer's Mental Health by Detecting Depression in YouTube Videos
text:
Mental health disorders represent one of the most pressing public health challenges of the modern era, with depression affecting more than 280 million people worldwide according to the World Health Organization. Despite its staggering prevalence, a substantial proportion of individuals experiencing depressive symptoms remain undiagnosed due to persistent stigma, limited access to clinical resources, or a lack of self-awareness. Concurrently, the proliferation of social media and video-sharing platforms has fundamentally altered how individuals express emotional states, with users increasingly turning to venues such as YouTube to share personal narratives and struggles with mental well-being. These user-generated videos contain rich multimodal signals—including vocal prosody, facial expressions, and linguistic content—that may serve as latent biomarkers of psychological distress, offering unprecedented opportunities for passive, large-scale screening outside clinical settings.

While traditional depression assessment relies heavily on self-reported questionnaires and structured clinical interviews, recent advances in affective computing and deep learning have enabled increasingly sophisticated automated analysis of behavioral cues in digital media. Existing research has predominantly focused on text-based sentiment analysis of social media posts or static image classification, leaving a critical gap in understanding how dynamic, long-form audiovisual content on platforms like YouTube can reveal nuanced depressive symptomatology. Video data encapsulates temporal patterns of psychomotor retardation, reduced affective variability, and anomalous speech patterns that single-modality approaches frequently fail to capture, necessitating robust multimodal frameworks that integrate computer vision, natural language processing, and acoustic analysis.

This paper presents a comprehensive computational approach for detecting depression in YouTube videos to infer and assess viewer mental health states. By extracting and fusing visual, acoustic, and textual features from video content, the proposed methodology aims to identify subtle behavioral manifestations associated with major depressive disorder while accounting for the unstructured nature of online vlogs. The findings contribute to the emerging field of digital phenotyping and lay the groundwork for non-invasive, scalable tools that could complement traditional diagnostic practices, facilitate early intervention, and ultimately bridge the gap between online self-expression and evidence-based mental healthcare delivery.

title: Computation of single-cell metabolite distributions using mixture models
text:
We applied a Bayesian Gaussian mixture model to single-cell metabolomic profiles from 3,847 individual HeLa cells measuring 142 polar metabolites. For each metabolite, model selection via Bayesian information criterion (BIC) favored multimodal distributions in 89 of 142 cases (62.7%), with the remaining 53 metabolites adequately described by single Gaussian components. The average number of mixture components across all metabolites was 2.4 ± 0.8, with ATP exhibiting the most complex architecture (five components, BIC = -14,230) and lactate showing clear bimodality (components at 2.3 fmol/cell and 8.7 fmol/cell, weight ratio 1.8:1). All models converged within 500 expectation-maximization iterations, with median parameter uncertainty below 5%.

The mixture framework significantly improved log-likelihood over unimodal null models (mean ΔLL = 34.7 ± 12.4; p < 0.001, parametric bootstrap). Posterior assignment of cells to metabolic subpopulations achieved a mean silhouette score of 0.71, indicating robust cluster separation. Notably, 23 metabolites displayed near-zero inflation captured by an additional exponential-decay component, with dropout rates ranging from 4.2% to 31.5% (median 11.3%). Posterior 95% credible intervals for component means excluded the population average in 67% of multimodal metabolites.

Cross-validation on a held-out set of 769 cells (20% split) yielded a mean absolute percentage error of 6.8% for metabolite quantile estimation, compared with 14.2% under standard kernel density estimation. Analysis of glucose-6-phosphate and fructose-1,6-bisphosphate revealed coordinated bimodal structure across the glycolytic axis, with 34% of cells mapping to a high-flux subpopulation (mean fructose-1,6-bisphosphate 18.4 fmol/cell) distinct from the low-flux majority. These results demonstrate that mixture models recover physiologically meaningful heterogeneity obscured by population-average approaches.

title: Heterogeneity Learning for SIRS model: an Application to the COVID-19
text:
This study presented a heterogeneity learning framework integrated with the classical SIRS model to better capture the diverse transmission dynamics of COVID-19 at the population level. By embedding individual-level variations in susceptibility, infectivity, and recovery rates directly into the compartmental structure, the proposed approach addressed a critical limitation of traditional mean-field assumptions that homogenize population interactions and obscure subpopulation differences. Our empirical results demonstrated that explicitly accounting for heterogeneity significantly improves the model's predictive accuracy and provides more reliable estimates of epidemic trajectories, peak timings, and the comparative effectiveness of non-pharmaceutical interventions relative to standard SIRS formulations. The learned heterogeneity parameters further offered interpretable insights into distinct risk profiles across demographic and behavioral subgroups, thereby supporting more targeted and efficient public health resource allocation.

Despite these methodological advances, several limitations warrant consideration. The current framework primarily relies on aggregated case and mortality data, which may obscure finer demographic, spatial, and socioeconomic differences within the population. Additionally, the assumption that heterogeneity can be effectively captured through learned parameter distributions rather than explicit dynamic contact networks may limit the model's applicability in settings where interaction structures dominate transmission dynamics. The constant recruitment and waning immunity assumptions inherent to the SIRS framework also simplify the complex, temporally evolving immunological landscape observed throughout the COVID-19 pandemic.

Future research should extend this framework to incorporate spatial heterogeneity, time-varying transmission parameters, and higher-resolution individual-level mobility and contact data. Integrating the proposed learning architecture with network-based or agent-based approaches could further enhance epidemiological realism. Nevertheless, this work underscores the necessity of moving beyond homogeneous approximations in compartmental modeling, offering a scalable, data-driven, and interpretable pathway to understand, monitor, and predict the heterogeneous spread of infectious diseases such as COVID-19.

title: Landmark detection in Cardiac Magnetic Resonance Imaging Using A Convolutional Neural Network
text: Accurate landmark detection in cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMR) is essential for ventricular function quantification, anatomical segmentation, and diagnostic assessment. However, manual annotation remains labor-intensive, time-consuming, and susceptible to inter-observer variability. This study proposes a fully automated framework based on a deep convolutional neural network (CNN) to precisely localize anatomical landmarks in CMR images. Our network architecture integrates deep hierarchical feature extraction with multi-scale context aggregation, enabling robust representation learning across diverse cardiac phases, imaging planes, and patient populations. We formulated landmark detection as a coordinate regression task and optimized the model using a composite loss function to enhance spatial localization accuracy and convergence stability. The proposed method was extensively evaluated on multi-center CMR datasets against manual annotations and conventional handcrafted feature-based approaches. Quantitative experiments demonstrated sub-pixel localization errors with high robustness to variations in image quality, anatomical morphology, and scanner protocols. Additionally, the optimized network achieved real-time inference capability, facilitating seamless integration into clinical workflows. These findings indicate that the proposed CNN-based approach provides a reliable, efficient, and reproducible solution for automated landmark detection in CMR, offering significant potential to advance computational cardiac image analysis and support clinical decision-making.

title: GPU-Accelerated Drug Discovery with Docking on the Summit Supercomputer: Porting, Optimization, and Application to COVID-19 Research
text: The rapid identification of therapeutic candidates against emerging pathogens such as SARS-CoV-2 demands computational approaches capable of evaluating massive chemical libraries with high fidelity and unprecedented speed. Molecular docking, a cornerstone structure-based virtual screening methodology, remains prohibitively expensive when applied to billion-scale compound databases on conventional CPU-only architectures, creating a critical bottleneck in early-stage drug discovery. We present the porting, optimization, and extreme-scale deployment of a GPU-accelerated docking workflow on the Summit supercomputer at Oak Ridge National Laboratory. Our work details the architectural adaptations required to exploit heterogeneous IBM AC922 nodes, leveraging the massive thread parallelism of NVIDIA Volta V100 GPUs alongside multi-core IBM POWER9 CPUs to maximize per-node throughput of the docking engine. We describe algorithmic optimizations including batched ligand pose generation and genotype evaluation, fine-grained parallelization of empirical scoring functions, asynchronous CPU-GPU task orchestration, and explicit memory hierarchy tuning that collectively mitigate memory bandwidth bottlenecks and warp divergence inherent to irregular, data-dependent docking workloads. The optimized implementation achieves orders-of-magnitude speedups over CPU baselines, enabling the screening of billions of molecular conformations across thousands of GPUs within clinically relevant timeframes. We deployed this workflow to conduct one of the largest published structure-based virtual screening campaigns against SARS-CoV-2 therapeutic targets, including the main protease (Mpro) and spike glycoprotein, evaluating hundreds of millions of commercially available and synthetically accessible compounds from the ZINC20 and Enamine REAL libraries. The campaign identified diverse, high-affinity hit compounds with favorable ADMET profiles that were subsequently prioritized for experimental validation and crystallographic follow-up, demonstrating that leadership-class GPU supercomputing can compress years of conventional computational screening into mere days. This study establishes a reusable, scalable framework for accelerated drug discovery and underscores the critical role of GPU optimization and heterogeneous HPC architectures in rapidly responding to global health emergencies through extreme-scale computational chemistry.

title: Is Factor Momentum More than Stock Momentum?
text:
The momentum anomaly remains one of the most pervasive challenges to the efficient market hypothesis. Since the seminal work of Jegadeesh and Titman (1993), the predictability of stock returns from past performance has been established across asset classes, geographies, and sample periods. More recently, however, a growing body of literature has documented robust momentum not merely among individual securities, but at the level of aggregate factor returns themselves.
