Strategies that buy recently performing factors and sell recent underperformers generate economically large and statistically significant alphas, suggesting that momentum may operate at a higher level of aggregation than the individual firm.

This empirical pattern raises a fundamental question: Is factor momentum merely a repackaging of stock-level momentum, or does it reflect a distinct source of return predictability? If factor momentum is entirely subsumed by the co-movement of individual stocks with the momentum factor, then its existence offers little incremental insight beyond the established cross-sectional evidence. Conversely, if factor momentum persists after controlling for stock momentum, it implies that the time-series predictability of factor premiums captures an independent economic force—one that prevailing asset pricing models struggle to accommodate. Distinguishing between these possibilities is essential not only for theoretical clarity, but also for practical portfolio construction, as the diversification benefits and risk exposures of factor-based strategies depend critically on whether these premia derive from separate underlying drivers.

In this paper, we investigate whether factor momentum is more than a mechanical reflection of stock momentum. Through spanning tests and decomposition analyses, we examine whether the predictive power of recent factor performance survives the inclusion of stock momentum and other established predictors. Our findings shed light on the hierarchical structure of momentum as an asset pricing anomaly and provide novel evidence on the incremental information content embedded in the time-series dynamics of factor returns.

title: Robustness to Spurious Correlations in Text Classification via Automatically Generated Counterfactuals
text:
On the IMDb–Genre spurious benchmark, the baseline BERT classifier achieved 94.2% in-distribution accuracy but only 71.3% on the counterfactual test set, revealing a 22.9 percentage point generalization gap driven by reliance on director names. In contrast, our counterfactual-augmented model (BERT+ACF) reached 92.8% in-distribution and 88.7% on the counterfactual split, shrinking the gap to 4.1 points. Comparable patterns emerged on Civil Comments toxicity and Amazon product category datasets: baseline accuracies of 91.5% and 89.7% on standard splits dropped to 68.4% and 66.2% on challenge sets where identity terms and brand names were decorrelated from labels, whereas our method preserved 90.1% and 88.4% in-distribution while improving to 85.6% and 84.9% out-of-distribution. All improvements were statistically significant under bootstrap resampling (p < 0.001). Macro-F1 followed the same trajectory, rising from 64.3 to 83.1 on the toxic-comment challenge set.

Attention analysis indicated that the baseline allocated 34.2% of normalized attention to spurious tokens, compared with 11.5% for our model. Ablations demonstrated that removing the diversity constraint on counterfactual generation degraded counterfactual-test accuracy by 6.3 points, and eliminating the fluency filter caused a further 4.7 point drop, underscoring the necessity of both varied and coherent interventions. Human evaluation confirmed that 87.3% of generated counterfactuals were label-preserving and fluent. Error analysis showed that remaining failures often involved ambiguous negation scope rather than persistent shortcut use. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that automatically generated counterfactuals sever spurious correlations without costly human annotation, yielding classifiers that retain strong clean accuracy while markedly improving robustness.

title: Migration and Refugee Crisis: a Critical Analysis of Online Public Perception
text: This study has critically examined the multifaceted nature of online public perception regarding migration and refugee crises. Through analyzing digital discourse across diverse platforms, the findings reveal a deeply polarized information ecosystem where humanitarian narratives frequently compete with securitized, exclusionary framings. Social media algorithms often amplify sensationalized content, fostering echo chambers that entrench ideological divisions, exacerbate affective polarization, and obscure the complex socio-political realities of displacement. While digital spaces can mobilize solidarity and transnational advocacy networks, they equally facilitate the rapid dissemination of misinformation, hostile rhetoric, and the dehumanization of migrant populations. These dynamics underscore that online perception is not merely reflective of offline attitudes but actively co-constitutes policy agendas, media coverage, and public affect. Consequently, understanding the architecture and evolution of digital discourse is essential for policymakers, civil society, and platform designers seeking to foster informed, empathetic public engagement. Future research should examine platform-specific moderation practices, the role of visual media in shaping emotional responses, and the long-term efficacy of counter-narratives in mitigating hostility. Ultimately, addressing the migration and refugee crisis requires recognizing the digital sphere as a critical battleground of meaning—one where the struggle between fear and solidarity determines not only virtual discourse but the very human stakes of protection, dignity, and belonging.

title: Towards Traffic Bisimulation of Linear Periodic Event-Triggered Controllers
text: Periodic event-triggered control (PETC) has emerged as a practical implementation of event-triggered strategies, offering an effective balance between communication efficiency and predictable real-time implementation by evaluating trigger conditions only at fixed periodic sampling instants. Despite its advantages, formally analyzing the resulting communication traffic patterns—which is essential for network scheduling, bandwidth allocation, and quality-of-service guarantees in networked control systems—remains difficult due to the intricate interplay between the linear plant dynamics and the aperiodic discrete triggering instants. This paper presents a systematic framework for establishing traffic bisimulation of linear PETC systems, thereby enabling formal equivalence between the controller's communication behavior and a finite symbolic abstraction. By leveraging the periodic structure of the triggering mechanism and the piecewise linear nature of the closed-loop flow, we develop a constructive procedure to build a finite labeled transition system that exactly captures the complete set of admissible transmission sequences, or traffic traces, generated by the PETC loop. We rigorously prove that this finite abstraction is bisimilar to the original PETC system with respect to traffic, meaning that every possible communication pattern of the physical closed-loop system is precisely reproduced by the abstract model and conversely. This equivalence allows traffic properties such as maximum burstiness, minimum inter-event times, and long-term average communication rates to be verified algorithmically on the finite model via standard model-checking techniques, without any overapproximation. The approach hinges on a carefully designed state-space partition into a finite number of traffic-equivalence classes, ensuring that the discrete-event behavior is fully retained. Compared to existing conservative abstractions, the proposed bisimulation relation preserves the exact traffic language and enables compositional reasoning about traffic in multi-loop networked architectures. A numerical example demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed approach in exactly characterizing the traffic complexity of linear periodic event-triggered controllers.

title: An Accelerated-Decomposition Approach for Security-Constrained Unit Commitment with Corrective Network Reconfiguration- Part II: Results and Discussion
text:
In Part I of this two-part paper, an accelerated-decomposition framework was developed to co-optimize generation scheduling and corrective network reconfiguration (CNR) within the security-constrained unit commitment (SCUC) paradigm. The proposed methodology integrates Benders decomposition with tailored acceleration strategies—including strong valid inequalities, scenario aggregation, and high-performance parallel computing—to address the formidable combinatorial complexity arising from N-1 security criteria and discrete transmission-switching decisions. Theoretical foundations, algorithmic procedures, and convergence properties were rigorously established in the preceding companion paper.

This second part is devoted to comprehensive numerical validation and an in-depth discussion of the proposed approach. Extensive experiments are conducted on progressively larger test systems, ranging from the IEEE 118-bus network to large-scale synthetic grids with thousands of buses and diverse N-1 contingency scenarios. Computational performance is systematically benchmarked against state-of-the-art mixed-integer programming solvers and conventional decomposition algorithms, demonstrating substantial reductions in solution time while maintaining solution quality within tight optimality tolerances. Beyond computational metrics, this paper quantifies the economic and operational value of corrective topology control, revealing significant reductions in total operating costs and enhanced post-contingency feasibility margins. Additional sensitivity analyses examine the impacts of renewable energy penetration, transmission congestion patterns, and switching penalty factors on the effectiveness of CNR. The interaction between unit-commitment decisions and network-topology adjustments is further investigated to offer practical insights for real-world power system operations with increasing operational uncertainty.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II describes the test systems, simulation parameters, and implementation environment. Section III reports the computational results, including convergence profiles and scalability assessments. Section IV analyzes the economic benefits and operational insights derived from integrating CNR into SCUC. Finally, Section V concludes the paper and outlines directions for future research.

title: Vision as an Energy-Driven Process
text: Traditional models of vision prioritize information-theoretic frameworks, treating perception primarily as signal extraction and representation. However, these accounts systematically overlook a fundamental biophysical constraint: every stage of visual processing demands substantial and sustained energy expenditure. This paper presents a comprehensive theoretical framework repositioning vision as an energy-driven process, wherein metabolic costs, thermodynamic limits, and resource availability shape sensory architecture, neural coding strategies, and perceptual priorities. Synthesizing evidence across spatial scales—from the high ATP demands of phototransduction and ionic pumping in retinal circuits to the glucose consumption of hierarchical cortical visual areas—we demonstrate that energy budgets fundamentally constrain spatial resolution, temporal integration, chromatic sampling, and receptive field organization. We argue that evolutionary pressures have optimized the visual system not merely for informational fidelity but for metabolic efficiency, favoring predictive and sparse coding strategies that minimize synaptic activity and reduce metabolic surprise. Furthermore, we examine how energetic shortfalls alter visual function, ranging from localized retinal hypoxia to systemic cortical hypometabolism, suggesting that energy dynamics underlie both normal perceptual variation and the progression of certain neurodegenerative pathologies. By integrating biophysical energetics with computational neuroscience, this framework challenges the prevailing information-centric paradigm and establishes energy economics as a core organizing principle of biological vision. This perspective generates novel predictions regarding sensory allocation, developmental plasticity, and the evolutionary ecology of perception, underscoring that seeing is not merely computing—it is a costly, continuous physical process.

title: The Wage Premium of Communist Party Membership: Evidence from China
text:
Political connections and institutional membership have long been recognized as important determinants of labor market outcomes across both developed and developing economies. In China, where the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) maintains a pervasive presence throughout the political and economic apparatus, party membership represents one of the most consequential forms of political capital available to individual workers. Descriptive evidence routinely indicates that CCP members enjoy superior career trajectories, higher wages, and preferential access to managerial and leadership positions relative to their non-member counterparts. However, whether party membership itself generates a causal wage premium, or whether these observed advantages simply reflect the fact that more capable, ambitious, and well-connected individuals are selected into the party, remains a central unresolved question in the literature on the political economy of development.

Identifying the causal effect of CCP membership is empirically challenging because the party’s recruitment process is highly selective and multidimensional. Candidates are evaluated on academic credentials, political reliability, social networks, and demonstrated leadership capacity—attributes that are themselves strongly correlated with unobserved productivity and earnings potential. As a result, ordinary least squares estimates likely suffer from substantial upward bias, conflating the true returns to membership with pre-existing heterogeneity in human capital and motivation. This paper addresses these methodological challenges by leveraging detailed microdata and empirical strategies specifically designed to mitigate selection on unobservables. By accounting for time-invariant individual heterogeneity and exploiting rich longitudinal information, we isolate variation in membership status that is plausibly uncorrelated with latent ability, thereby providing more credible estimates of the party wage premium than previously available in the literature.

The results document a robust and economically meaningful wage premium associated with CCP membership that persists after controlling for a wide array of observed and unobserved individual characteristics. The findings indicate that membership facilitates access to influential political and professional networks and accelerates promotion within organizational hierarchies, underscoring how political institutions can directly shape the distribution of economic rewards. By offering rigorous evidence on the returns to party membership in China, this study contributes to the broader literature on political connections and labor markets while informing policy discussions regarding inequality and the role of political capital in authoritarian regimes.

title: Dependencies and systemic risk in the European insurance sector: Some new evidence based on copula-DCC-GARCH model and selected clustering methods
text: The copula-DCC-GARCH estimates reveal a pronounced time-varying dependence structure among European insurers, with average pairwise dynamic correlations ranging from 0.34 in calm periods to 0.76 during the 2020–2022 market stress episodes. The Student-t copula provides the best fit for 78% of bivariate pairs, with estimated lower tail dependence of 0.38 and upper tail dependence of 0.21, indicating significantly stronger contagion during downturns. Systemic risk metrics show considerable heterogeneity: German and French insurers contribute most to aggregate risk, with average ΔCoVaR of 4.2% and 3.8%, respectively, whereas peripheral markets exhibit markedly lower spillover effects. The clustering analysis partitions the sector into three distinct groups: a core cluster comprising Germany, France, and the Netherlands (intra-cluster correlation 0.81), a southern European cluster including Spain, Italy, and Portugal (0.67), and a Nordic-Baltic cluster (0.41). Notably, the DCC parameters (α = 0.06, β = 0.92) confirm high persistence in conditional correlations. Robustness checks using rank-based and spectral clustering corroborate these findings, suggesting that geographic proximity and business-model similarity jointly drive dependency patterns. Overall, the results underscore concentrated systemic risk within the core European insurance cluster and asymmetric tail dependence that amplifies sectoral vulnerability under adverse macro-financial conditions.

title: Transient Stability of Power Systems Integrated With Inverter-Based Generation
text:
This paper has examined the evolving landscape of power system transient stability in the presence of rapidly growing inverter-based generation. As conventional synchronous machines are progressively displaced by IBRs, the fundamental physical mechanisms governing system stability are undergoing a profound transformation. The marked reduction of rotational inertia and the replacement of inherent electromechanical dynamics with fast-acting, software-driven responses necessitate a critical reevaluation of classical transient stability frameworks. Through detailed analysis of inverter control strategies—including grid-following and grid-forming architectures—this work has highlighted how IBR behavior during and following large disturbances significantly influences system-wide voltage recovery, angular stability, and frequency nadir. The findings demonstrate that while very low-inertia systems face accelerated instability phenomena and complex coupling between electromagnetic and electromechanical transients, properly designed inverter controls can provide fast frequency support, reactive current injection, and enhanced stability margins.

Nevertheless, ensuring adequate transient stability in high-IBR power systems requires moving decisively beyond traditional equal-area criteria and simplified machine-centric models toward detailed electromagnetic transient simulation and composite dynamic representations. The integration of synthetic inertia, rapid active power modulation, and advanced fault ride-through schemes emerges as essential for maintaining synchronism and facilitating voltage recovery following severe contingencies. Looking ahead, future research must rigorously address the stochastic variability of renewable sources, develop harmonized grid connection codes for diverse inverter technologies, and establish stability metrics and assessment methodologies specifically tailored to hybrid synchronous-inverter networks. Ultimately, the transition toward inverter-dominated grids demands coordinated efforts across dynamic modeling, control design, and system operational planning to guarantee robust transient performance and secure, reliable operation of future low-carbon power systems.

title: Sum Throughput Maximization in Multi-Tag Backscattering to Multiantenna Reader
text: This paper studies a multi-tag backscatter communication (BackCom) system, where multiple low-power tags simultaneously transmit information to a multiantenna reader by reflecting ambient or dedicated radio-frequency (RF) carrier signals. In such a setup, severe co-channel interference among concurrent tags, the doubly near-far effect, and stringent energy constraints of passive circuits fundamentally bottleneck the achievable sum throughput. To address these challenges, we formulate a sum throughput maximization problem by jointly optimizing the receive beamforming vectors at the multiantenna reader and the reflection coefficients of individual tags, subject to practical hardware constraints including per-tag power budgets and circuit power consumption. The resulting optimization problem is inherently non-convex and highly coupled across antenna and tag variables, making it computationally intractable to solve optimally. To circumvent this difficulty, we develop an efficient alternating optimization (AO) framework that decomposes the original problem into two tractable subproblems. Specifically, given the tag reflection coefficients, the optimal receive beamforming is derived in closed form via linear minimum mean-square error (LMMSE) or zero-forcing (ZF) combining; subsequently, with fixed beamforming, the tag-side variables are updated through sequential convex approximation (SCA) or fractional programming techniques that ensure a locally optimal solution. We rigorously prove the convergence of the proposed algorithm and analyze its computational complexity. Extensive simulation results demonstrate that the proposed scheme significantly outperforms baseline methods, such as single-antenna reception and equal reflection strategies, in terms of sum throughput, particularly under high tag density and strong interference conditions.

title: The structure of multiplex networks predicts play in economic games and real-world cooperation
text: Social networks fundamentally shape human cooperation, yet most studies isolate single-layer relationships, overlooking the fact that real-world interactions are inherently multiplex. Individuals are simultaneously embedded in overlapping networks of friendship, kinship, and professional ties, and the interplay between these layers may critically determine behavioral outcomes. Although economic games provide controlled settings to study cooperative decision-making, their external validity remains debated, and few studies have linked multiplex network architecture to both experimental play and field observations of cooperation. Here, we address this gap by analyzing how the structure of multiplex networks—encompassing multiple relational dimensions—predicts strategic behavior in economic games and real-world cooperative acts. Leveraging comprehensive network data, we demonstrate that multiplex centrality, interlayer correlation, and community structure consistently explain variance in cooperation across contexts. Our findings reveal that integrating multiplex topology bridges the laboratory and the field, offering a unified framework for understanding the network foundations of human cooperation.

title: OER Recommendations to Support Career Development
text: Open Educational Resources (OER) offer scalable, equitable pathways for lifelong learning and workforce preparation, yet their potential to support structured, intentional career development remains largely underutilized across formal and informal learning ecosystems. This paper synthesizes interdisciplinary scholarship and emerging practice to propose evidence-based recommendations for designing, curating, and deploying OER that align with dynamic labor market demands and diverse individual career trajectories. Drawing on an integrative review of major OER repositories, industry competency frameworks, and adult career construction theory, we identify critical gaps in skills signaling, modular pathway architecture, and wraparound learner supports. We present a conceptual framework organized around four pillars: (1) rigorous competency alignment with transparent, industry-recognized standards; (2) modular, stackable learning units that enable incremental credentialing; (3) embedded career guidance, self-assessment, and mentorship affordances; and (4) sustainable cross-sector partnerships that ensure ongoing content relevance and labor market validity. The recommendations emphasize accessibility, interoperability, and learner agency so that OER function as effective bridge mechanisms between education and employment. Findings indicate that when OER are intentionally mapped to career competencies and integrated with holistic support services, they significantly enhance employability, career adaptability, and mobility, particularly for non-traditional and underserved learner populations. This study contributes actionable strategies for educators, policymakers, and instructional designers seeking to leverage open resources as instruments for equitable, lifelong career advancement.

title: Energy Scheduling for Residential Distributed Energy Resources with Uncertainties Using Model-based Predictive Control
text:
The rapid proliferation of residential distributed energy resources (DERs)—including rooftop photovoltaic systems, battery storage, and flexible loads—has transformed traditional households from passive consumers into active prosumers. While this shift offers opportunities for reducing electricity costs and supporting grid decarbonization, it introduces significant operational challenges. The intermittency of renewable generation, coupled with stochastic demand and dynamic electricity pricing, creates a highly uncertain environment for real-time energy scheduling. Conventional rule-based or open-loop optimization strategies often fail to adapt to these disturbances, leading to suboptimal dispatch decisions, increased costs, and violations of constraints such as battery state-of-charge limits or grid import capacity.

Model Predictive Control (MPC) offers a compelling solution through its receding horizon framework, which repeatedly solves an optimal control problem using updated forecasts and measured system states. Unlike static schedulers, MPC accommodates uncertainties via inherent feedback correction and rolling trajectory updates, enabling proactive compensation for prediction errors. Its explicit handling of dynamics and physical constraints makes it well-suited for orchestrating heterogeneous DER assets within residential microgrids. However, ensuring reliable performance depends critically on how uncertainties are modeled within the prediction horizon, whether through stochastic scenarios, robust bounds, or chance-constrained formulations.

This paper investigates model-based predictive control strategies for residential DER scheduling under multiple sources of uncertainty. By formulating the problem within an MPC framework and analyzing its effectiveness in mitigating forecast inaccuracies, this work aims to provide a computationally tractable, closed-loop optimization approach that balances economic performance with operational reliability and user comfort requirements.

title: A Bayesian method for inference of effective connectivity in brain networks for detecting the Mozart effect
text: Application of a hierarchical Bayesian dynamic causal model to resting-state fMRI data from 28 healthy adults revealed robust, measurable changes in effective connectivity following 12 minutes of Mozart exposure. Posterior estimates indicated significantly increased self-inhibition in the left superior temporal gyrus (mean = –0.52 Hz, 95% credible interval [CI] = [–0.79, –0.28]) and strengthened forward coupling from Heschl’s gyrus to the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (mean = 0.34 Hz, CI = [0.14, 0.55]). Bayesian model comparison decisively favored the Mozart condition over the scrambled-music control (Bayes factor BF₁₀ = 24.6, posterior model probability = 0.96). Furthermore, the posterior probability of a direct effective connection from the right inferior frontal gyrus to the auditory cortex was 0.91 under Mozart, compared to only 0.43 under control. Network entropy decreased by 14.2%, reflecting more efficient information transfer. These findings demonstrate that brief exposure to Mozart’s music reliably alters top-down effective connectivity, furnishing network-level neural evidence for the Mozart effect.

title: Roadmap to a Roadmap: How Could We Tell When AGI is a 'Manhattan Project' Away?
text:
The challenge of anticipating when artificial general intelligence becomes achievable through a national-level mobilization comparable to the Manhattan Project is not merely a technical forecasting exercise—it is a prerequisite for prudent governance. This paper has argued that recognizing the “Manhattan Project threshold” requires a structured, multi-dimensional roadmap-to-a-roadmap: a monitoring framework that tracks converging technical preconditions, resource availability, and organizational feasibility rather than relying on singular metrics or expert intuition alone. By disaggregating the path to AGI into observable milestones—such as the resolution of foundational algorithmic bottlenecks, the commodification of requisite compute at scale, the emergence of compelling prototype systems, and the convergence of research agendas toward scalable architectures—we can move beyond binary speculation toward a more nuanced state of readiness assessment.

Nevertheless, the indicators proposed here remain deliberately provisional. History cautions against excessive confidence in technological prognostication, and the emergence of AGI may yet be shaped by discontinuities, covert research programs, or architectural paradigms that evade contemporary forecasting tools. Our framework is therefore offered not as a predictive algorithm but as a scaffold for ongoing deliberation, one that demands iterative refinement as the scientific frontier evolves and as societal values shift. The broader implication is unmistakable: democratic societies should not wait for unambiguous, universally visible signals before building governance capacity. If the transition to a Manhattan-scale AGI project can only be confirmed in hindsight, the window for constructive policy intervention, public deliberation, and international coordination will likely have already closed.

Ultimately, the question is not whether we can pinpoint the exact calendar moment when AGI becomes imminently buildable, but whether we can cultivate the institutional foresight to recognize when the remaining distance has narrowed from a marathon to a sprint. Constructing that perceptual and governance infrastructure—robust, adaptive, transparent, and humbly aware of its own limitations—is perhaps the most urgent roadmap of all.

title: On forward invariance in Lyapunov stability theorem for local stability
text: The Lyapunov direct method remains the fundamental tool for establishing local stability of nonlinear dynamical systems. In standard formulations of Lyapunov's stability theorem, the requirement that the time derivative of a positive definite function be negative definite in a neighborhood of the equilibrium is typically accompanied by the implicit assumption that corresponding sublevel sets are forward invariant, ensuring trajectories remain within the domain where stability conditions apply. This paper investigates the precise role and necessity of forward invariance in local stability analysis. We demonstrate that while local asymptotic stability can be established without explicitly assuming forward invariance, the construction of invariant sublevel sets is essential for obtaining quantitative estimates of the domain of attraction and guaranteeing that solutions do not exit the region of negative definiteness before converging. By analyzing the topological properties of Lyapunov sublevel sets and their relationship with system trajectories, we establish refined sufficient conditions under which forward invariance emerges as a structural consequence of the Lyapunov derivative conditions rather than an independent a priori requirement. Furthermore, we clarify scenarios where the lack of forward invariance may lead to conservative stability estimates or technical complications in nonlinear and hybrid systems. These results bridge an important gap in classical Lyapunov theory and provide practical guidance for constructing valid Lyapunov functions and invariant estimates in control applications.

title: Summer vacation and COVID-19: effects of metropolitan people going to summer provinces
text: The seasonal migration of metropolitan populations to cooler provinces during summer months represents a longstanding demographic pattern in numerous countries. Yet, the COVID-19 pandemic introduced unprecedented complexities to these large-scale movements, raising critical concerns about disease transmission dynamics across regional boundaries. Although existing literature has extensively analyzed urban mobility during public health emergencies, scant attention has been devoted to the specific epidemiological and socioeconomic risks posed by vacation-driven travel from densely populated metropolitan areas to traditionally cooler, often medically underserved, destination provinces. This study examines the multifaceted impacts of such population inflows on regional COVID-19 spread, healthcare system resilience, and local economic stability. By integrating mobility datasets with epidemiological records, we quantify how summer tourism reshaped infection trajectories and resource allocation patterns in receiving communities. Our findings offer evidence-based insights for crafting targeted interventions that reconcile seasonal economic activities with infectious disease prevention in an era of persistent pandemic threats.

title: Using Multiple Imputation to Classify Potential Outcomes Subgroups
text: Potential outcomes subgroups, such as those arising in principal stratification, are central to studying heterogeneous treatment effects and causal mediation. A persistent challenge is that subgroup membership depends on potential outcomes under counterfactual treatment conditions, yet the fundamental problem of causal inference ensures that at least one potential outcome per unit is necessarily unobserved. Consequently, subgroup indicators are partially missing, and deterministic classification rules ignore critical uncertainty in assignment. We propose a multiple imputation framework that treats missing potential outcomes as imputation targets to probabilistically classify units into latent subgroups. By drawing missing potential outcomes from their posterior predictive distribution conditional on observed covariates and measured outcomes, we generate multiple completed datasets, apply principled classification rules, and aggregate results using standard combination rules. This procedure propagates classification uncertainty into downstream analyses, yields valid frequentist inferences, and mitigates the bias inherent in single-imputation or modal assignment strategies. Through simulation studies and an empirical illustration, we demonstrate that the proposed method improves classification accuracy and produces more reliable standard errors for subgroup-specific causal estimands compared to conventional approaches that fail to account for imputation variability in the presence of partially observed potential outcomes.

title: The Snowball Earth transition in a climate model with drifting parameters
text:
The Neoproterozoic era witnessed one of the most dramatic climate transitions in Earth history, wherein the planet apparently descended into near-global glaciation during the so-called Snowball Earth events of the Cryogenian period. Understanding the physical mechanisms that permitted such a catastrophic ice-albedo feedback remains a central challenge in paleoclimate research. Energy balance models and more sophisticated general circulation models have consistently demonstrated that, under sufficiently reduced solar forcing or declining atmospheric greenhouse gas concentrations, the climate system can exhibit pronounced bistability between warm and ice-covered states separated by an unstable threshold. In this classical picture, the Snowball Earth transition is viewed as a bifurcation—a saddle-node or Hopf bifurcation in low-dimensional models—where a stable warm state loses stability and collapses to a globally frozen attractor. Yet these idealized frameworks typically treat control parameters as static, mapping out equilibrium hysteresis curves without adequately addressing how the system responds when boundary conditions evolve gradually over geological timescales.

In reality, the forcing that drove the Cryogenian glaciations likely changed continuously over millions of years, driven by tectonically regulated CO₂ drawdown, silicate weathering feedbacks, and modest secular variations in solar luminosity. When parameters drift slowly across a bifurcation point, the resulting dynamics can differ markedly from the quasi-static approximation: critical transitions may be delayed, noise-induced escape can precede deterministic thresholds, and the effective stability landscape itself becomes inherently time-dependent. Despite growing recognition of rate-dependent tipping in contemporary climate research, the implications of drifting parameters for deep-time Snowball Earth initiation remain largely unexplored.

This study addresses that gap by introducing sustained time-dependent parameter drift into a conceptual climate model capable of capturing the warm-to-Snowball transition. By systematically varying the rate at which radiative forcing decreases, we examine how the threshold for global glaciation depends on drift velocity, quantify bifurcation delays, and characterize the transient dynamics that precede the critical transition. Our results highlight that the route to a Snowball Earth is not simply a matter of crossing a fixed bifurcation point but involves a subtle interplay between ice-albedo feedback strength, parameter drift rate, and system thermal inertia, offering a refined dynamical perspective on one of Earth's most extreme climate shifts.

title: Exploring the Endogenous Nature of Meme Stocks Using the Log-Periodic Power Law Model and Confidence Indicator
text:
We calibrated the LPPL model to daily price series of five heavily shorted meme stocks—designated MEM-A through MEM-E—over the January–March 2021 window (n = 1,240 total observations). The model converged for 78% of the 120 rolling-window fits, yielding a mean critical-time estimate tc of 14.3 days (SD = 2.1) ahead of the observed local price maxima. The power-law exponent m averaged 0.42 (SE = 0.04, R² = 0.91), consistent with an unsustainable super-exponential regime, while the log-periodic angular frequency ω centered on 7.2 rad (95% CI: [6.4, 8.0]), indicating persistent endogenous oscillations. A placebo test on 500 reshuffled series produced a mean LPPL-CI of only 0.12, confirming that the structure is not spurious.

The LPPL Confidence Indicator (LPPL-CI), constructed from the normalized residual variance and parameter stability across nested windows, registered 0.81 for the aggregate meme-stock index at peak activity, compared with 0.34 for the matched control sample of non-meme retail favorites (t = 4.72, p < 0.001). At the individual level, MEM-C exhibited the highest LPPL-CI score (0.89) and the smallest damping ratio (γ = 0.11), signaling strong self-reinforcing feedback loops.

Regression analysis confirmed that a one-standard-deviation increase in the LPPL-CI corresponded to a 2.4-percentage-point rise in the probability of a subsequent >30% drawdown within ten trading days (p < 0.01). These findings suggest that meme-stock price trajectories are not driven solely by exogenous news shocks; rather, the statistically significant LPPL signatures and elevated confidence indicators reveal an endogenous bubble dynamic generated by self-referential investor behavior and reflexive momentum.

title: IAN: Combining Generative Adversarial Networks for Imaginative Face Generation
text: We presented IAN, a novel framework that synergistically combines multiple generative adversarial networks for imaginative and highly realistic facial image synthesis. By integrating complementary adversarial architectures through a collaborative optimization scheme, IAN leverages diverse generative priors to produce faces that transcend the limitations of single-model approaches, enabling both photorealistic rendering and creative facial attribute manipulation. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves superior visual quality, diversity, and semantic consistency compared to baseline GANs, effectively balancing fidelity and imagination. The framework offers broad applicability in digital content creation, virtual character design, and privacy-preserving face synthesis. Future work will explore extending IAN to temporal video generation, incorporating fine-grained semantic control, and investigating adaptive weighting mechanisms to further enhance interpretability and user controllability. We believe that principled multi-GAN collaboration represents a promising direction for next-generation generative models, paving the way toward more creative, robust, and versatile neural face synthesis systems.

title: The impact of small changes in thoroughfare connectivity on the potential for student walking
text: Active school travel is widely recognized as a critical means of enhancing children’s physical activity and independent mobility, yet the built environment often constrains walking potential. While existing research has extensively examined macro-level street connectivity, the effects of small-scale, incremental changes in thoroughfare networks remain underexplored. This study investigates how minor modifications to thoroughfare connectivity influence the potential for student walking. Using spatial network analysis and GIS-based pedestrian accessibility modeling, we compared connectivity metrics and walking catchments before and after targeted micro-interventions—such as opening cul-de-sacs, adding mid-block crossings, and optimizing intersection configurations—across selected school neighborhoods. Student residential locations and school sites were integrated to calculate changes in walking potential. Results indicate that even modest connectivity enhancements significantly improved pedestrian route directness and expanded the proportion of students within a walkable distance. Notably, small changes yielded disproportionately large benefits in low-density suburban areas where discontinuities in the street network previously imposed substantial detours. These findings suggest that low-cost, targeted alterations to thoroughfare connectivity can effectively increase student walking rates without requiring large-scale infrastructure investment. The study provides actionable evidence for planners and policymakers seeking to promote active travel through incremental urban design interventions.

title: Economics of disagreement -- financial intuition for the Rényi divergence
text:
Disagreement among economic agents regarding future states of the world constitutes a foundational element of modern financial theory, profoundly influencing asset prices, portfolio choices, and market dynamics. While an extensive literature has examined the pricing implications of heterogeneous beliefs through various statistical divergence measures—most notably the Kullback-Leibler divergence—the economic substance and financial intuition underlying generalized information-theoretic distances remain largely opaque to economists. This paper bridges this conceptual gap by establishing a rigorous financial interpretation of the Rényi divergence, a parametric family of divergence measures that nests numerous conventional metrics as special cases and occupies a central role in information geometry.

We demonstrate that the Rényi divergence of order α naturally emerges from the equilibrium analysis of economies where agents evaluate speculative opportunities under differentially distorted probability measures. Specifically, we show that this divergence quantifies the shadow price of belief disagreement in incomplete contingent claim markets, wherein the parameter α governs the curvature of agents' ambiguity attitudes and determines endogenous risk-sharing rules. Our framework reveals that distinct orders within the Rényi family correspond to alternative market microstructures and bargaining protocols among heterogeneous investors, thereby connecting information geometry to the wealth dynamics of disagreement. By embedding the Rényi divergence into the economics of disagreement, this study not only enriches the information-theoretic foundations of behavioral and quantitative finance but also delivers novel, testable implications for the term structure of disagreement premiums and the propagation of belief dispersion across financial markets.

title: Generalised linear models for prognosis and intervention: Theory, practice, and implications for machine learning
text:
Generalised linear models have long served as a cornerstone of statistical modelling in clinical and epidemiological research, providing a principled framework for relating covariates to outcomes through a flexible yet interpretable structure. From logistic regression in prognostic risk stratification to Poisson models in evaluating intervention effects, GLMs offer transparent parameter estimates and well-characterised uncertainty that remain essential for evidence-based decision-making. Their theoretical elegance and computational tractability have cemented their role in both explanatory and predictive paradigms.

Yet the ascendancy of machine learning has precipitated a methodological tension, wherein algorithmic flexibility and predictive accuracy are often privileged over parametric parsimony and causal interpretability. While modern approaches such as gradient boosting and deep learning capture complex non-linearities, they frequently obscure the quantification of intervention effects and individual prognoses that GLMs readily afford. This disconnect raises pressing questions about how classical regression theory can inform, and be extended by, contemporary computational methods without sacrificing the inferential rigour required for clinical and policy applications.

This paper examines the theoretical foundations and practical deployment of GLMs across prognostic and interventional settings, delineating their enduring utility alongside emerging hybrid methodologies. By interrogating the intersection between established generalised linear theory and machine learning practice, we identify opportunities for leveraging parametric insights within flexible algorithmic frameworks, ultimately advocating for modelling strategies that balance predictive performance with actionable inferential clarity.

title: No data? No problem! A Search-based Recommendation System with Cold Starts
text: We evaluated the proposed search-based recommender against Popularity, Random, Content-Based (CB), and MetaMatrix baselines on MovieLens-1M and Amazon-Books, restricting evaluation strictly to users with fewer than three historical interactions. The proposed system achieved a Hit Ratio@10 of 0.34 and NDCG@10 of 0.18 on MovieLens-1M, substantially outperforming Popularity (HR@10 0.21, NDCG@10 0.09), Random (HR@10 0.08, NDCG@10 0.03), and CB (HR@10 0.26, NDCG@10 0.12). On Amazon-Books, it attained HR@10 of 0.28 and NDCG@10 of 0.14, compared with 0.15 and 0.07 for Popularity, and 0.19 and 0.08 for CB. Ablation studies demonstrated that removing the query-expansion module reduced HR@10 by 12%, while disabling the semantic re-ranking layer caused an 8% drop in precision and a 6% decline in recall. Runtime analysis showed an average latency of 45 ms per recommendation, well within interactive thresholds. Notably, for zero-shot cold-start users with no prior ratings, the system maintained an NDCG@10 of 0.11 and a catalog coverage score of 0.42, whereas collaborative filtering variants collapsed to 0.03 and 0.15 respectively. Statistical significance was confirmed using a paired t-test (p < 0.01) across all metrics. These results indicate that leveraging external search indices and synthetic query generation effectively mitigates data sparsity without requiring historical interaction logs.

title: Multi-layered Network Structure: Relationship Between Financial and Macroeconomic Dynamics
text: This study demonstrates that the multi-layered network structure provides a critical framework for understanding the intricate relationship between financial and macroeconomic dynamics. By modeling financial institutions, markets, and macroeconomic variables as interconnected layers, we reveal how shocks propagate across the system through both direct and indirect contagion channels. Our findings indicate that network topology significantly amplifies or dampens macroeconomic fluctuations, highlighting the importance of cross-layer dependencies for systemic risk assessment. The results underscore that financial stability cannot be analyzed in isolation from real economy linkages, and that macroeconomic conditions reciprocally shape financial network resilience. These insights carry important implications for macroprudential policy, suggesting that effective regulation must account for the complex web of multi-layered interdependencies rather than focusing on single-layer metrics. Future research should extend this framework to incorporate evolving network architectures, time-varying linkages, and nonlinear feedback effects to further enhance our understanding of integrated economic systems.

title: Stuttering Speech Disfluency Prediction using Explainable Attribution Vectors of Facial Muscle Movements
text: Stuttering is a complex speech fluency disorder characterized by involuntary disruptions, including sound repetitions, prolongations, and blocks. While traditional assessment predominantly relies on acoustic analysis, mounting evidence suggests that facial muscle movements encode critical biomarkers for predicting speech disfluencies. However, leveraging visual physiological cues for stuttering prediction remains largely underexplored, and the black-box nature of deep learning models limits their clinical applicability. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a novel framework for stuttering speech disfluency prediction using explainable attribution vectors derived from facial muscle movements. Our approach first extracts fine-grained facial action unit intensities and dense landmark trajectories from video recordings to capture subtle kinematic patterns associated with disfluent speech production. These spatiotemporal features are then fed into a deep temporal architecture that models long-range dependencies in orofacial dynamics. Critically, we integrate gradient-based attribution mechanisms to compute explainable attribution vectors, which precisely quantify the contribution of individual facial muscle groups to the model’s prediction. This enables the identification of physiologically meaningful regions—such as the orbicularis oris, mentalis, and levator labii superioris—that serve as early indicators of impending disfluency events. Extensive experiments on a curated dataset of stuttered speech videos demonstrate that our method achieves superior predictive performance compared to both audio-only and existing multimodal baselines, as measured by F1-score and frame-level accuracy. Furthermore, the extracted attribution vectors reveal distinct muscular activation signatures preceding different disfluency types, offering interpretable insights that align with established clinical observations. This work not only advances the state of the art in automatic stuttering detection but also provides a transparent, clinically interpretable tool to support speech-language pathologists in objective diagnosis and personalized intervention planning.

title: Neural document expansion for ad-hoc information retrieval
text:
Ad-hoc information retrieval remains a fundamental challenge in modern search systems, where the goal is to retrieve relevant documents in response to one-off, user-initiated queries. A long-standing obstacle in this task is the vocabulary mismatch problem: users and authors often employ different words to express the same concepts, causing relevant documents to be missed when query terms do not exactly appear in the text. Traditional document expansion techniques, such as pseudo-relevance feedback and thesaurus-based methods, have been proposed to alleviate this issue by appending related terms to original document representations. However, these approaches typically rely on term co-occurrence statistics or shallow linguistic resources, struggling to capture deep semantic relationships and contextual nuances.

The emergence of deep learning and pre-trained language models has opened new avenues for bridging semantic gaps in information retrieval. Neural document expansion, which leverages sequence-to-sequence architectures—such as T5 and BART—or large language models to predict and inject query-like expansions into documents, has recently garnered significant attention. Unlike classical methods that merely append statistically associated terms, neural approaches generate fluent, semantically rich paraphrases, anticipated questions, or contextual elaborations that align more closely with real user intent. Consequently, they bridge the lexical chasm between queries and documents more effectively and have shown remarkable promise when coupled with learned sparse retrievers or dense dual-encoders for first-stage candidate generation.

In this paper, we present a comprehensive study on neural document expansion for ad-hoc retrieval. We systematically analyze the impact of diverse expansion strategies, investigate the interplay between expansion fidelity, length, and downstream retrieval effectiveness, and propose an enhanced framework that optimizes expansion generation through task-specific fine-tuning and selective filtering. Extensive experiments on standard TREC and MS MARCO benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed approach significantly outperforms both traditional expansion baselines and existing neural methods, yielding consistent gains in recall and ranking metrics while maintaining computational efficiency.

title: Can Insider Trading Be Committed Without Trading?
text: This Article challenges the foundational premise that insider trading necessarily requires a securities transaction. While federal jurisprudence has long conceptualized insider trading through the paradigm of buying or selling securities while in possession of material nonpublic information, recent enforcement actions and doctrinal developments reveal a growing regulatory and judicial willingness to penalize non-trading conduct that exploits informational asymmetries. Drawing on tipping liability, selective disclosure frameworks, and the "possession versus use" debate, this Article argues that the animating concern of insider trading law—protecting market integrity and remedying breaches of fiduciary duty—can be implicated even in the absence of an executable trade. Through a comparative analysis of SEC enforcement patterns and circuit court decisions, the study identifies three categories of non-trading insider trading: constructive trading through proxies, coordinated abstention from trading, and the strategic disclosure of information to third parties for pecuniary gain. The Article contends that although expanding liability beyond traditional trading raises significant due process and fair notice concerns, a properly cabined theory of non-trading insider trading better aligns with the purposes of Section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5. It concludes by proposing a framework for distinguishing culpable non-trading conduct from legitimate investment behavior.

title: Learning Opinion Dynamics From Social Traces
text:
Social media platforms, online forums, and digital communication networks have become primary arenas for public discourse, generating unprecedented volumes of observational data about how individuals express, share, and revise their views. These social traces offer a unique window into the microscopic processes that drive collective opinion formation, yet they remain underutilized by classical theoretical models of opinion dynamics, which typically rely on stylized interaction rules and small-scale experiments.

Traditional approaches such as the DeGroot model or bounded confidence dynamics provide elegant mathematical frameworks, but their fixed assumptions about agent heterogeneity, network structure, and influence mechanisms often fail to capture the complexity of real-world behavior. Bridging this gap requires moving beyond handcrafted rules toward data-driven methods that can uncover opinion evolution directly from observed social signals.

In this paper, we propose a framework for learning opinion dynamics from large-scale social traces. By combining temporal interaction data with expressive machine learning architectures, we infer how opinions propagate and transform through social networks without presupposing a specific parametric form. Our approach enables both accurate prediction of opinion trajectories and novel insights into the mechanisms governing collective attitude shifts.

title: A deep network approach to multitemporal cloud detection
text: The proposed multitemporal cloud detection network achieved an overall pixel-level accuracy of 94.3%, an F1-score of 0.912, and an Intersection over Union (IoU) of 0.847 on the test set comprising 1,240 Sentinel-2 image pairs acquired over heterogeneous landscapes spanning agricultural, urban, and coastal biomes. Corresponding precision and recall were 0.928 and 0.897, respectively. When evaluated against the single-temporal baseline, which attained an accuracy of 89.7% and an F1-score of 0.854, the multitemporal framework reduced omission errors by 38.2% and commission errors by 24.6%. The inclusion of a temporal attention module improved cloud boundary delineation, raising the IoU for thin cirrus regions from 0.61 to 0.78. Cross-sensor generalization tests on Landsat-8 imagery yielded an accuracy of 92.1% without fine-tuning, demonstrating robustness across spatial resolutions. The analysis of inference speed showed that the proposed model processes a 512×512 pixel tile at 10 m spatial resolution in 0.18 seconds on a single GPU, compared to 0.12 seconds for the single-temporal counterpart, with the additional cost attributed to the temporal feature fusion layer. Ablation studies indicated that removing the bidirectional LSTM branch decreased the F1-score by 4.3 percentage points, while substituting the custom cloud-refinement decoder with a standard U-Net reduced accuracy to 91.2%. Error analysis revealed that 73% of misclassifications occurred at cloud-shadow interfaces and over bright built-up surfaces during seasonal snow cover. These results confirm that leveraging temporal consistency significantly enhances cloud mask reliability, particularly for transient and optically thin clouds, while maintaining computational feasibility for large-area applications.

title: Constraints in Random Effects Age-Period-Cohort Models
text: Random effects age-period-cohort models offer flexibility for hierarchical and correlated data, yet they do not resolve the fundamental identification problem inherent to the APC framework. This paper demonstrates that the choice of identifying constraints—whether placed on fixed effects, random effects, or variance components—profoundly influences estimated trends, variance partitioning, and best linear unbiased predictions. Unlike conventional fixed-effect approaches where constraints merely rotate the solution plane, restrictions in random-effects formulations can alter the assumed covariance structure and shrinkage properties, yielding divergent substantive conclusions across specifications. Consequently, researchers must recognize that no single constraint is neutral or uniquely "correct." We recommend that empirical applications routinely report sensitivity analyses across multiple theoretically justified constraints, explicitly state the assumptions embedded in each choice, and examine the stability of both fixed and random variance component estimates. Furthermore, transparency regarding how constraints interact with the random-effects covariance matrix is essential for valid interpretation and replication. Future work should continue to develop data-driven or prior-based strategies that mitigate the influence of arbitrary restrictions while preserving the advantages of hierarchical modeling. Ultimately, careful attention to constraint selection remains indispensable for credible inference in random effects APC analyses.

title: Twin Estimates of the Effects of Prenatal Environment, Child Biology, and Parental Bias on Sex Differences in Early Age Mortality
text: Sex differences in early-age mortality are well documented, yet disentangling the contributions of biological predispositions from environmental and behavioral influences remains empirically challenging. This study leverages a twin research design to separately identify the effects of the prenatal environment, child biology, and parental bias on sex-specific mortality risks during infancy and early childhood. Using twin fixed-effects models that exploit variation within twin pairs, we parse the relative importance of shared prenatal conditions, biological endowments, and postnatal parental investment behavior. Our findings indicate that biological factors contribute to a baseline male survival disadvantage, whereas parental sex preferences and unequal resource allocation significantly amplify observed mortality differentials. Prenatal environmental constraints further modulate these gaps. Collectively, the results demonstrate that the early-life sex mortality gap stems from an interplay of biological vulnerability and socially mediated factors, highlighting the potential for policy interventions targeting prenatal care and parental incentives to improve child survival equitably.

title: Towards Smart Sustainable Cities: Addressing semantic heterogeneity in building management systems using discriminative models
text: The rapid urbanization worldwide has spurred the development of smart sustainable cities, where Building Management Systems (BMS) serve as the critical backbone for energy efficiency and operational optimization. However, the widespread deployment of heterogeneous BMS platforms across different vendors and building generations has resulted in severe semantic heterogeneity, hindering seamless data integration and interoperability among distributed assets. Existing ontology-based alignment approaches often struggle with scalability and dynamic adaptation to continuously evolving building schemas. To address this challenge, this paper proposes a novel discriminative modeling framework that automatically identifies and resolves semantic discrepancies in multi-source BMS data. By leveraging machine learning-based classification techniques, our method distinguishes semantically equivalent entities without relying on exhaustive manual mappings or rigid predefined rules. Experimental evaluations on real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed approach significantly improves integration accuracy while reducing engineering overhead, thereby offering a scalable pathway toward interoperable and sustainable urban infrastructures.

title: The Mechanism of the Origin and Development of Lightning from Initiating Event to Initial Breakdown Pulses (v.2)
text: Despite decades of research, the precise mechanism linking lightning initiation to the onset of initial breakdown pulses (IBPs) remains incompletely understood. This study presents an updated physical model describing the cascade from initiating event to IBP emission in cloud-to-ground flashes. We integrate high-speed optical observations, electric field change measurements, and particle-based discharge simulations to track pre-breakdown evolution. Our results indicate that lightning originates from localized streamer bursts initiated by hydrometeor-enhanced field amplification, which thermalize into hot leader channels. These nascent leaders propagate in inhomogeneous cloud regions, generating space charge layers that modulate the ambient potential. The transition to the IBP phase occurs when the developing leader system reaches critical length and charge density, producing characteristic bipolar electric field signatures. This framework reconciles microscale plasma processes with macroscale discharge morphology, offering a unified explanation for the origin of lightning and the generation of its earliest electromagnetic emissions.

title: Modeling Dispositional and Initial learned Trust in Automated Vehicles with Predictability and Explainability
text:
The successful deployment of automated vehicles (AVs) hinges on passenger willingness to cede control, a decision governed fundamentally by trust. However, trust in automation is not a static attitude but a dynamic construct shaped by both stable individual differences and early interaction experiences. Dispositional trust reflects a user’s generalized propensity to rely on automated systems, rooted in personality traits and prior beliefs about technology, whereas initial learned trust emerges from the first direct encounters with an AV and rapidly calibrates subsequent reliance intentions. Understanding how these distinct forms develop during initial exposure is essential for designing interfaces that foster appropriate reliance rather than overtrust or disuse.

Central to this calibration are the system properties of predictability and explainability. Predictability—the ability to anticipate an AV’s future states and actions—reduces environmental uncertainty and enables learned trust to form through observable behavioral consistency. Explainability, which concerns the transparency and interpretability of an AV’s decision-making rationale, may particularly moderate how users with varying dispositional trust orientations interpret system behaviors in ambiguous scenarios. Although both properties are widely advocated as pillars of trustworthy automation, their distinct roles in shaping dispositional versus initial learned trust remain theoretically underdeveloped.

This paper addresses this gap by proposing a model linking predictability and explainability to dispositional and initial learned trust in AV contexts. By disentangling stable user characteristics from early experiential factors, the model clarifies how design features contribute to trust formation at the outset of human-automation interaction. Implications for transparent interface design are discussed, offering a foundation for cultivating well-calibrated trust in automated driving.

title: Key Borrowers Detection by Long-Range Interactions
text: We evaluated our method on the Financial Contagion Network (FCN-2019) comprising 12,450 borrowers and 89,300 lending ties, with key borrowers defined as the top 5% default contributors. Our Long-Range Interaction Network (LRIN) achieved an AUC of 0.947, an F1-score of 0.891, and a Precision@50 of 0.820, substantially outperforming GraphSAGE (AUC 0.912, F1 0.854) and GAT (AUC 0.921, F1 0.863). The ablation removing interactions beyond two hops reduced AUC by 0.031 and F1 by 0.028, confirming that long-range dependencies are critical for detection accuracy. Specifically, borrowers connected via latent paths of length ≥4 contributed 34.2% of the total predictive signal for systemic defaults. Attention weight visualization revealed that 18.7% of the highest-attention edges spanned disjoint communities with no direct local overlap, indicating that LRIN captures hidden risk channels. Furthermore, on the smaller Regional Bank Dataset (RBD-2020) with 3,100 nodes, LRIN maintained an AUC of 0.938, whereas baseline performance dropped by over 0.04. Runtime scaled linearly with network size, processing the full graph in 4.3 seconds per epoch on a single GPU. These results demonstrate that explicit modeling of long-range interactions significantly improves key borrower detection and uncovers non-local systemic risk pathways invisible to localized neighborhood aggregation methods.

title: GARCH(1,1) model of the financial market with the Minkowski metric
text: This study has introduced a novel extension of the standard GARCH(1,1) framework by embedding volatility dynamics within the Minkowski metric space. By reformulating the conditional variance equation through the lens of spacetime geometry, we established a geometrically informed approach to modeling financial market volatility that distinguishes between timelike and spacelike market shocks. The proposed model preserves the parsimonious structure of the traditional GARCH(1,1) specification while offering an alternative interpretation of persistence and clustering through invariant interval measures. Our theoretical development demonstrates that the Minkowski-based formulation captures asymmetric propagation of information across trading horizons, suggesting that volatility transmission may be better understood as a geometric phenomenon governed by pseudo-Euclidean distance rather than purely temporal dependence. Although the current exposition focused primarily on model specification and analytical properties, the framework opens several avenues for future research, including empirical estimation with high-frequency data, multivariate extensions using Lorentzian geometry, and exploration of causal structures implied by the metric signature. While practical implementation requires careful treatment of the signature constraints and stationarity conditions, the integration of relativistic geometric concepts into financial econometrics provides a promising conceptual bridge between physics-inspired methodologies and stochastic volatility modeling, potentially enriching our understanding of complex market dynamics.

title: Evaluating Semantic Interaction on Word Embeddings via Simulation
text: Word embeddings underpin most modern natural language processing systems, yet systematically evaluating how they encode complex semantic interactions remains a persistent challenge. This paper proposes a simulation-based framework to rigorously assess how distributional representations capture semantic operations, including compositionality, analogy, and relational reasoning. By generating controlled synthetic tasks and manipulating linguistic variables in a principled manner, we isolate the effects of specific semantic phenomena on embedding geometry without confounding corpus artifacts. Our large-scale simulations reveal substantial disparities across architectures: contextualized embeddings demonstrate superior stability in compositional tasks, whereas static embeddings exhibit systematic biases in analogical reasoning. Moreover, we quantify robustness under adversarial perturbations and low-frequency lexical combinations, identifying failure modes invisible to standard benchmarks. These results demonstrate that simulation-driven evaluation provides a reproducible, fine-grained diagnostic tool for semantic representation. This work establishes a methodological foundation for understanding and improving how vector space models encode meaning through interaction.

title: Learning-based Prediction and Uplink Retransmission for Wireless Virtual Reality (VR) Network
text:
Virtual reality (VR) has emerged as a transformative paradigm for immersive communications, with applications spanning gaming, telemedicine, and remote collaboration. However, delivering seamless VR experiences over wireless networks imposes stringent requirements, including ultra-high data rates and ultra-reliable low-latency communication (URLLC). In interactive VR systems, the uplink transmission of tracking data—including head-mounted display (HMD) orientations, controller movements, and gesture signals—plays a pivotal role in enabling real-time rendering at edge servers. Even minor uplink delays or packet losses can severely degrade motion-to-photon latency, leading to cybersickness and a poor quality of experience (QoE).

Conventional uplink retransmission protocols, such as hybrid automatic repeat request (HARQ), often fail to satisfy these demanding latency constraints due to rigid timing structures and their inability to adapt to rapidly varying wireless channels. Although extensive research has addressed predictive rendering and downlink VR streaming, uplink reliability remains comparatively underexplored. Recently, learning-based techniques have demonstrated remarkable potential in forecasting human head movements and wireless channel dynamics. Nevertheless, most existing works treat prediction and communication as decoupled processes, leaving predictive insights underutilized for enhancing uplink transmission resiliency.

To bridge this gap, this paper proposes a novel learning-based prediction and uplink retransmission framework specifically tailored for wireless VR networks. By leveraging deep learning models to anticipate VR traffic patterns and fading channel states, we design a predictive retransmission mechanism that proactively optimizes radio resource allocation and retransmission decisions before packet errors occur. Specifically, predictive information is exploited to pre-allocate uplink resources and determine optimal retransmission timing, thereby avoiding congestion during channel fading. Unlike conventional reactive HARQ that merely responds to negative acknowledgments, the proposed approach tightly couples predictive intelligence with the uplink transmission process, minimizing unnecessary retransmission overhead while guaranteeing ultra-reliable transmission. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed scheme significantly outperforms benchmark reactive mechanisms in terms of packet success rate and average latency, offering a promising solution for latency-sensitive VR uplink communications.

title: Economics of carbon-dioxide abatement under an exogenous constraint on cumulative emissions
text: This paper examines the optimal intertemporal allocation of carbon-dioxide abatement when climate policy is subject to an exogenous, binding constraint on cumulative emissions. Treating the carbon budget as a finite exhaustible resource, we derive the cost-minimizing path of emissions reductions and the associated trajectory of the carbon price. We show that the shadow price of CO2 rises at the social rate of discount, reflecting a dynamic scarcity rent on the remaining atmospheric carbon stock. The optimal abatement schedule balances marginal mitigation costs across periods, front-loading reductions when costs decline over time but respecting the intertemporal budget cap. Our results provide a benchmark for the timing of net-zero transitions and highlight that under a hard cumulative constraint, the initial carbon price is determined by total abatement requirements and the discount rate rather than contemporaneous marginal damages. The framework reconciles Hotelling-based carbon pricing with temperature-target policies and derives implications for optimal climate finance and technology investment.

title: Human brain activity for machine attention
text:
Attention is a cornerstone of human cognition, dynamically allocating neural resources to salient stimuli while filtering irrelevant distractions. In artificial systems, attention mechanisms have become equally indispensable, enabling deep learning models to focus on task-relevant features and achieving breakthrough performance across vision, language, and multimodal tasks. Yet despite their shared nomenclature, machine attention remains largely an algorithmic construct—optimized through end-to-end gradient descent without grounding in the biological mechanisms that govern human perception. This disconnection raises fundamental questions about whether computational models capture the efficiency and flexibility of neural attention, and whether artificial systems might benefit from deeper integration with the brain's own selection processes.

Recent advances in non-invasive neuroimaging have opened new avenues to bridge this divide by making the neural correlates of human attention accessible at scale. Techniques such as electroencephalography and functional magnetic resonance imaging provide rich signals that reveal where, when, and how the brain prioritizes information. By treating these neural recordings as implicit supervision or inductive bias, researchers can align computational attention with biologically grounded selection criteria, moving beyond purely data-driven optimization toward neurophysiologically informed architectures.

In this work, we investigate how human brain activity can directly guide machine attention. We present a framework that integrates neural recordings into the training and inference of attention-based models, demonstrating that brain-derived supervision improves alignment between human and machine behavior while enhancing model generalization and interpretability. Our findings suggest that leveraging human brain activity offers a compelling path toward more human-centric and cognitively plausible artificial intelligence.

title: The Life and Death of SSDs and HDDs: Similarities, Differences, and Prediction Models
text:
The Results and Analysis section examined 14,200 consumer HDDs and 6,800 SSDs over a 48-month observation window. HDDs exhibited an annualized failure rate (AFR) of 3.8% in year one, escalating to 8.4% by year four, with a mean time to failure (MTTF) of 45,000 hours. In contrast, SSDs demonstrated a significantly lower AFR of 1.2% initially, rising to only 2.9% by year four, with an MTTF of 120,000 hours. However, SSD failure modes were predominantly wear-related: once NAND program/erase cycles exceeded 2,800, failure probability spiked sharply from 0.4% to 18.7% within 90 days.

Our predictive models revealed divergent precursors across technologies. For HDDs, a logistic regression model using reallocated sector count, seek error rate, and operating temperature achieved an AUC-ROC of 0.89 at the 95% confidence level, predicting failures 14 days in advance with 82% precision. For SSDs, a gradient-boosted model incorporating wear leveling count, grown bad blocks, and thermal throttling events yielded an AUC-ROC of 0.84, forecasting failures 21 days prior. Notably, ambient temperature correlated weakly with SSD mortality (Pearson r = 0.12) but strongly with HDD mortality (r = 0.61).

The survival analysis indicated that while HDDs follow a classical Weibull distribution (shape parameter β = 2.3), SSDs exhibit a delayed wear-out phase best modeled by a log-logistic curve with a median survival of 52 months. These findings suggest that unified prediction frameworks must explicitly account for fundamentally different degradation physics: mechanical attrition and head-stack degradation in HDDs versus cumulative oxide damage and charge-trap wear in SSDs.

title: Quantifying Volatility Reduction in German Day-ahead Spot Market in the Period 2006 through 2016
text: This study quantified a pronounced and statistically significant reduction in price volatility within the German day-ahead spot market throughout the decade from 2006 to 2016. The empirical results demonstrate that the deepening integration of European electricity markets, sustained expansion of renewable generation capacity, and substantially enhanced market liquidity collectively contributed to a structurally more stable pricing environment. While the early years were characterized by frequent price spikes and pronounced variance, the latter period exhibited significantly dampened fluctuations, reflecting improved market efficiency and maturity. These findings indicate that regulatory frameworks supporting cross-border market coupling and renewable energy deployment have concurrently facilitated wholesale price stabilization, thereby offering more reliable short-term investment signals for market participants. Nevertheless, the ongoing transformation of the generation mix continues to pose emerging challenges related to supply intermittency and negative price events.
