Overall, the analysis confirms that the German day-ahead market underwent a measurable transition toward lower volatility during the observed period, providing a critical empirical foundation for future research on electricity market design and energy transition dynamics.

title: Loss Rate Forecasting Framework Based on Macroeconomic Changes: Application to US Credit Card Industry
text: Accurate forecasting of credit card loss rates is critical for risk management, regulatory capital allocation, and timely loan loss provisioning under forward-looking accounting standards such as CECL and IFRS 9. However, traditional models often rely on historical averages or static roll-rate methodologies that inadequately capture regime shifts driven by macroeconomic cycles. This paper proposes a comprehensive loss rate forecasting framework that explicitly links credit card charge-off dynamics to macroeconomic fluctuations, with a specific empirical application to the U.S. credit card industry. Leveraging quarterly aggregate portfolio data spanning multiple business cycles from 1990 to 2023, we first identify and extract a set of macroeconomic drivers—including unemployment rates, real GDP growth, Treasury yield spreads, household debt service burdens, and consumer confidence indices. We then employ a multi-stage econometric strategy that combines dynamic factor analysis to distill common macroeconomic trends, vector error correction modeling to preserve long-run equilibrium relationships among co-integrated variables, and a regime-switching or gradient-boosting augmentation to account for non-linearities during periods of economic stress. Out-of-sample validation across baseline, adverse, and severely adverse macroeconomic scenarios demonstrates that the proposed framework substantially improves forecast accuracy, reducing root mean squared error compared with traditional autoregressive benchmarks. Our findings indicate that unemployment rates and short-term funding costs serve as powerful leading predictors, while the interaction between household leverage and GDP contractions significantly amplifies downside tail risks. Scenario-based projections further reveal that industry-wide charge-off rates can escalate rapidly under stressed conditions, highlighting the necessity of dynamic, forward-looking provisions. By translating macroeconomic forecasts into granular, scenario-contingent portfolio risk estimates, this study provides a robust, empirically grounded tool that supports regulatory stress testing, strategic capital planning, and balance-sheet resilience for credit card issuers and policymakers. The framework’s modular architecture also allows for seamless integration of alternative data sources and real-time macroeconomic nowcasts, enhancing its adaptability to rapidly evolving economic environments.

title: A Nonparametric Bayesian Item Response Modeling Approach for Clustering Items and Individuals Simultaneously
text: Item response theory (IRT) models have been widely used in educational and psychological measurement to characterize the relationship between latent traits and item responses. However, conventional IRT approaches typically assume homogeneity across items and individuals, thereby overlooking potential heterogeneity in both domains. While existing clustering techniques often treat item grouping and respondent classification separately, such disjoint strategies may fail to capture the intricate interplay between item characteristics and individual ability structures. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a nonparametric Bayesian IRT modeling framework that simultaneously clusters items and individuals within a unified hierarchical structure. By incorporating Dirichlet process priors, the proposed method enables data-driven inference on the number of clusters and flexibly adapts to complex data patterns without prespecifying group memberships. This approach not only enhances measurement precision but also provides deeper insights into the latent structure underlying item response data.

title: Considerations for Eye Tracking Experiments in Information Retrieval
text:
Eye tracking has established itself as an indispensable method in interactive information retrieval (IIR) research, offering fine-grained insights into how users allocate visual attention during search and browsing tasks. By recording gaze position and movement with high temporal precision, researchers gain access to implicit behavioral signals—such as fixation duration, scan paths, and pupil dilation—that complement explicit interactions like clicks and query reformulations. These measures have been widely used to investigate core phenomena including result relevance assessment, snippet readability, interface layout effects, and cognitive load during complex sessions. As retrieval interfaces evolve from static result pages toward dynamic, multimodal, and conversational systems, understanding visual behavior remains central to designing effective, user-centered information systems.

Yet the apparent accessibility of modern eye trackers belies the substantial methodological complexity inherent in designing and analyzing rigorous experiments. Factors ranging from hardware sampling rate, calibration accuracy, and head-movement tolerance to ambient lighting and participant characteristics such as visual acuity can introduce noise or systematic bias that threatens internal validity. Moreover, analyzing eye movement data requires consequential yet often underreported decisions—including the definition of areas of interest, the selection of metrics, the handling of data loss and blink artifacts, and the treatment of individual differences—that vary considerably across studies. This inconsistency complicates replication efforts and limits cumulative knowledge development, raising questions about the robustness of eye tracking evidence in the IR literature.

This paper examines the methodological landscape of eye tracking research within information retrieval, identifying critical considerations that shape experimental design, data quality, and analytical interpretation. Rather than advocating a single prescriptive protocol, we synthesize best practices and trade-offs across diverse IR contexts—from desktop search to mobile and conversational interfaces—to help researchers align their technical choices with their research questions. By highlighting underappreciated sources of variance and offering practical recommendations for transparency and reporting standards, we aim to strengthen the reliability and comparability of eye tracking studies. Ultimately, our goal is to support the IR community in harnessing gaze data more effectively to build richer, more robust theories of search behavior.

title: Markovian And Non-Markovian Processes with Active Decision Making Strategies For Addressing The COVID-19 Pandemic
text: The Markovian framework yielded a mean prediction error of 12.3% (RMSE = 847 cases) over a 14-day horizon, whereas the non-Markovian formulation reduced this error to 6.8% (RMSE = 412 cases) when incorporating variable infectiousness windows and hospitalization memory kernels. Under passive policy scenarios, the Markovian model projected a peak ICU occupancy of 342 beds on day 47; the non-Markovian model, accounting for Erlang-distributed stay durations, forecasted 398 beds on day 52, aligning within 4.1% of observed admissions. In the 65+ cohort, Markovian projections underestimated mortality by 18.4% relative to observed weekly fatalities, whereas the non-Markovian approach with age-specific recovery time distributions narrowed this gap to 3.2%. Active decision strategies triggered at a seven-day incidence threshold of 50 per 100,000 produced markedly divergent outcomes. The Markovian policy suite reduced the effective reproduction number (Re) from 2.4 to 0.95 after 21 days, averting an estimated 14,200 infections at a compliance cost of $2.1 million per day. In contrast, the non-Markovian active process, leveraging history-dependent contact tracing efficacy declining from 78% to 61% after day 10 post-exposure, achieved Re = 0.82 in 18 days and averted 19,600 infections with a marginally higher operational cost of $2.4 million daily. Vaccination rollout simulations further showed that prioritizing the top two risk tiers under non-Markovian rules prevented 8,400 additional hospitalizations compared to the memoryless allocation. Computational cost differed substantially: the Markovian decision cycle averaged 0.4 seconds per iteration, while non-Markovian history-augmented states required 3.2 seconds but improved policy precision by 23%. Sensitivity analysis indicated that a 10% increase in testing latency eroded the Markovian advantage by 31%, whereas the non-Markovian framework exhibited robustness with only an 8% degradation in outcome accuracy. These findings indicate that memory-aware processes significantly enhance pandemic response fidelity despite increased computational demands.

title: Gamification of Enterprise Systems: A Synthesis of Mechanics, Dynamics, and Risks
text: This paper synthesized the multifaceted landscape of enterprise gamification, delineating how distinct mechanics—including points, badges, leaderboards, and narrative frameworks—interact with underlying system dynamics to reshape user engagement, collaboration, and organizational workflows. Our analysis reveals that while gamification can significantly enhance productivity and enterprise system adoption, its efficacy remains contingent upon thoughtful alignment with specific organizational contexts, user motivations, and task complexities. Critically, we underscored that poorly designed implementations risk fostering superficial compliance, counterproductive gaming behaviors, and data privacy vulnerabilities, thereby undermining long-term strategic outcomes. The findings suggest that sustainable enterprise gamification requires a balanced socio-technical architecture that prioritizes intrinsic motivators over extrinsic rewards and incorporates robust governance and risk mitigation frameworks. Future research should advance longitudinal investigations into user fatigue, ethical algorithmic design, and cross-cultural applicability. Ultimately, gamification should not be treated as a universal panacea but as a nuanced strategic intervention, carefully calibrated to the complex realities of modern organizations.

title: Adaptive Precision Training for Resource Constrained Devices
text: Training deep neural networks on resource-constrained devices, such as microcontrollers, embedded systems, and mobile edge nodes, is increasingly vital for privacy-preserving edge intelligence and federated learning. However, the substantial memory footprint and computational cost of standard full-precision training render it infeasible for devices with severely limited storage, energy budgets, and processing capabilities. Although low-precision quantization mitigates resource demands, statically fixing numerical precision throughout the entire training process often induces gradient underflow, convergence instability, or non-negligible accuracy degradation, particularly in deep architectures with heterogeneous layer sensitivities. To address this challenge, we propose Adaptive Precision Training (APT), a novel framework that dynamically adjusts the numerical precision of weights, activations, and gradients across different layers and training stages according to real-time gradient statistics, loss landscape curvature, and instantaneous hardware resource availability. APT introduces a lightweight precision controller that employs a feedback-driven policy to determine optimal bit-width configurations, seamlessly transitioning between floating-point and fixed-point representations without requiring exhaustive offline searches. Furthermore, we develop an error-compensated gradient scaling mechanism coupled with a precision-aware momentum buffer to mitigate the adverse effects of precision reduction on backward propagation and weight updates. We theoretically analyze the convergence properties of APT under standard smoothness assumptions, establishing that it retains the same asymptotic convergence rate as full-precision stochastic gradient descent up to a controlled precision-dependent constant. Extensive experiments conducted on multiple benchmark datasets, including CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny-ImageNet, using resource-limited hardware platforms such as ARM Cortex-M4 and Raspberry Pi 4, demonstrate that APT achieves comparable test accuracy to full-precision training while reducing peak memory usage by up to 4.2× and computational latency by 3.5×. Additionally, APT exhibits strong generalization across diverse neural architectures ranging from compact CNNs to lightweight transformers. These results validate that adaptive precision strategies offer a principled balance between model performance and resource efficiency, establishing a scalable foundation for practical on-device training in next-generation embedded AI applications.

title: Urban volumetrics: spatial complexity and wayfinding, extending space syntax to three dimensional space
text: The overwhelming majority of urban morphological studies and spatial cognition research have historically relied upon two-dimensional representations, treating cities as planar configurations in which vertical stratification is either simplified or entirely neglected. Yet contemporary urban environments are increasingly characterized by profound volumetric complexity—encompassing multilevel transport networks, stacked public realms, and vertically integrated pedestrian systems—that fundamentally challenges conventional planar analytical frameworks. While space syntax has provided robust insights into the relationship between spatial configuration, human movement, and wayfinding, its conventional reliance on axial lines and visibility graphs remains largely confined to horizontal planes. Although recent scholarship has attempted to extend these principles to multilevel structures, such efforts frequently remain “two-and-a-half-dimensional,” flattening vertical relationships into stacked layers rather than embracing true volumetric continuity and topological depth. Consequently, the intricate interplay between three-dimensional spatial complexity and wayfinding behavior in vertically articulated cities remains insufficiently theorized. This paper proposes a rigorous extension of space syntax into genuine three-dimensional volumetric space to address this critical gap. By reconceptualizing urban systems as continuous volumetric fields rather than discrete horizontal planes, we develop an analytical framework that captures spatial complexity through metrics of volumetric accessibility, three-dimensional visual permeability, and integrated topological depth. We argue that wayfinding in multilevel environments is shaped not merely by horizontal integration, but by the holistic volumetric configuration of space, wherein vertical permeability and inter-level connectivity play equally decisive roles. The remainder of this paper details the theoretical foundation, methodological innovation, and empirical validation of this volumetric approach.

title: Relative utility bounds for empirically optimal portfolios
text: We derive non-asymptotic bounds on the relative utility loss of empirically optimal portfolios in multi-asset investment problems. When expected utility is maximized using estimated market parameters rather than the true unknown distribution, the resulting data-driven portfolio suffers an out-of-sample performance degradation. For a general class of concave utility functions—including exponential, power, and mean–variance objectives—we establish explicit upper bounds on the shortfall between the expected utility of the empirically optimal portfolio and that of the oracle optimal portfolio. These relative utility bounds depend on the number of observations, the dimension of the asset universe, the risk-aversion profile encoded in the utility curvature, and the condition number of the returns covariance structure. Under standard moment and mixing conditions, the utility loss decays at a rate of at least $n^{-1/2}$, with faster rates achievable for smoother utilities or sub-Gaussian return tails. The results are distributionally robust and allow for mild model misspecification. Our findings yield a quantitative guideline for the sample size required to ensure that an estimated portfolio attains a prescribed fraction of the maximum achievable expected utility.

title: A general solution to the preferential selection model
text:
Preferential selection models provide a fundamental framework for understanding how choice processes amplify small initial differences into persistent structural inequalities. Whether describing the accumulation of citations in scientific networks, the concentration of market share among competing products, or the distribution of resources in organizational hierarchies, these models formalize the tendency of selectors to favor alternatives with greater current endowments. Yet despite their broad application across statistical physics, economics, and computer science, analytical progress has remained fragmented: existing solutions typically depend on asymptotic approximations, restrictive functional forms for the selection kernel, or continuum limits that obscure finite-size effects.

This paper presents a closed-form general solution to the preferential selection model that transcends these limitations. By treating the selection dynamics as a discrete-time stochastic process governed by an arbitrary preferential kernel, we derive exact expressions for the time-dependent distribution of selected quantities without recourse to mean-field assumptions or large-system expansions. Our approach employs a generating-function transformation that diagonalizes the evolution operator, yielding compact formulas for both transient behavior and stationary states that are valid for any finite population and any well-defined initial condition.

The resulting framework unifies previously disparate special cases and exposes the precise dependence of asymptotic outcomes on the functional form of preferential bias and initial heterogeneity. We illustrate the practical utility of the general solution through applications to citation network growth, brand competition, and stratification dynamics, demonstrating that earlier models emerge as particular parameterizations. These findings establish a comprehensive analytical foundation for predicting and controlling preferential selection processes across disciplinary boundaries.

title: Learning abstract structure for drawing by efficient motor program induction
text:
We presented a framework for learning abstract structural representations of drawings through efficient motor program induction. By treating drawings as sequences of compositional motor actions generated by latent programs, our approach bridges the gap between high-level symbolic structure and low-level perceptual execution. The proposed model efficiently searches the space of possible programs, discovering reusable primitives, hierarchical relations, and stochastic variation that capture the underlying generative process behind visual concepts. This program induction approach enables strong generalization: once an abstract structure is learned, it can be flexibly reinstated to produce novel exemplars, interpolate between styles, and parse new drawings into interpretable constituent parts.

Our results demonstrate that learning to draw involves more than memorizing pixel patterns or reproducing fixed trajectories; it requires acquiring a compact, causal model of how images are constructed from sequential actions. By factorizing knowledge into abstract motor programs and their execution parameters, the model achieves systematicity, compositionality, and data efficiency that purely neural generative models struggle to attain. The induced programs furthermore provide an explicit, human-interpretable representation of visual concepts, opening avenues for human-machine collaboration in artistic, educational, and design domains.

Several important directions remain for future work. Current limitations include the assumption of a fixed library of drawing primitives and the computational challenges of scaling to highly complex scenes with many interacting objects. Extending the framework to jointly learn primitive vocabulary from raw motor data, rather than assuming predefined stroke types, would further reduce inductive bias. Additionally, integrating visual attention mechanisms with online program synthesis could enable real-time drawing assistance, interactive tutoring systems, and grounded language learning. Ultimately, we believe that grounding visual understanding in the motor programs that produce images offers a principled and powerful avenue toward artificial systems that can create, reason about, and communicate visual structure in human-like ways.

title: Modeling and simulating the spatial spread of an epidemic through multiscale kinetic transport equations
text: We present a multiscale kinetic transport framework for modeling and simulating the spatial spread of infectious diseases. Classical compartmental models, such as SIR-type systems, rely on the homogeneous-mixing assumption and consequently fail to resolve the spatial heterogeneities, anisotropic diffusion, and mobility-driven propagation mechanisms observed in real-world epidemics. To address this limitation, we introduce a mesoscopic description based on kinetic transport equations governing the evolution of distribution functions for susceptible, infected, and recovered populations. Here, the transport operator accounts for microscopic individual velocities and directional movement preferences, while collisional integral operators model both localized contacts and nonlocal contagion interactions across social and geographic networks. By performing a systematic Chapman–Enskog asymptotic expansion in diffusion and hyperbolic scaling limits, we derive consistent macroscopic approximations—including reaction–diffusion and advection–reaction–diffusion systems—that rigorously bridge individual-level mobility with coarse-grained epidemic dynamics. The kinetic approach intrinsically preserves finite propagation speeds and enables seamless transitions between rarefied kinetic and collective hydrodynamic regimes. To circumvent computational stiffness from disparate scales, we design asymptotic-preserving numerical schemes that remain uniformly stable and accurate across all regimes without resolving the small mean free path. Extensive simulations demonstrate sharp traveling infection wavefronts, spontaneous spatial hotspot formation, and the quantitative impact of mobility reductions and nonlocal interactions on epidemic velocity and final size. The results confirm that multiscale kinetic transport equations provide a flexible, mathematically rigorous foundation for spatial epidemic modeling, offering theoretical insight into cross-scale disease propagation and a robust computational platform to inform public health interventions.

title: Social networks, confirmation bias and shock elections
text: The rapid proliferation of social media has fundamentally transformed political communication, enabling voters to actively curate information environments that increasingly align with their preexisting beliefs. This self-selection mechanism, further amplified by algorithmic curation, fosters echo chambers where confirmation bias—the tendency to favor information that validates prior convictions—flourishes unchecked. While considerable scholarship has documented the polarizing effects of online networks, less understood is how the interplay between social network structures and confirmation bias systematically produces electoral surprises. Traditional forecasting models often fail to anticipate "shock elections," where outcomes deviate sharply from ex-ante expectations, partly because they underestimate the endogenous reinforcement of biased beliefs within digitally mediated peer groups. This study bridges this gap by examining how network topology and cognitive bias jointly distort information aggregation, leading to collective misperceptions and unexpected voting outcomes. Leveraging computational modeling and empirical evidence from recent electoral cycles, we demonstrate that confirmation bias within tightly clustered online communities not only amplifies ideological extremity but also masks underlying preference shifts until they suddenly materialize at the ballot box. Our findings offer novel insights into the microfoundations of political uncertainty and contribute to a deeper understanding of when and why networked democracies remain vulnerable to unpredicted political shocks.

title: Modelling Covid-19 epidemic in Mexico, Finland and Iceland
text: The COVID-19 pandemic manifested heterogeneously across national contexts, necessitating comparative epidemiological modelling to disentangle the effects of demographics, geography, and non-pharmaceutical interventions. This study presents a comparative analysis of the COVID-19 epidemic in Mexico, Finland, and Iceland—three countries with markedly different population sizes, densities, and public health strategies. Using a compartmental SEIR model calibrated to reported case and mortality data from February 2020 to December 2021, we estimated time-varying reproduction numbers, epidemic peaks, and the relative impact of intervention measures. Parameter estimation was performed via Bayesian inference, incorporating country-specific contact patterns, mobility reductions, and vaccination rollouts. Results indicate that Iceland’s intensive test-trace-isolate strategy and small population enabled rapid suppression of transmission, yielding the lowest effective reproduction number and shortest epidemic waves. Finland’s geographically dispersed population and timely lockdown measures flattened the curve considerably, whereas Mexico experienced prolonged, higher-magnitude waves driven by dense urban centres and delayed mobility restrictions. Model projections underscore that early, sustained interventions and healthcare capacity scaling were critical determinants of cumulative mortality. These findings highlight how country-specific contexts modulate epidemic dynamics and inform tailored pandemic preparedness frameworks for diverse demographic and geographic settings.

title: Event Prediction in the Big Data Era: A Systematic Survey
text:
The past decade has witnessed an unprecedented explosion of digital data generated by social media platforms, sensor networks, financial transactions, and online information systems. This big data revolution has fundamentally transformed how information is collected, processed, and analyzed, offering extraordinary opportunities to understand complex patterns in human behavior, natural phenomena, and organizational dynamics. At the core of these observations lie events—discrete occurrences that carry significant semantic meaning, ranging from disease outbreaks and stock market fluctuations to social protests and traffic accidents. The ability to anticipate such events before they materialize holds profound implications for proactive decision-making across science, industry, and governance.

Despite substantial advances in machine learning and data mining, event prediction in the big data era confronts unique challenges stemming from the four Vs: massive Volume, high Velocity, diverse Variety, and uncertain Veracity. Researchers from disparate communities—including natural language processing, time series analysis, spatial data mining, and complex network theory—have independently developed methodologies tailored to their specific domains. This fragmentation has resulted in a heterogeneous landscape of techniques, datasets, and evaluation protocols that are rarely compared or synthesized, impeding knowledge transfer and systematic progress.

While several focused reviews have examined event prediction within isolated contexts, a comprehensive, cross-domain systematic survey remains conspicuously absent. This paper fills that gap by providing a holistic overview of event prediction methodologies in the age of big data. We systematically categorize existing approaches based on data modalities, algorithmic paradigms, and application domains, identify prevailing trends and technological enablers, and highlight critical open challenges. Our analysis aims to bridge disciplinary silos and offer researchers a unified foundation for advancing the state of the art in predictive analytics.

title: Addressing the Privacy Implications of Mixed Reality: A Regulatory Approach
text:
Our survey of 1,247 mixed reality users and 84 hardware developers revealed systemic privacy vulnerabilities in current MR ecosystems. Seventy-eight percent of users reported significant discomfort with continuous environmental scanning, while 63% were unaware that their gaze data was being retained for an average of 14 months. Developers indicated that 91% of current MR headsets collect at least six distinct biometric data streams, yet only 12% of privacy policies disclosed this practice explicitly. Additionally, 54% of applications transmitted raw spatial mapping data to third-party servers without end-to-end encryption.

We evaluated three regulatory models across a simulated 24-month deployment period in twelve jurisdictions. The baseline self-regulation scenario resulted in an estimated 342 privacy incidents per 10,000 active users, with an average remediation cost of $4,200 per breach and a median response time of 38 days. By contrast, our proposed tiered regulatory framework—which mandates real-time anonymization of spatial maps, requires on-device processing for biometric inference, and limits raw biometric retention to 72 hours—reduced incidents to 41 per 10,000 users, representing an 88.0% decrease. Compliance costs under this model averaged $180,000 per platform annually, compared to $2.3 million in projected liability and remediation costs under the baseline scenario.

Further analysis showed that regulatory mandates for granular, just-in-time user consent dashboards increased opt-out rates for non-essential data collection from 11% to 34% and reduced unauthorized data sharing by 57%. However, jurisdictions implementing strict data localization requirements observed a 27% decrease in cross-border MR service availability and a 15% increase in consumer prices, suggesting a tangible trade-off between privacy protection and market access. Regression analysis indicated that every additional month of biometric data retention correlated with a 3.2% increase in the probability of re-identification within shared virtual environments. These findings demonstrate that proactive, technically specific regulation substantially mitigates privacy risks in mixed reality without imposing economically prohibitive burdens on operators.

title: Exact Combinatorial Optimization with Graph Convolutional Neural Networks
text:
This paper introduced a principled framework for integrating graph convolutional neural networks into exact combinatorial optimization solvers. By treating mixed-integer linear programs as bipartite graphs with variable and constraint nodes, we enable a GCN to learn high-dimensional embeddings that jointly encode the structural, numerical, and logical properties of a problem instance. Our results demonstrate that a GCN trained to imitate the strong branching rule can match the quality of these expensive expert decisions while reducing the online computational overhead by orders of magnitude. Through extensive experiments on canonical NP-hard benchmarks, we showed that the proposed approach consistently produces smaller branch-and-bound trees than classical hand-crafted branching heuristics and generalizes to instances substantially larger and more constrained than those encountered during training. These findings empirically confirm that modern deep learning architectures, when equipped with an appropriate relational inductive bias, can effectively distill latent combinatorial structure and substantially enhance the efficiency of exhaustive search algorithms.

Nevertheless, several important challenges remain. The current policy exhibits diminished effectiveness on out-of-distribution problem families, suggesting that more robust domain-adaptation techniques, self-supervised pretraining regimes, or invariant architectural choices are needed to broaden applicability across diverse application domains. Furthermore, scaling the approach to industrial-scale formulations containing millions of variables and constraints demands careful balancing of model expressiveness against the strict latency constraints inherent to every branch-and-bound node, particularly when deploying within existing commercial solver frameworks. Future research should also seek rigorous theoretical characterizations of GCN representational capacity in the context of polyhedral combinatorics, which could inform architecture design and yield actionable generalization bounds. Finally, extending learned components to other critical solver decisions—including node selection, cutting-plane generation, and primal heuristics—offers a promising path toward fully hybrid optimization engines. We anticipate that such structure-aware, data-driven methods will become essential building blocks in next-generation exact optimization software, forging deeper and more productive connections between machine learning and discrete decision making.

title: Multiple Sclerosis disease: a computational approach for investigating its drug interactions
text: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic autoimmune disorder of the central nervous system characterized by progressive demyelination and neurodegeneration. The complex pathogenesis and heterogeneous clinical course of MS necessitate long-term administration of disease-modifying therapies combined with symptomatic treatments, thereby elevating the risk of pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic drug-drug interactions (DDIs) that may compromise therapeutic efficacy and patient safety. This study presents an integrative computational framework that combines network pharmacology, molecular docking simulations, and machine learning-based prediction models to systematically investigate potential interactions among established and emerging MS therapeutics. By constructing comprehensive drug-target-disease networks and performing pathway enrichment analysis, we identified critical molecular hubs and signaling cascades underlying MS pathophysiology and drug response. Our results revealed several significant synergistic and antagonistic interactions, particularly among immunomodulatory agents, sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor modulators, and repurposed compounds, alongside clinically relevant metabolic interactions mediated by cytochrome P450 enzymes. Furthermore, adverse event profiling highlighted potential cardiotoxic and hepatotoxic liabilities. These computational predictions provide mechanistic insights into MS polypharmacology and offer a cost-effective, high-throughput strategy for prioritizing drug combinations, supporting personalized medicine, and facilitating the rational design of safer therapeutic regimens.

title: Future Smart Connected Communities to Fight COVID-19 Outbreak
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has posed unprecedented challenges to global public health systems, exposing critical vulnerabilities in traditional epidemic response mechanisms. Conventional containment strategies, which rely heavily on manual contact tracing and centralized healthcare infrastructures, often struggle to balance timeliness, accuracy, and privacy protection during rapid outbreak phases. In this context, the concept of smart connected communities (SCCs)—underpinned by the Internet of Things (IoT), artificial intelligence (AI), and ubiquitous communication networks—has emerged as a transformative paradigm for resilient pandemic management. By enabling real-time health monitoring, intelligent resource allocation, and seamless remote interactions, SCCs can substantially enhance early warning capabilities and reduce transmission risks at the community level. Nevertheless, existing literature predominantly focuses on isolated technological interventions, lacking a holistic framework that orchestrates sensing, connectivity, and governance for community-wide epidemic resilience. To bridge this gap, this paper presents a comprehensive architecture for future smart connected communities, exploring how interconnected infrastructures, data-driven decision-making, and citizen-centric digital services can collectively strengthen preparedness and coordinated response against COVID-19 and potential future public health emergencies. Moreover, by fostering multi-stakeholder collaboration among governments, enterprises, and residents, such intelligent community ecosystems offer a scalable and sustainable pathway toward post-pandemic societal recovery.

title: Synthetic Data Generation for Economists
text: Synthetic data generation has emerged as a critical methodological tool for empirical economists navigating the tension between expanding data availability and stringent privacy constraints. As administrative microdata, longitudinal household surveys, and granular firm-level records become indispensable for causal inference, structural estimation, and policy simulation, legal and ethical barriers to data access increasingly impede scientific reproducibility and collaboration. This paper provides a comprehensive framework for generating high-fidelity synthetic datasets tailored to the distinctive features of economic data—including temporal dependence, panel attrition, heavy-tailed distributions, zero-inflated outcomes, and complex causal structures that govern behavioral responses. We systematically evaluate modern generative approaches, ranging from classical copula methods, multiple imputation by chained equations, and Bayesian networks to deep generative architectures such as generative adversarial networks (GANs), variational autoencoders, diffusion models, and transformer-based large language models, assessing their capacity to preserve marginal distributions, conditional means, regression coefficients, and treatment effect heterogeneity. Our analysis demonstrates that while off-the-shelf algorithms often fail to capture the skewed income distributions, autocorrelated macroeconomic dynamics, and network dependencies characteristic of economic datasets, domain-specific adaptations—incorporating economic equilibrium constraints, temporal embeddings, hierarchical structures, and formal differential privacy guarantees—substantially improve both fidelity and confidentiality protection. We introduce practical validation metrics designed specifically for econometric inference, encompassing coefficient stability, counterfactual prediction accuracy, rank preservation, and disclosure risk quantification. Drawing on applications to longitudinal labor surveys, censored firm balance sheets, spatial employment data, and synthetic control settings, we show that meticulously constructed synthetic data can facilitate reproducible research, enable secure remote access environments, and accelerate methodological innovation without substantially compromising analytical validity. We conclude with actionable guidelines for implementation, dissemination, and the ethical boundaries of synthetic data deployment in economic research.

title: Towards Social & Engaging Peer Learning: Predicting Backchanneling and Disengagement in Children
text:
Peer learning offers rich opportunities for children's cognitive and social development, yet its success depends critically on the subtle social dynamics that unfold between young learners. Backchanneling behaviors—such as nodding, verbal acknowledgments, and reciprocal gaze—serve as vital social glue in collaborative interactions, signaling active listening and mutual understanding. Conversely, moments of disengagement can quickly undermine the learning process, making early identification essential for timely supportive intervention. However, these fleeting socio-behavioral signals remain difficult to detect and respond to automatically, particularly in the unstructured, multimodal contexts characteristic of child-centered education.

This paper addresses the challenge of computationally predicting backchanneling and disengagement during children's peer learning activities. By modeling these dynamic interaction phenomena, we aim to lay groundwork for responsive educational technologies that foster socially attuned and engaging collaborative experiences. Our work contributes novel predictive models for automatically detecting when children are socially connecting with or drifting away from their peers, opening avenues for adaptive systems that promote sustained engagement and mutual support in learning environments.

title: I like fish, especially dolphins: Addressing Contradictions in Dialogue Modeling
text:
We evaluated our Contradiction-Aware Dialogue Model (CADM) against a standard Transformer baseline and a fact-checking augmented variant on the Contradictory Conversations benchmark. Our model achieved a contradiction detection F1 score of 78.4%, compared to 34.2% for the baseline and 51.7% for the fact-checking model. In response generation, CADM obtained a BLEU-4 score of 22.1 and a ROUGE-L of 41.3, slightly lower than the baseline’s 24.7 and 43.8, reflecting an expected trade-off between fluency and factual consistency. However, BERTScore precision was 87.3% for CADM versus 81.5% for the baseline, indicating stronger semantic alignment with factually consistent references.

Human annotators rated 500 dialogues on consistency and coherence using a 5-point Likert scale. CADM scored 4.2 on factual consistency, significantly outperforming the baseline (2.8) and the fact-checking model (3.4), while maintaining comparable coherence at 3.9 versus 4.1 and 3.8 respectively. On the biological taxon subset containing statements such as "I like fish, especially dolphins," CADM reduced taxonomic contradictions by 63.5% relative to the baseline and corrected 89.2% of such errors when explicitly prompted with definitional questions.

Ablation studies indicated that removing the entailment loss decreased consistency scores by 11.3 points, while omitting the contradiction memory bank increased hallucinated facts by 18.7%. Error analysis showed that 72% of remaining contradictions involved subtle temporal shifts or coreference ambiguities, such as "I used to live in Paris" followed by "I have never been to France." These results demonstrate that targeted architectural modifications substantially improve logical coherence, though nuanced spatiotemporal reasoning remains an open challenge.

title: Corona-Warn-App: Tracing the Start of the Official COVID-19 Exposure Notification App for Germany
text: The launch of the Corona-Warn-App marked a pivotal moment in Germany’s digital response to the COVID-19 pandemic, representing one of the largest open-source public health technology deployments in the country’s history. Developed in an unprecedented collaboration between public institutions and private technology partners under immense time pressure, the app demonstrated both the considerable potential and the inherent limitations of decentralized exposure notification systems when deployed at national scale. By prioritizing a privacy-preserving architecture from its inception and ensuring transparency through immediate open-source publication, the project successfully fostered significant public trust while navigating complex technical, legal, and societal challenges throughout its initial rollout. Nevertheless, the early operational phase revealed critical lessons regarding the integration of digital notification infrastructure with existing medical workflows, the absolute necessity of broad testing capacity and laboratory reporting interoperability, and the importance of sustained user engagement strategies that extend far beyond initial download metrics. As the pandemic evolved, the Corona-Warn-App served not merely as a functional tool for individual risk notification but also as an influential blueprint for future digital public health interventions in democratic societies. Its development underscored that effective health technology requires continuous iterative improvement, robust cross-sectoral governance frameworks, and clear, consistent communication strategies to achieve meaningful epidemiological impact. Ultimately, while the app alone could not contain viral transmission chains, its establishment laid essential foundational groundwork for Germany’s emerging digital health sovereignty and continues to offer enduring, actionable insights for the responsible architecture of responsive, privacy-respecting health technologies during future public health emergencies.

title: Principles to Practices for Responsible AI: Closing the Gap
text: The rapid proliferation of high-level ethical principles for artificial intelligence (AI) has not been matched by effective implementation mechanisms, leaving a persistent and well-documented gap between aspirational commitments and day-to-day operational practices. This paper examines the systemic challenges that public and private organizations face when translating abstract responsible AI principles into concrete, verifiable actions across the entire AI development and deployment lifecycle. Through a systematic analysis of existing governance frameworks, longitudinal case studies, and cross-sectoral implementation models, we identify critical barriers to operationalization, including inherent ambiguity in principle interpretation, structural misalignment between technical engineering teams and socio-ethical objectives, insufficient resource allocation, and the absence of clear institutional accountability mechanisms. To bridge this divide, we propose an integrative, multi-layered framework that connects normative ideals with engineering practices by translating ethical principles into measurable technical and organizational requirements, embedding them within standard software development and procurement pipelines, and establishing robust continuous monitoring, auditing, and participatory feedback loops. Our analysis demonstrates that successful implementation requires sustained multidisciplinary collaboration, context-sensitive risk assessment tools, iterative impact evaluations, and fundamental organizational cultural shifts at all levels that prioritize transparency, accountability, and meaningful stakeholder engagement. Furthermore, we argue that closing the principles-to-practices gap necessitates adaptive governance structures that empower diverse communities, align incentive systems, and respond dynamically to evolving technological capabilities and societal contexts. The findings offer actionable pathways for practitioners, managers, and policymakers to move beyond principle-setting toward accountable, sustainable, and human-centered AI deployment, emphasizing that responsible AI constitutes an ongoing organizational commitment rather than a static, one-time design objective.

title: Towards Earnings Call and Stock Price Movement
text:
The earnings call has emerged as a pivotal channel through which publicly traded firms communicate forward-looking guidance and strategic outlook to market participants. Unlike regulated financial reports, these quarterly conferences offer unstructured, real-time interactions between management and analysts, rendering them a rich source of information for investors. However, the extent to which earnings call content—spanning textual disclosures, vocal cues, and sentiment dynamics—drives subsequent stock price movements remains insufficiently understood. Prior literature has predominantly focused on hard accounting metrics or aggregated news sentiment, leaving the nuanced information embedded in managerial discourse and question-and-answer sessions underexplored.

This study investigates the predictive linkage between earnings call characteristics and abnormal stock returns. By leveraging natural language processing and audio feature extraction, we decompose multimodal signals from conference transcripts and voice recordings to examine how markets assimilate soft information. Our analysis reveals that linguistic sentiment, vocal emotion, and unexpected topics in the Q&A segment exhibit significant explanatory power for post-announcement price drifts, even after controlling for earnings surprises. These findings contribute to the literature on information disclosure and market efficiency by highlighting the role of paralinguistic features and interactive dialogue in shaping investor behavior. Ultimately, this research offers practical implications for algorithmic trading and corporate disclosure policies in emerging and developed markets alike.

title: Neural Joint Entropy Estimation
text: Estimating joint entropy is fundamental to information-theoretic analysis, yet classical nonparametric methods suffer from the curse of dimensionality and fail to capture complex statistical dependencies in high-dimensional continuous spaces. We introduce Neural Joint Entropy Estimation (NJEE), a neural network-based approach that formulates joint entropy as a tractable variational lower bound. By training a deep architecture to implicitly model the underlying probability distribution, our method bypasses explicit density estimation, histogram binning, and costly nearest-neighbor searches. We establish theoretical consistency guarantees under mild smoothness assumptions and demonstrate favorable scaling to high-dimensional variables. Through extensive experiments on synthetic benchmarks and real-world datasets, we show that NJEE substantially outperforms traditional k-NN and kernel-based estimators, particularly in small-sample regimes and distributions with strong nonlinear dependencies. These results establish a scalable, differentiable framework for joint entropy estimation with direct applications to mutual information estimation, independence testing, and representation learning.

title: Personalized fall detection monitoring system based on learning from the user movements
text:
Falls represent one of the most critical public health challenges affecting older adults, often resulting in severe injuries, reduced mobility, and loss of independence. With aging populations worldwide, the incidence of fall-related accidents continues to rise, placing substantial burdens on healthcare systems and caregivers. Timely detection of falls is essential to ensure rapid medical intervention and minimize long-term complications. Consequently, automated fall detection systems have emerged as a promising technological solution to support continuous monitoring in home environments and assisted living facilities. However, despite significant advances in wearable sensors and ambient monitoring technologies, many existing solutions struggle to balance sensitivity and specificity in real-world scenarios.

Conventional fall detection approaches typically rely on generic thresholds and predefined activity models that are applied uniformly across diverse user populations. Such standardized methods frequently fail to account for individual variations in gait, body morphology, and daily activity patterns, leading to high rates of false positives and missed detections. Moreover, activities of daily living that resemble falling motions—such as bending, sitting abruptly, or lying down—often trigger unnecessary alarms, causing user frustration and decreased adherence to monitoring protocols. These limitations highlight the pressing need for adaptive systems capable of recognizing personalized movement signatures rather than depending on broad population-based assumptions.

This paper presents a personalized fall detection monitoring system that addresses these challenges by learning and adapting to the unique movement patterns of individual users. By leveraging machine learning techniques to construct user-specific behavioral models, the proposed system distinguishes between genuine falls and benign activities that are characteristic of each person's lifestyle. This personalized approach not only enhances detection accuracy but also significantly reduces false alarm rates, thereby improving user acceptance and system reliability. The remainder of this paper details the system architecture, the learning methodology, experimental validation across diverse user profiles, and a comparative analysis demonstrating the advantages of personalization in continuous fall monitoring applications.

title: Initialization of a Disease Transmission Model
text:
The initialized model was parameterized using demographic and epidemiological data from a synthetic population of N = 2,400,000 individuals partitioned across four age strata: 0–19 (26%), 20–44 (34%), 45–64 (25%), and 65+ (15%). Baseline transmission coefficients were calibrated to early outbreak incidence reports, yielding an effective contact rate β = 0.48 day⁻¹ and a basic reproduction number R₀ = 2.8 (95% CI: 2.4–3.2). The incubation period was fixed at 1/σ = 5.2 days and the infectious period at 1/γ = 8.1 days, producing a generation time Tg = 6.4 days. Initial conditions at t = 0 were set to S(0) = 2,399,850, E(0) = 100, I(0) = 50, and R(0) = 0, reflecting a nascent outbreak seeded by 150 total infections. Geographic initialization across twelve administrative districts allocated 62% of index infections to the two urban core districts, generating a spatial R₀ gradient from 3.1 in dense nodes to 1.9 in peripheral zones.

Sensitivity analysis revealed that peak prevalence varied nonlinearly with initial infected prevalence. A 20% increase in I(0) advanced the epidemic peak by 11 days and increased cumulative incidence by 4.3%. Conversely, halving the initial exposed pool delayed the peak by 7 days but reduced total cases by only 1.8%. The age-structured initialization showed that assigning 40% of initial infections to the 20–44 stratum accelerated early growth (r = 0.18 day⁻¹) compared to uniform seeding (r = 0.14 day⁻¹). Parameter estimation via least-squares fitting to the first 21 days of reported cases achieved a normalized root-mean-square error of 0.032.

These results indicate that model initialization is highly sensitive to the spatial and demographic distribution of initial infections, whereas aggregate counts exert weaker influence on long-term dynamics. The calibrated baseline reproduces observed early trajectories with fidelity sufficient for scenario projection, though uncertainties in the initial exposed compartment and spatial seeding warrant ensemble-based forecasting approaches.

title: Adversarial Robustness of Deep Convolutional Candlestick Learner
text: This paper investigated the adversarial robustness of deep convolutional neural networks trained to predict market movements directly from candlestick chart images. By treating technical analysis as a computer vision task, we demonstrated that state-of-the-art candlestick learners, despite achieving strong predictive performance and attractive risk-adjusted returns under benign market conditions, remain highly vulnerable to carefully crafted adversarial perturbations. Our comprehensive experiments revealed that imperceptible modifications to historical price visualizations—constrained by tight L-infinity bounds—induce severe degradation in both directional classification accuracy and practical profitability metrics, with attacks exhibiting strong black-box transferability across diverse network architectures, training seeds, and underlying asset classes. We further evaluated several defense strategies, finding that adversarial training yields the most consistent robustness gains, albeit at a modest cost to clean-market performance and computational efficiency, while input preprocessing, feature squeezing, and randomization techniques provide only limited protection against adaptive threat models. These findings reveal a critical and previously underexplored attack surface in vision-based algorithmic trading systems, whereby malicious actors could exploit perceptual predictors through compromised data feeds, manipulated brokerage charting interfaces, or synthetically generated market imagery. Nonetheless, our analysis is subject to important limitations. The current threat model primarily assumes full white-box access and static two-dimensional representations, which may not fully encapsulate the non-stationary, high-frequency dynamics of live markets, the sequential structure underlying tick-level price formation, or regulatory constraints on execution. Future work should pursue certifiable robustness bounds, examine the nuanced distinction between benign market microstructure noise and malicious perturbations, and develop multimodal architectures that synergistically fuse candlestick imagery with temporal order-book or alternative data features. As deep learning systems become increasingly embedded in quantitative finance, rigorously characterizing and mitigating the adversarial vulnerability of chart-based predictors will be indispensable for building trustworthy, secure, and resilient automated trading infrastructure.

title: Competitive pricing despite search costs if lower price signals quality
text: This paper examines the interplay between consumer search costs and quality signaling in markets with asymmetric information. Conventional search theory suggests that search frictions soften price competition and sustain supracompetitive markups. We demonstrate, however, that competitive pricing can emerge precisely because lower prices credibly signal high quality. In a sequential search model where consumers cannot observe product quality prior to purchase, high-type firms voluntarily set prices near or even below cost to separate themselves from low-type competitors. Because consumers rationally interpret low prices as evidence of superior, cost-efficient quality, the downward signaling distortion fully offsets the upward pressure typically created by search costs. The unique separating equilibrium exhibits competitive pricing despite positive search costs, and survives standard refinements. Our results imply that informational incentives can discipline markets more powerfully than search frictions distort them, and provide a theoretical foundation for aggressive introductory pricing in experience-good markets.

title: Can Testing Ease Social Distancing Measures? Future Evolution of COVID-19 in NYC
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has imposed unprecedented public health and socioeconomic burdens globally, prompting widespread adoption of non-pharmaceutical interventions, particularly social distancing measures. While demonstrably effective in flattening epidemic curves and mitigating viral transmission, prolonged lockdowns and mobility restrictions have precipitated severe economic contractions, widespread unemployment, profound psychological distress, and systemic educational losses. These escalating costs have rendered long-term adherence to stringent distancing increasingly untenable, compelling policymakers to explore alternative strategies that might preserve public health gains while restoring socioeconomic activity. Expanded diagnostic testing has emerged as a particularly promising candidate, theoretically enabling early case identification, rapid contact tracing, and targeted isolation. Nevertheless, the quantitative capacity of testing to substitute for—or merely supplement—broad social distancing mandates remains inadequately characterized, particularly in densely populated urban environments where transmission dynamics are complex. New York City, the pandemic's early epicenter in the United States, presents an especially critical case study for examining this trade-off, given its extreme population density, extensive public transit utilization, and evolving policy landscape. In this study, we develop a compartmental epidemiological model calibrated to NYC-specific epidemiological and mobility data to investigate whether enhanced testing regimes can sufficiently ease social distancing measures while preventing healthcare system overload and secondary epidemic waves. By simulating various scenarios encompassing differential testing scales, frequencies, and population coverage alongside graded relaxation of mobility restrictions, we assess the future trajectory of COVID-19 in NYC and identify critical thresholds for test-driven mitigation strategies. Our findings aim to provide actionable, evidence-based policy frameworks for balancing epidemic control with socioeconomic restoration in large metropolitan contexts.

title: Corporate Governance and Firms Financial Performance in the United Kingdom
text:
This study examines the relationship between corporate governance mechanisms and firm financial performance among publicly listed companies in the United Kingdom. Against the backdrop of successive revisions to the UK Corporate Governance Code and heightened regulatory scrutiny following the 2008 financial crisis and subsequent corporate governance reforms, understanding the efficacy of internal governance structures remains critical for academics, policymakers, and practitioners. Drawing on agency theory and stakeholder theory, this paper investigates how specific board attributes and ownership characteristics influence both accounting-based and market-based performance outcomes in one of the world’s leading capital markets. Utilizing a sample of non-financial firms listed on the main market of the London Stock Exchange over the period 2010–2022, we employ panel data regression techniques with firm fixed effects and system Generalized Method of Moments estimators to analyze the effects of board size, board independence, Chief Executive Officer duality, audit committee diligence, board gender diversity, and institutional ownership concentration on return on assets, return on equity, and Tobin’s Q.

The empirical findings reveal a statistically significant positive association between board independence and firm performance, suggesting that a higher proportion of non-executive directors enhances monitoring quality and strategic oversight. Conversely, CEO duality is found to exert a negative influence on accounting profitability, consistent with predictions derived from the entrenchment hypothesis. Board gender diversity demonstrates a significant positive relationship with market valuation, while board size exhibits an inverted U-shaped association with performance, indicating that excessively large boards incur coordination and decision-making inefficiencies. Furthermore, concentrated institutional ownership is positively related to both accounting returns and market valuations, underscoring the pivotal monitoring role played by long-term institutional investors.

These results remain robust across alternative model specifications, endogeneity treatments using instrumental variables, and subsample analyses segregated by firm size and industry classification. The study contributes to the corporate governance literature by providing contemporary UK-specific evidence that bridges the gap between compliance with governance codes and realized economic outcomes. Our findings offer practical implications for policymakers and board practitioners seeking to optimize governance architectures, supporting recent regulatory emphases on board independence and diversity while cautioning against unchecked board expansion and concentrated executive power.

title: Learning Undirected Graphs in Financial Markets
text:
Financial markets constitute complex adaptive systems where assets interact through intricate webs of latent dependencies. Understanding the underlying network structure among financial instruments is essential for risk management, portfolio allocation, and the detection of systemic vulnerabilities. Undirected graphical models provide a principled framework for representing conditional independence relationships, offering a sparse and interpretable characterization of market interconnectedness that distinguishes direct linkages from spurious correlations.

Despite their theoretical appeal, learning such graphs from financial data presents distinct methodological challenges. Market dynamics are inherently high-dimensional, non-stationary, and contaminated by heavy-tailed noise, complicating the recovery of meaningful dependency structures from limited historical observations. Traditional correlation-based approaches often conflate direct and indirect relationships, yielding dense networks that obscure true economic mechanisms and amplify estimation error.

This paper addresses these challenges by developing methodology for learning undirected graphs tailored to the stylized features of financial time series. We propose robust approaches for estimating sparse inverse covariance structures while accommodating the temporal dependence and distributional complexities prevalent in market data. By bridging statistical graph learning with financial econometrics, our framework enables more reliable discovery of cross-asset dependencies and supports enhanced network-based decision-making in investment and regulatory contexts.

title: Why are Developers Struggling to Put GDPR into Practice when Developing Privacy-Preserving Software Systems?
text:
Our study surveyed 127 software developers and 34 privacy officers across 42 organizations. We found that 78% of respondents reported significant difficulties translating GDPR requirements into concrete technical specifications. Specifically, 63% cited Article 25 (Data Protection by Design and by Default) as particularly challenging to operationalize, with developers noting that phrases such as "state of the art" and "appropriate safeguards" lack measurable technical boundaries or engineering benchmarks.

When asked about implementation barriers, 71% identified ambiguity in legal language as the primary obstacle, while 58% pointed to insufficient tooling for verifying privacy controls. For instance, only 19% of teams reported having automated mechanisms to validate the right to erasure (Article 17) across distributed backup systems, and 44% admitted to retaining residual personal data in unidentified logs despite implementing manual deletion procedures. Additionally, 56% expressed uncertainty about whether pseudonymization techniques met GDPR standards for anonymization.

Organizational factors exacerbated these technical challenges. In 67% of cases, legal and engineering teams used conflicting terminology, leading to misinterpreted requirements that required an average of 3.2 revision cycles per feature. Furthermore, 52% of developers stated they received no formal GDPR training, relying instead on ad-hoc online resources. Time constraints compounded these issues: 81% reported that privacy considerations were routinely deprioritized under tight release schedules, resulting in 39% admitting to shipping features without completing required privacy impact assessments.

Cross-border development added further complexity. Teams operating across multiple jurisdictions reported that reconciling GDPR with other regulatory frameworks consumed an average of 14.3 hours per sprint. Collectively, these findings indicate that developer struggles stem not from disinterest but from systemic gaps between legal abstraction and technical implementation, compounded by organizational silos, inadequate tooling, and persistent resource constraints.

title: Uncovering the structure of clinical EEG signals with self-supervised learning
text: This work presented a self-supervised learning framework for uncovering the latent structure inherent in clinical EEG signals without relying on scarce manual annotations. By leveraging large-scale unlabeled recordings, our approach learns rich, generalizable representations that capture physiologically relevant patterns, including transient events and background dynamics, which are often obscured by the high dimensionality, non-stationarity, and noise characteristic of scalp recordings. Through systematic analysis, we demonstrated that these learned representations cluster into semantically meaningful structures and transfer effectively to downstream clinical tasks, outperforming both traditional hand-crafted features and fully supervised baselines in critical applications such as patient stratification and anomaly detection. Our results suggest that self-supervised pre-training can substantially mitigate the data inefficiency and annotation bottleneck that have historically limited deep learning applications in clinical electrophysiology. While this study focused on single-center recordings, future work should extend these methods to diverse multi-center cohorts, incorporate multimodal clinical data, and explore hierarchical architectures that explicitly model long-range temporal dependencies across multiple scales. By unlocking structure from abundant unlabeled data, self-supervised learning offers a promising and scalable path toward realizing the full clinical potential of EEG as an interpretable, data-efficient biomarker in neurological care.

title: Digital image processing to detect subtle motion in stony coral
text: Stony corals exhibit subtle micromorphological movements that reflect their physiological state, yet these motions often remain imperceptible to the unaided eye and are overlooked by conventional visual survey techniques. This study presents a non-invasive digital image processing framework to detect and quantify minute motions in scleractinian corals as a sensitive indicator of coral health and environmental stress. Using high-resolution time-lapse imaging sequences acquired under controlled laboratory and in situ reef conditions, we implemented an integrated computational pipeline comprising rigid image registration for geometrical stabilization, adaptive temporal noise filtering, and phase-based motion magnification to amplify imperceptible displacements falling below the nominal pixel resolution. Subpixel optical flow analysis was subsequently applied to extract spatiotemporal motion vectors across coral polyp tissues and coenosarc surfaces over extended durations. Our results demonstrate that the proposed method successfully resolves micron-scale cyclic motions associated with polyp expansion, tissue pulsation, and passive sediment-shedding behaviors that are completely invisible in raw video footage. Comparative physiological experiments revealed distinct motion signatures between healthy colonies and those undergoing early thermal stress, with stressed specimens exhibiting significantly reduced oscillation amplitude and markedly altered periodicity in tissue movement before visible bleaching appeared. The algorithm maintained robust performance under natural turbidity and diurnally varying illumination, improving signal-to-noise ratios by over an order of magnitude relative to unprocessed sequences. These findings establish that computational motion analysis of stony corals can serve as a powerful, non-contact biosensor for the early detection of sublethal stress responses, offering a cost-effective and scalable complement to molecular and physiological monitoring in both reef conservation programs and experimental marine biology.

title: Inference of a universal social scale and segregation measures using social connectivity kernels
text:
The quantification of social structure and spatial segregation represents a foundational challenge across sociology, urban science, and computational social science. Conventional segregation indices, including the Dissimilarity Index and Theil's entropy measure, have served as standard tools for demographic analysis for decades. Nevertheless, these metrics predominantly depend on predefined administrative boundaries and arbitrary spatial units, thereby failing to capture the continuous, multi-scale nature of social interactions that characterize contemporary urban environments. Furthermore, the lack of a universal, data-driven metric for social distance complicates cross-contextual comparisons of residential patterns and social cohesion across diverse metropolitan systems.

Recent advances in geospatial big data and network science have enabled unprecedented fine-grained analyses of human mobility and social connectivity. Yet existing approaches frequently treat spatial proximity and social affinity as decoupled processes, neglecting their inherent co-evolutionary dynamics and the kernel-like decay of interaction probability with distance. To bridge this gap, we present an integrated framework based on social connectivity kernels to simultaneously infer a universal social scale and construct boundary-free segregation measures. By modeling social interaction intensity as a continuous kernel function of both geographic and latent social distances, we derive a scale parameter that emerges organically from empirical interaction patterns rather than exogenous administrative definitions. The resulting segregation measures generalize classical indices while remaining robust across heterogeneous urban contexts. This work establishes a principled, mathematically consistent foundation for comparative segregation analysis, with direct implications for urban planning and policies aimed at fostering spatial equity and social integration.

title: Deep Learning with Heterogeneous Graph Embeddings for Mortality Prediction from Electronic Health Records
text: Accurate mortality prediction from electronic health records (EHRs) is critical for early clinical intervention and resource allocation, yet it remains challenging due to the high dimensionality, temporal irregularity, sparsity, and complex relational structure inherent in longitudinal patient data. Conventional deep learning approaches often treat EHRs as sequential feature vectors or homogeneous graphs, overlooking the rich semantic distinctions among diverse medical entities—such as diagnoses, medications, procedures, and laboratory tests—and their intricate, time-varying interactions. To address these limitations, we propose a novel deep learning framework that leverages heterogeneous graph embeddings for inpatient mortality prediction. Our method constructs a temporal heterogeneous graph from structured EHR data, wherein nodes represent distinct entity types and edges capture semantic relations including temporal adjacency, co-occurrence, prescription, and hierarchical dependencies. We introduce a hierarchical graph attention network that learns context-aware embeddings by propagating information across heterogeneous neighborhoods via type-specific linear transformations, metapath-based aggregation, and multi-head attention mechanisms. This enables the model to jointly encode longitudinal patient trajectories and global clinical knowledge without manual feature engineering. We evaluate our approach on the publicly available MIMIC-III dataset, comparing it against strong baselines including recurrent neural networks, Transformer-based sequence models, and homogeneous graph neural networks. Experimental results demonstrate that our model achieves state-of-the-art performance, with statistically significant improvements of up to 4.8% in area under the receiver operating characteristic curve and 7.2% in area under the precision-recall curve over the best baseline. Furthermore, qualitative analysis of attention distributions reveals that the learned weights align with clinically meaningful patterns, such as acute organ dysfunction and abnormal laboratory trends, thereby enhancing model interpretability and trustworthiness. These findings suggest that explicitly modeling EHR data as heterogeneous graphs offers a powerful paradigm for clinical prediction tasks and may facilitate more reliable, transparent decision support in intensive care settings.

title: Predicting COVID-19 Pneumonia Severity on Chest X-ray with Deep Learning
text:
The COVID-19 pandemic placed unprecedented strain on healthcare systems worldwide, with viral pneumonia representing the primary driver of severe illness, respiratory failure, and mortality. Rapid and accurate assessment of disease severity upon hospital admission is critical for guiding treatment decisions, predicting clinical outcomes, and allocating limited intensive care resources effectively. Chest X-ray (CXR) remains one of the most widely available and frequently used imaging modalities for evaluating pulmonary involvement in COVID-19, offering a rapid, cost-effective, and easily repeatable alternative to computed tomography in acute care settings.

However, manual interpretation of CXRs is inherently subjective and susceptible to substantial inter-observer variability, particularly during surges in patient volume when experienced radiologists are in short supply. Conventional severity scoring systems require significant human effort and may overlook subtle radiographic patterns that precede clinical deterioration. Recent advances in deep learning have demonstrated remarkable potential in medical image analysis, enabling automated detection, quantification, and risk stratification from routine imaging with performance comparable to or exceeding human experts in specific tasks.

In this study, we develop and validate a deep learning framework to predict COVID-19 pneumonia severity directly from frontal chest X-rays. By leveraging large-scale, multi-institutional datasets and state-of-the-art convolutional neural network architectures, our approach aims to provide an objective, reproducible, and scalable tool for early severity assessment, ultimately supporting clinical decision-making and triage in emergency departments and resource-limited environments.

title: Digital Currency and Economic Crises: Helping States Respond
text:
Our panel dataset covers 42 economies that introduced retail central bank digital currencies (CBDCs) between 2019 and 2023, compared against a control group of 38 states relying on conventional monetary tools. During acute crisis episodes—defined as sovereign-debt stress or inflation shocks exceeding 8% annually—CBDC-adopting states demonstrated measurably faster stabilization. Within six months of deploying direct fiscal transfers via programmable digital wallets, recipient states reduced average unemployment by 2.3 percentage points (from a baseline mean of 9.1%), versus a 0.7-point reduction in the control group. Inflation volatility, measured by the standard deviation of monthly CPI changes, fell by 34% in the treatment group compared with 12% in non-adopters, while sovereign bond spreads narrowed by an average of 58 basis points and currency-substitution pressures declined markedly.

Transmission speed emerged as the primary channel. Emergency disbursements reached households in a median of 3.8 hours through tokenized CBDC rails, whereas conventional banking channels required a mean of 11.5 days. Consequently, the fiscal multiplier for digital-transfer states averaged 1.48 during the 0–12 month window, significantly higher than the 0.92 multiplier observed in analog-system states (p < 0.05). Real GDP contraction was likewise attenuated, with CBDC economies shrinking by 1.2% peak-to-trough versus 3.4% in the control sample.

Nevertheless, the benefits were contingent on pre-existing digital infrastructure.
