States with baseline internet penetration below 65% saw attenuated welfare gains, with multipliers dropping to 1.09 and administrative costs consuming 14% of transfer values—more than triple the 4.2% cost ratio in high-connectivity economies. These findings indicate that digital currency can materially enhance crisis response capacity, yet its efficacy remains bounded by digital inclusion thresholds.

title: Getting to Know One Another: Calibrating Intent, Capabilities and Trust for Human-Robot Collaboration
text: Effective human-robot collaboration demands more than technical interoperability; it requires the gradual construction of mutual understanding. In this paper, we have argued that successful teaming depends on the continuous calibration of three interdependent dimensions: intent, capabilities, and trust. By treating these elements as bidirectional properties rather than unilateral robot features, we move beyond traditional models that cast the robot as either a passive tool or an omniscient agent. Instead, we position both partners as adaptive entities that must learn to read, respect, and update their mental models of one another over time. Our framework suggests that explicit communication of goals, transparent signaling of competence boundaries, and dynamic trust management are not isolated system features but jointly constitute the foundation of resilient, human-centered collaboration. As robots transition from controlled environments into complex social and industrial settings where ambiguity is inevitable, the ability to align expectations and recover gracefully from misalignment becomes paramount. We contend that calibration should not be viewed as a one-time registration step, but as an ongoing dialogic process that unfolds across interaction histories. Future work must therefore develop formal methods for real-time calibration, account for stable and situational individual differences among human partners, and investigate how repeated encounters reshape the dynamics of intent, capability, and trust. Ultimately, getting to know one another is not a preliminary phase to be completed before work begins, but the very work of collaboration itself. Only by embracing this reciprocity can we realize partnerships in which humans and robots complement each other not merely through what they do, but through a shared understanding of why, within what limits, and with what confidence they can rely on one another.

title: Mixed-Reality Robotic Games: Design Guidelines for Effective Entertainment with Consumer Robots
text: The increasing availability and affordability of consumer robots have opened new opportunities for interactive entertainment, yet designing compelling gaming experiences that seamlessly blend physical robots with mixed-reality (MR) environments remains a significant challenge. While both robotics and MR have matured independently, effective integration requires addressing unique interaction dynamics, spatial alignment, and user engagement factors that differ from conventional video games or purely physical robot interactions. This paper presents a comprehensive set of design guidelines for developing mixed-reality robotic games that leverage consumer-grade robots to create immersive and enjoyable entertainment experiences. Through a systematic literature review, iterative prototyping of three distinct MR robotic games, and a user study involving 48 participants, we identified critical design dimensions including physical-digital synchronization, robot embodiment and behavior design, user agency and safety perception, gameplay pacing, and adaptive difficulty. Our findings reveal that successful MR robotic games must balance the robot's physical constraints with virtual augmentation, utilize spatial audio and visual feedback to bridge the real-virtual gap, and maintain coherent narrative embodiment to sustain player immersion. We synthesize these insights into eight evidence-based design guidelines, offering practical recommendations for game designers and HCI researchers. This work contributes a foundational framework for entertainment applications with consumer robots, highlighting how thoughtful MR integration can transform standalone robotic toys into rich, socially engaging gaming platforms. The guidelines are intended to inform future development and inspire novel hybrid experiences at the intersection of robotics, mixed reality, and interactive entertainment.

title: Teaching Economics with Interactive Browser-Based Models
text:
The teaching of economics has long grappled with a fundamental pedagogical challenge: how to convey abstract theoretical constructs—such as market equilibrium, comparative statics, and strategic interactions—in ways that foster deep conceptual understanding. Traditional instruction, dominated by static diagrams and algebraic derivations, frequently positions students as passive recipients rather than active explorers of economic mechanisms. This pedagogical mode risks obscuring the inherently dynamic nature of behavioral adjustments and systemic feedback loops central to economic reasoning.

While various computational tools have been introduced to ameliorate these limitations, many require costly licenses, steep learning curves, or local installation, creating barriers to scalable adoption across diverse educational contexts. The maturation of modern web standards, however, offers an underexploited alternative. Browser-based interactive models, built upon lightweight, open-web technologies such as HTML5 and JavaScript, enable instantaneous, device-agnostic access to dynamic simulations without proprietary dependencies. These environments facilitate “learning by doing” by allowing users to manipulate exogenous variables and immediately observe endogenous responses, bridging the gap between mathematical formalism and economic intuition. Despite this potential, the systematic integration of such tools into economics curricula remains sparse in the extant literature, and evidence regarding their efficacy in non-Western higher-education settings remains limited.

This paper addresses this gap by examining the design, implementation, and pedagogical impact of interactive browser-based models in undergraduate economics courses. By embedding manipulable visualizations directly into the instructional workflow, educators can transform passive content delivery into guided discovery, enabling students to perturb parameters, test hypotheses, and intuitively grasp counterintuitive causal relationships that static expositions often fail to convey. Drawing on implementation experiences from university courses in China, we demonstrate how low-cost, web-deployable simulations can substantively enhance student engagement, classroom interactivity, and conceptual retention without imposing additional technical burdens on instructors or learners. The remainder of this article proceeds as follows. Section 2 reviews related scholarship. Section 3 outlines design principles. Section 4 describes classroom strategies and analyzes student feedback. Section 5 discusses implications, and Section 6 concludes.

title: Estimation of number of runaway electrons per avalanche in Earth's atmosphere
text: Runaway electron avalanches in strong atmospheric electric fields are central to understanding high-energy phenomena associated with thunderstorms, including terrestrial gamma-ray flashes (TGFs) and gamma-ray glows. Despite extensive modeling of the avalanche multiplication factor and characteristic energy spectrum, a direct quantitative estimate of the absolute number of runaway electrons produced in a single avalanche initiated by a single primary seed electron remains poorly constrained across the varying density and electric field conditions of Earth's atmosphere. In this study, we present a comprehensive numerical calculation of the runaway electron population per avalanche using a three-dimensional Monte Carlo model of relativistic runaway electron avalanches (RREA) self-consistently coupled with a realistic atmospheric density profile and sub-breakdown electric field configurations representative of mesoscale convective systems. We track the full cascade development from a single seed electron at altitudes ranging from sea level to 20 km, accounting for elastic scattering, ionization losses, and Moller scattering in dry air under standard atmospheric conditions. Our results demonstrate that the total number of runaway electrons per avalanche, N_RREA, scales exponentially with the potential difference encountered by the corresponding avalanche front, following N_RREA ~ exp(αΔz), where α is the Townsend-like ionization coefficient modified for relativistic electrons. For typical thundercloud electric fields of 0.5–1.0 MV m⁻¹ at altitudes of 5–10 km, a single avalanche yields between 10⁴ and 10⁸ runaway electrons over propagation distances of 1–3 km, with the upper bound approaching 10¹² electrons in extreme fields conducive to TGF production. We further show that atmospheric density gradients significantly modulate avalanche growth, causing a rapid termination of multiplication at lower altitudes where collisional energy losses dominate. These estimates provide a critical link between microscopic discharge processes and macroscopic observable emissions, offering quantitative constraints for models of TGF source mechanisms and the role of runaway breakdown in lightning initiation.

title: Synthesis of Supervisors Robust Against Sensor Deception Attacks
text:
Cyber-physical systems rely on networked sensors for supervisory feedback, yet this dependency exposes control architectures to sensor deception attacks. By falsifying measurement data, adversaries can induce unsafe plant behavior, threatening safety-critical infrastructures such as automated manufacturing and traffic networks. Although prior work has extensively studied attack detection and resilient estimation, the synthesis of supervisors that proactively guarantee specification enforcement despite compromised observations remains largely unexplored.

Traditional supervisory control theory presumes faithful sensor information, an assumption that fails under adversarial corruption. This paper addresses this gap by formalizing the robust supervisor synthesis problem against sensor deception attacks. We model attacks as bounded manipulations of the observed event sequence and derive necessary and sufficient conditions for the existence of robust supervisors. Furthermore, we present a synthesis procedure that ensures the controlled plant satisfies the desired safety specification even when sensor measurements are adversarially manipulated.

title: Overlapping-sample Mendelian randomisation with multiple exposures: A Bayesian approach
text: Applying the Bayesian overlapping-sample MR model to summary statistics for 142 genetic variants, we estimated independent causal effects of BMI, systolic blood pressure, and LDL cholesterol on type 2 diabetes risk using entirely overlapping genome-wide association study samples (n = 320,000). The posterior mean causal effect for BMI was 0.42 log-odds per standard deviation (95% credible interval [CrI] 0.18–0.67), with a Bayes factor of 12.3 against the null. For systolic blood pressure, the posterior mean was 0.15 (95% CrI –0.02 to 0.33), yielding inconclusive evidence (Bayes factor = 2.1). LDL cholesterol showed a posterior mean of 0.08 (95% CrI –0.05 to 0.22; Bayes factor = 1.4). The posterior median overlap-correlation was 0.74 (95% CrI 0.68–0.79). In contrast, a standard inverse-variance weighted analysis that ignored overlap produced a biased BMI estimate of 0.58 (95% CI 0.35–0.81) with artificially narrow intervals. Markov chain Monte Carlo convergence was satisfactory (R-hat < 1.01 for all parameters across four chains of 10,000 iterations). These results demonstrate that the proposed method yields well-calibrated posterior inference for multiple correlated exposures even with complete sample overlap, correctly widening credible intervals to reflect correlated instrument-exposure and instrument-outcome estimation errors.

title: Distributed Consensus of Nonlinear Multi-Agent Systems With Mismatched Uncertainties and Unknown High-Frequency Gains (Extended Version)
text: This paper has investigated the distributed consensus problem for a class of nonlinear multi-agent systems in the presence of mismatched uncertainties and unknown high-frequency gains. By combining Nussbaum-type gain functions with a distributed adaptive backstepping design, a decentralized consensus protocol was developed without requiring prior knowledge of the control directions or the bounds of mismatched uncertainties. It was rigorously proved that under an undirected connected communication graph, the proposed control scheme guarantees that all follower agents achieve consensus while ensuring the boundedness of all closed-loop signals. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that the detrimental effects of unknown high-frequency gains and mismatched nonlinearities can be effectively compensated via local neighbor-based interactions. Simulation results further validated the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed approach. Future research will be devoted to extending the proposed methodology to directed communication topologies, switching networks, and more general multi-agent systems subject to output constraints and actuator faults.

title: Evolutionary dynamics of cryptocurrency transaction networks: An empirical study
text: The rapid proliferation of cryptocurrencies has fundamentally transformed digital finance, with blockchain systems generating massive, publicly accessible transaction records. These records naturally form complex networks where nodes represent addresses and edges capture financial flows, offering a unique lens to examine economic behavior in decentralized ecosystems. While prior research has extensively studied static topological properties of cryptocurrency networks, the evolutionary dynamics underlying their long-term growth and structural adaptation remain insufficiently understood. This gap limits our ability to model network resilience, detect anomalous activities, and predict systemic risks in volatile crypto markets. To address this limitation, we present a comprehensive empirical study analyzing the temporal evolution of cryptocurrency transaction networks using large-scale on-chain data. By tracking network metrics and community structures over extended periods, we uncover distinct phases of network development and characterize the mechanisms driving topological changes. Our findings provide novel insights into the interplay between market events and network architecture, contributing to a deeper understanding of financial dynamics in blockchain-based economies.

title: Sizing of Movable Energy Resources for Service Restoration and Reliability Enhancement
text:
Power distribution networks are increasingly exposed to high-impact, low-probability events, including extreme weather and natural disasters, that cause prolonged outages and threaten critical infrastructure. While traditional restoration strategies rely primarily on network reconfiguration and manual repair, these approaches often result in significant delays before loads are re-energized, particularly in remote or severely affected areas. Movable energy resources (MERs)—such as mobile emergency generators, truck-mounted battery energy storage systems, and portable renewable generation units—have emerged as flexible, rapidly deployable alternatives capable of supplying temporary power to critical loads and bridging the gap until permanent repairs are completed. By physically transporting energy to the point of need, MERs offer distinct advantages in enhancing distribution system resilience and reducing customer interruption durations beyond what stationary assets can provide.

However, the effective integration of MERs into distribution system planning introduces complex decision-making challenges, particularly regarding optimal sizing. Determining the appropriate capacity, quantity, and technology mix of movable resources requires carefully balancing capital and operational costs against expected reliability and resilience benefits. Oversizing leads to excessive investment and underutilized assets, whereas undersizing risks failing to restore priority loads during emergencies. The sizing problem is further complicated by the spatiotemporal dynamics of outages, travel time constraints, and the need for coordination with conventional restoration schemes. Existing planning frameworks typically treat energy resources as stationary, overlooking mobility dimensions that fundamentally alter cost-performance trade-offs in network hardening.

This paper addresses the strategic sizing of movable energy resources designed to support post-disturbance service restoration and enhance distribution system reliability. By explicitly modeling mobility characteristics, deployment logistics, and temporal availability of MERs, the proposed framework identifies optimal resource configurations that minimize outage costs while respecting budgetary and operational constraints. The subsequent sections present a comprehensive methodology for MER sizing, demonstrating how strategically dimensioned mobile assets can complement traditional infrastructure investments to create more adaptive and reliable distribution networks.

title: Custom Edge-Element FEM Solver and its Application to Eddy-Current Simulation of Realistic 2M-Element Human Brain Phantom
text:
The custom edge-element solver was validated on an unstructured tetrahedral mesh of the human head comprising 2,047,832 elements and 3,142,685 edges. At 64 MHz, the iterative solver converged in 87 iterations of preconditioned BiCGSTAB (ILU(1)) to a relative residual below 1e-8, requiring 4.2 minutes per excitation and a peak memory footprint of 12.4 GB on a single workstation. The discrete system contained 3.1 million degrees of freedom with an average of 32 nonzeros per row. A direct MUMPS solution on a 512,000-element reference mesh agreed within 0.9% in the L2-norm of the magnetic field, confirming implementation correctness. The Nédélec edge basis suppressed spurious modes; the divergence-free residual remained below 2.3e-12 throughout the domain.

Within the realistic brain phantom, peak induced current density reached 3.18 A/m² in the cerebrospinal fluid and 0.74 A/m² in cortical grey matter, while dropping to 0.21 A/m² in white matter. The volume-averaged specific absorption rate was 0.041 W/kg, with a 95th-percentile value of 0.089 W/kg and a maximum of 0.15 W/kg near the nasal cavity. Magnetic field perturbations at the cortical surface exhibited a maximum deviation of 5.7% from the incident homogeneous field. Relative to a nodal scalar-potential formulation on an equivalent mesh, the edge-element approach reduced the L2 error by 18% in high-conductivity regions and eliminated non-physical oscillations at tissue interfaces. Weak-scaling tests demonstrated near-linear complexity from 500,000 to 2,000,000 elements. These findings demonstrate that the proposed solver achieves experimentally viable accuracy and computational efficiency for high-resolution eddy-current analysis in anatomically detailed human models.

title: Analysis of Safe Ultrawideband Human-Robot Communication in Automated Collaborative Warehouse
text: This paper presented a comprehensive analysis of ultrawideband (UWB) technology as a communication and localization solution for safe human-robot collaboration in automated warehouse environments. Our findings demonstrate that UWB's high temporal resolution, robustness to multipath fading, and centimeter-level positioning accuracy enable reliable real-time proximity detection and collision avoidance between mobile robots and human workers. The low-power, short-pulse characteristics of UWB satisfy stringent safety requirements while maintaining minimal interference with existing wireless infrastructure. Comparative evaluation against conventional RF alternatives confirms that UWB provides superior performance in dense, metallic, and highly dynamic industrial settings typical of modern fulfillment centers. Furthermore, the analysis reveals that integrating UWB-based safety envelopes with adaptive trajectory planning significantly reduces collision risks without compromising operational throughput or system latency. Future work should address scalability challenges associated with coordinating large fleets of autonomous mobile robots, mitigate potential interference from co-located UWB networks, and explore deeper integration of UWB with 5G and edge computing frameworks for enhanced system resilience and real-time decision-making. Ultimately, safe UWB human-robot communication represents a critical enabler for next-generation collaborative warehouses, harmonizing productivity demands with stringent occupational safety standards and paving the way for more adaptive, trustworthy automation ecosystems.

title: Robust Transient Stability Constrained Optimal Power Flow with Power Flow Routers Considering Renewable Uncertainties
text: The increasing penetration of renewable energy sources introduces significant uncertainties into power systems, posing severe challenges to transient stability and economic operation. This paper proposes a robust transient stability constrained optimal power flow (TSCOPF) model incorporating power flow routers (PFRs) to address renewable uncertainties. By leveraging the flexible power flow control capability of PFRs, the proposed model enhances both economic efficiency and transient stability margins under uncertain renewable generation. A robust optimization framework is formulated to guarantee operational feasibility against worst-case renewable fluctuations, while transient stability constraints are explicitly integrated via time-domain simulation. The resulting mixed-integer nonlinear programming problem is solved through an efficient decomposition algorithm. Case studies on modified IEEE test systems demonstrate that the proposed method effectively mitigates renewable uncertainty impacts, improves transient stability performance, and reduces operational costs compared to conventional TSCOPF approaches without PFRs.

title: Weather regimes linked to daily precipitation anomalies in Northern Chile
text: Northern Chile, encompassing the hyper-arid Atacama Desert, constitutes one of the driest environments on Earth. Although mean annual precipitation is negligible, sporadic daily rainfall anomalies can trigger destructive flash floods, disrupt critical mining operations, and cause significant ecological disturbances in fragile desert ecosystems. These precipitation events are fundamentally governed by large-scale atmospheric circulation, yet the specific weather regimes controlling daily rainfall variability across this region remain insufficiently characterized. Existing literature has predominantly emphasized seasonal to interannual drivers such as the El Niño–Southern Oscillation and the Madden–Julian Oscillation, while the synoptic-scale circulation patterns directly associated with day-to-day precipitation extremes have received comparatively limited scrutiny. Establishing a robust link between dominant weather regimes and localized precipitation anomalies is essential for improving sub-seasonal forecasting capabilities and advancing hydrological risk management in water-scarce regions. In this study, we employ an objective weather typing approach to identify recurrent daily circulation regimes over Northern Chile and quantify their relationship with observed precipitation anomalies. Our analysis aims to isolate the key synoptic configurations responsible for wet extremes and elucidate the underlying dynamic and thermodynamic mechanisms that drive regional rainfall generation in hyper-arid environments.

title: Security Analysis for Distributed IoT-Based Industrial Automation
text: The proliferation of Internet of Things (IoT) devices in industrial automation has catalyzed the transition toward decentralized, distributed control architectures that enhance operational flexibility and scalability. However, the convergence of information technology and operational technology in these environments introduces a broadened attack surface, exacerbated by resource-constrained endpoints, heterogeneous communication protocols, and stringent real-time requirements. This paper presents a comprehensive security analysis framework tailored for distributed IoT-based industrial automation systems. We systematically model the threat landscape across device, network, and application layers, identifying critical vulnerabilities inherent to edge-node deployments, mesh topologies, and cloud-edge orchestration paradigms. Through a combination of attack surface analysis, formal verification of coordination protocols, and empirical evaluation on a representative testbed, we quantify the exploitability of identified vectors and assess the efficacy of existing mitigation strategies. Our findings reveal that distributed consensus mechanisms and legacy interoperability gateways constitute the weakest links, susceptible to man-in-the-middle, firmware tampering, and denial-of-service attacks. Based on these results, we propose a layered defense architecture integrating lightweight cryptographic primitives, zero-trust network segmentation, and anomaly detection calibrated for industrial latency constraints. This work provides actionable insights for securing next-generation industrial ecosystems without compromising deterministic performance.

title: Clinical connectivity map for drug repurposing: using laboratory tests to bridge drugs and diseases
text:
Drug repurposing presents a compelling strategy to accelerate therapeutic discovery and reduce development costs, yet traditional computational approaches rely heavily on genomic, transcriptomic, or structural similarities that frequently fail to translate into clinical efficacy. Despite being among the most abundant and standardized data collected in routine care, laboratory test results—which capture integrated physiological and pathological states—remain underexploited as a systematic resource for connecting pharmacological perturbations with disease mechanisms.

To address this gap, we introduce a clinical connectivity map that uses laboratory test signatures as an intermediate layer to link drugs and diseases. By quantifying drug-induced alterations in clinical laboratory profiles and comparing them against the abnormal laboratory patterns characteristic of specific diseases, this framework identifies repurposing candidates whose therapeutic effects may reverse or compensate for pathological perturbations. The approach effectively positions routine laboratory measurements as a translational bridge between molecular targets and observable patient phenotypes.

Grounded in real-world clinical data, this strategy offers an interpretable, scalable complement to existing omics-based methods. By framing repurposing hypotheses within the familiar vocabulary of clinical laboratory medicine, it holds potential to expedite the identification of new treatments for diseases with substantial unmet medical needs.

title: Modeling, Vibration Control, and Trajectory Tracking of a Kinematically Constrained Planar Hybrid Cable-Driven Parallel Robot
text:
The proposed model was validated through finite-element simulation and experimental prototyping on a 2 m × 1.5 m testbed. Modal analysis revealed fundamental frequencies of 4.2 Hz, 7.8 Hz, and 12.3 Hz for the first three bending modes, closely matching the analytical predictions within an average deviation of 3.5%. Under active vibration control, the fundamental modal damping ratio increased from 2.1% to 8.7%, reducing end-effector residual oscillation amplitude by 76% and settling time from 1.85 s to 0.42 s when subjected to an impulse disturbance of 15 N at the moving platform.

For trajectory tracking, a Lissajous curve with 0.8 m amplitude was executed at a maximum velocity of 1.2 m/s and peak acceleration of 3.5 m/s². Without vibration compensation, the root-mean-square tracking error was 4.6 mm, peaking at 11.3 mm during high-acceleration segments. Implementation of the hybrid controller reduced the RMSE to 0.9 mm and the maximum absolute error to 2.1 mm. Cable tensions remained bounded between 18 N and 142 N, fully respecting the kinematic constraints and avoiding slackness. These results demonstrate that the integrated modeling framework and hybrid control strategy effectively suppress coupled vibrations while maintaining sub-millimeter-scale tracking precision under aggressive maneuvers.

title: An Algorithm to find Superior Fitness on NK Landscapes under High Complexity: Muddling Through
text:
We have introduced Muddling Through, a deliberately myopic and incremental search algorithm designed to navigate the severe ruggedness of NK landscapes when epistatic complexity is high. Conventional optimization strategies, including standard hill-climbing and elitist genetic algorithms, typically falter under large K because the landscape becomes dense with local optima and fitness correlations decay over vanishingly short distances. Our experimental results demonstrate that by embracing severely limited foresight and making small, contextually bounded adjustments without global coordination, Muddling Through consistently locates regions of superior mean fitness that elude more globally ambitious methods.

The central theoretical implication is at once counter-intuitive and pragmatic: under conditions of extreme epistatic complexity, the pursuit of optimal global structure is not merely computationally expensive but structurally futile. Instead, adaptive success follows from tolerating local ambiguity, retaining viable partial solutions, and permitting extended fitness plateaus while incrementally shifting allele configurations. This aligns with Lindblom’s original insight that disjointed incrementalism can outperform synoptic planning when problem environments overwhelm analytic capacity.

While our experiments confirm these advantages across standard NK parameterizations, several limitations suggest avenues for future work. The algorithm’s sensitivity to mutation scheduling and neighborhood size deserves tighter analytic characterization, and its behavior on landscapes with neutral networks or dynamic K remains unexplored. Integrating Muddling Through with sparse long-jump mutations or minimal memory mechanisms may further improve asymptotic performance without sacrificing its core robustness. Nevertheless, the present findings strongly suggest that when complexity is high, the path to superior fitness is rarely found through grand design, but through persistent, modest muddling.

title: Sustainable financing of permanent CO2 disposal through a Carbon Takeback Obligation
text: Achieving the goals of the Paris Agreement requires not only rapid decarbonization but also the permanent disposal of residual carbon dioxide emissions through geological storage, mineralization, or analogous durable sequestration methods. Despite growing recognition of the need for gigatonne-scale carbon dioxide removal (CDR), existing policy frameworks—particularly emissions trading systems and carbon taxes—have failed to generate the stable, long-term capital flows necessary to finance permanent CO2 disposal infrastructure at the required scale. This paper introduces and rigorously evaluates the Carbon Takeback Obligation (CTBO) as a distinct governance mechanism to address this financing gap. Operating as an extended producer responsibility scheme applied to the fossil fuel sector, a CTBO mandates that extractors, producers, and importers progressively take back and permanently dispose of a rising fraction of the CO2 embodied in their products, ultimately reaching 100% as economies approach net zero. Using integrated economic modeling and policy analysis across representative jurisdictions, we demonstrate that embedding the full cost of permanent disposal into the fossil fuel supply chain creates a dedicated, predictable, and durable revenue stream for CDR and sequestration technologies. This approach internalizes end-of-pipe climate costs without depending on politically volatile carbon prices or competing government budget priorities. Our findings show that a phased implementation—beginning with a low takeback fraction and escalating linearly—minimizes economic disruption, stimulates innovation in direct air capture and geological storage, and prevents free-riding by ensuring that responsibility for safe, permanent elimination of CO2 rests with polluters rather than the public. Critically, the CTBO establishes sustainable financing for permanent disposal independently of emissions trading schemes, thereby guaranteeing funding even where carbon markets remain weak. We conclude that the Carbon Takeback Obligation provides a scalable, equitable, and financially robust policy architecture essential for achieving climate neutrality through the complete and funded geological elimination of fossil carbon.

title: Modeling a Nonlinear Biophysical Trend Followed by Long-Memory Equilibrium with Unknown Change Point
text: Many biophysical processes exhibit a distinct two-phase pattern: an initial period of nonlinear accumulation or growth followed by a stable equilibrium with persistent fluctuations. Typical examples include tree-ring development, physiological adaptation, and ecosystem succession, where an organism or system initially follows a biologically governed trend before settling into a long-run stationary state. While nonlinear trends and long-memory dynamics have been extensively studied in isolation, their coexistence with an unknown transition point poses significant methodological challenges. Existing models typically assume either a known change point or separable short-memory equilibrium, thereby overlooking the gradual shift between deterministic biophysical growth and stochastic long-memory dependence. Failure to account for this structural break can lead to biased parameter estimates and misleading inferences about the persistence properties of the equilibrium phase. This paper proposes a unified modeling framework that captures a nonlinear biophysical trend followed by a long-memory equilibrium, treating the change point as an unknown parameter to be estimated jointly with the trend and memory parameters. By integrating flexible semiparametric trend specification with fractional integration techniques, we develop estimators and inference procedures, providing a rigorous and flexible tool for analyzing biophysical time series subject to structural evolution.

title: Finite-time stabilization in optimal time of homogeneous quasilinear hyperbolic systems in one dimensional space
text: This paper addresses the finite-time stabilization in optimal time of homogeneous quasilinear hyperbolic systems in one space dimension. We consider general systems written in Riemann invariants with nonlinear coupling terms and propose explicit boundary feedback laws that stabilize the equilibrium state in the shortest possible time. By exploiting the wave propagation speeds along characteristic curves and constructing an appropriate Lyapunov functional, we establish that the proposed controls achieve exact stabilization within a finite time that matches the theoretical lower bound dictated by the system's characteristic velocities. The analysis relies on a careful study of the nonlinear transport equations and their interactions at the boundaries. The robustness of the feedback laws with respect to small perturbations of the system parameters is also investigated. The results are illustrated through application to models arising in traffic flow and hydraulic engineering, demonstrating the practical relevance of the optimal stabilization time framework.

title: Market laws
text:
Markets have long served as the primary institutional mechanism for coordinating economic activity, allocating resources, and distributing wealth across societies. Yet the phrase “market laws” captures a fundamental duality that persists at the intersection of economics and jurisprudence: on one hand, it refers to the endogenous regularities—supply and demand, price elasticity, competitive convergence—that appear to govern exchange relationships independent of human design; on the other, it denotes the explicit legal frameworks—property rights, contract enforcement, antitrust statutes, and regulatory oversight—that constitute, constrain, and sometimes correct market outcomes. This dual character raises enduring questions about the extent to which markets operate as spontaneous orders governed by immutable economic forces, and the degree to which their function and legitimacy depend upon deliberately constructed legal architectures.

Despite extensive scholarship in both law and economics, these two dimensions of market laws are frequently analyzed in isolation. Economic models often treat legal institutions as exogenous parameters, while legal scholarship tends to focus on normative prescriptions without fully integrating the dynamic feedback loops between regulation and market behavior. The resulting gap obscures how statutory interventions reshape the very regularities they seek to channel, and how market evolution continuously generates pressure for legal adaptation. A coherent account of market laws must therefore transcend disciplinary boundaries to examine how endogenous economic tendencies and exogenous legal norms co-evolve, producing distinct institutional configurations across different sectors, jurisdictions, and historical periods.

This paper advances an integrated framework for understanding market laws as simultaneously descriptive and prescriptive phenomena. By tracing the interplay between core economic mechanisms—such as information asymmetry, network effects, and competitive entry—and the legal structures that modulate them, the analysis illuminates why certain regulatory regimes succeed in aligning private incentives with public welfare while others generate unintended distortions. In doing so, it contributes to a richer conception of market governance, one that recognizes legal rules not merely as external constraints upon pre-political exchange, but as constitutive elements that shape what markets are and how they function.

title: Challenging Eukaryogenesis: The Story of the Eukaryotic Ancestor
text: Phylogenomic reconstruction of the last eukaryotic common ancestor (LECA) from 347 concatenated gene families yields a composite genome of 12,403 protein-coding genes, of which 34% (4,217) lack detectable archaeal or bacterial orthologs under stringent reciprocal best-hit criteria. Contrary to canonical endosymbiotic models predicting an Asgard archaeal host, only 18% (2,233) of LECA’s informational genes trace to this source, whereas 41% (5,085) exhibit strongest affinity to diversified bacterial clades, and 11% (1,364) show chimeric phylogenetic signals incompatible with strict vertical inheritance. Metabolic profiling further reveals 89 complete enzyme chains in central metabolism, yet only 23 (25.8%) retain clear alpha-proteobacterial topology; 37 (41.6%) resolve within Chloroflexi or Planctomycetota lineages, and 29 display mosaic ancestry involving three or more donor phyla. Quantitative cellular complexity indices score LECA at 0.74 relative to modern Saccharomyces cerevisiae (1.0), implying an estimated 1.2 × 10^9 years of prior evolution that exceeds the 0.8 Gyr window permitted by microfossil constraints. These data indicate that phagocytosis capacity, cytoskeletal machinery, and spliceosomal introns co-emerged gradually across 600,000 generations rather than via singular symbiogenetic jumps. Consequently, the eukaryotic ancestor appears less a product of abrupt merger and more a lineage that accreted complexity through prolonged, multilateral gene flux prior to mitochondrial endosymbiosis.

title: A Horserace of Volatility Models for Cryptocurrency: Evidence from Bitcoin Spot and Option Markets
text: This study conducts a comprehensive horserace among competing volatility forecasting models for Bitcoin, utilizing both spot and option market data. Our findings indicate that option-implied volatility and high-frequency realized volatility models deliver superior forecasting accuracy relative to traditional GARCH-type specifications, particularly at shorter horizons. The informational content of the Bitcoin options market significantly enhances volatility predictions, although spot-based models—especially HAR-RV variants—remain competitive during periods of market stress and tail events. These results highlight the incremental value of incorporating derivatives data when modeling the unique distributional features of cryptocurrency returns, characterized by extreme kurtosis, persistent jumps, and structural breaks. For risk managers and derivative traders, the evidence suggests that combining option-implied and realized measures yields the most robust forecasts, offering practical guidance for dynamic hedging and option pricing decisions in highly speculative environments. While our analysis is confined to Bitcoin, the methodological framework readily extends to other digital assets. Future research should explore the performance of these models across alternative cryptocurrencies, during major regulatory shocks, and following the rapid integration of decentralized finance protocols. As cryptocurrency markets continue to mature, accurate volatility measurement remains essential for ensuring financial market stability and supporting informed participant behavior.

title: Learning under Invariable Bayesian Safety
text:
Safety-critical applications of machine learning demand rigorous guarantees that system behavior remains within safe operating regions despite environmental uncertainty and distributional shifts. Existing safety frameworks often rely on point estimates or frequentist bounds that may fail to adequately capture epistemic uncertainty, leading to overly conservative or potentially unsafe decisions when deployed in out-of-distribution scenarios. To address these fundamental limitations, this paper introduces the framework of Learning under Invariable Bayesian Safety, which systematically integrates Bayesian inference with invariant safety constraints to provide probabilistic guarantees that remain robust across varying operational conditions, model updates, and unforeseen environmental perturbations.

We formulate safety as a Bayesian posterior constraint, wherein the probability of violating safety specifications is bounded by a risk tolerance calibrated through the posterior distribution over model parameters. Central to our approach is the notion of invariance: we construct safety sets that are guaranteed to persist under the learned posterior dynamics, ensuring that once the system enters a safe region, it remains therein with high probability throughout the learning process regardless of subsequent posterior updates. We derive finite-sample convergence rates for the Bayesian safety posterior and establish sufficient conditions under which the invariant safety property is preserved during online learning and sequential decision-making. Our theoretical analysis provides provable bounds on the probability of safety violations under posterior sampling strategies, even as the model continues to adapt to newly collected data.

Empirical validation on simulated robotics and autonomous driving benchmarks with high-dimensional continuous state spaces demonstrates that our approach achieves tighter risk-calibrated safety margins compared to frequentist and worst-case baselines while avoiding the excessive conservatism that typically hinders exploration and performance. These results suggest that embedding Bayesian uncertainty quantification within invariant safety constraints offers a principled, scalable, and reliable pathway toward deploying learning-based systems in real-world safety-critical domains.

title: Social Engagement versus Learning Engagement -- An Exploratory Study of FutureLearn Learners
text: Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs) have democratized access to higher education, yet they continue to be plagued by high attrition and superficial participation. Learner engagement, a multidimensional construct central to understanding persistence and achievement in digital learning environments, is typically differentiated into learning engagement—reflecting cognitive, behavioral, and emotional investment in course content—and social engagement, which captures interaction within the learning community. Although these dimensions are often theorized as complementary drivers of sustained participation, their empirical relationship in MOOC contexts remains ambiguous and underexplored. FutureLearn, a prominent UK-based platform architected around social learning pedagogy, presents an ideal setting to interrogate this relationship, as its interface explicitly foregrounds discussion forums and peer interaction. Nevertheless, whether active social participation invariably accompanies deeper learning engagement, or whether learners navigate these modes independently following distinct motivational trajectories, is still poorly understood. Prior research has largely treated social and learning engagement as separate phenomena, employing disparate analytical lenses that obscure how they manifest and interact within a single platform ecosystem. Against this backdrop, the current study adopts an exploratory approach to examine the nexus between social engagement and learning engagement among FutureLearn learners. By triangulating behavioral trace data with self-reported measures, this research seeks to discern whether socially active learners demonstrate correspondingly high levels of learning engagement, or if a decoupling pattern exists. The findings are anticipated to yield contextualized insights into MOOC learner behavior and offer evidence-based recommendations for balancing social design with individual learning pathways.

title: Kinetic-controlled hydrodynamics for multilane traffic models
text: We present a novel multiscale framework for multilane vehicular traffic, termed kinetic-controlled hydrodynamics, which rigorously couples lane-specific kinetic descriptions with systems of macroscopic balance laws through dynamic, data-informed closure relations. Motivated by the heterogeneous dynamics of lane-changing maneuvers and the strongly anisotropic nature of multilane vehicular interactions, our approach employs a hierarchical domain-decomposition strategy in which the traffic state on each lane is represented by a second-order hydrodynamic system whose constitutive fluxes and non-equilibrium corrections are actively governed by an underlying Boltzmann-type kinetic equation. Lane-exchange mechanisms are modeled as nonlocal, velocity-dependent source terms derived from the integral collision kernel, thereby capturing the transient behavioral dynamics of vehicles executing both discretionary and mandatory lane changes across heterogeneous lane conditions. By means of a Chapman–Enskog expansion around lane-specific local equilibrium distributions that incorporate desired velocities, finite spacing constraints, and relative-velocity dependencies, we derive a closed, coupled system of anisotropic balance laws for mass and momentum on each lane. The resulting multilane model preserves strict hyperbolicity and yields a non-equilibrium pressure tensor that naturally encodes the velocity variance and correlation structures induced by microscopic lane-changing interactions. We establish the well-posedness of the coupled kinetic–hydrodynamic system and rigorously identify the asymptotic limit connecting the multilane

title: Investor Emotions and Earnings Announcements
text:
Earnings announcements represent among the most significant information events in financial markets, providing timely updates on firm performance and guiding investor expectations regarding future cash flows and risk. For decades, the efficient market hypothesis has provided the dominant framework for understanding price formation around these disclosures, assuming that investors process new information rationally and impound it instantaneously into asset prices. However, an expanding body of research in behavioral finance demonstrates that market participants are subject to systematic psychological biases, cognitive constraints, and affective influences that can distort economic decision-making. Emotions—ranging from optimism and excitement to anxiety and fear—shape how investors interpret news, assess uncertainty, and execute trades, suggesting that the market reaction to earnings news may not be a purely rational affair and that affective forces warrant careful scrutiny.

While a vast literature has documented the relation between earnings surprises, abnormal returns, and trading volume, far less attention has been devoted to the emotional undercurrents that accompany these fundamental disclosures. Investor emotions may serve as a critical transmission mechanism, amplifying immediate price reactions to unexpected earnings, attenuating the incorporation of complex information into prices, or contributing to well-documented anomalies such as post-earnings announcement drift. High-stakes quarterly disclosures create natural laboratories for studying affective responses because they concentrate attention, trigger uncertainty resolution, and frequently generate conflicting signals about firm prospects. Understanding whether and how emotional states mediate the market's processing of earnings news remains essential for accurately modeling short-run price dynamics and assessing the practical limits of market efficiency.

This study examines the interplay between investor emotions and earnings announcements by analyzing sentiment dynamics and market-based affective proxies during quarterly reporting windows. By connecting measures of investor emotion to the magnitude, volatility, and persistence of earnings-related returns, we aim to disentangle emotional overreaction from rational reassessment of firm value. Our findings contribute to the literature on behavioral corporate finance by highlighting emotions not merely as background noise, but as a substantive economic force in the pricing of fundamental information. The results carry important implications for investors seeking to avoid affect-driven trading errors, for managers aiming to understand market reception of their disclosures, and for regulators monitoring the stability of informationally intensive markets.

title: Network desynchronization by non-Gaussian fluctuations
text:
We investigated the impact of non-Gaussian fluctuations on the synchronization of coupled phase oscillators arranged on a random network of size N = 100 with mean degree ⟨k⟩ = 10 and coupling strength K = 2.0. Under Gaussian noise of intensity D = 0.3, the system maintained a robust steady-state Kuramoto order parameter of r = 0.82 ± 0.03. Replacing the noise with skew-normal fluctuations (skewness γ = 1.5, kurtosis κ = 7.2) of identical variance reduced r to 0.41 ± 0.05. Similarly, Lévy-alpha-stable noise with stability index α = 1.4 and scale parameter σ = 0.25 yielded r = 0.29 ± 0.08, indicating nearly complete desynchronization.

The desynchronization onset occurred rapidly across topologies. Gaussian noise produced a characteristic phase decorrelation time of τ_c = 48 ms, whereas the skew-normal and Lévy cases exhibited τ_c = 11 ms and 6 ms, respectively. The probability of fluctuations exceeding three standard deviations was 8.4% under the skew-normal distribution versus 0.27% for the Gaussian benchmark. Analysis of the phase-slip density revealed that these heavy tails generated intermittent large jumps: the skewed distribution produced 0.9 ± 0.1 phase slips per unit time compared with 0.12 ± 0.02 for Gaussian noise. These rare, large events fragmented coherent clusters, and the coupling K = 2.0 could not restore order on the event timescale.

Further increasing the skewness to γ = 2.0 while holding the variance fixed depressed the order parameter below the critical threshold r_c ≈ 0.35. Beyond this point the network could not regain macroscopic synchrony even when the noise variance was subsequently reduced by 40%. These results demonstrate that higher-order statistics—particularly heavy tails and asymmetry—dominate network coherence, implying that fluctuation models constrained solely by mean and variance substantially overestimate synchronization stability in neuronal and power-grid systems.

title: Inflation Dynamics of Financial Shocks
text:
This paper has examined the transmission of financial shocks to inflation dynamics, bridging the gap between macrofinancial literature and price-setting behavior. By integrating credit market frictions into a New Keynesian framework with heterogeneous firms, we have shown that financial disruptions generate protracted, non-linear effects on aggregate price dynamics that standard demand-side channels fail to capture. Our main findings indicate that adverse financial shocks tighten firms' borrowing constraints, raising marginal costs through working capital and precautionary pricing channels, thereby exerting upward pressure on inflation even amid contracting output. These supply-side financial pressures interact with monetary policy responses, creating a complex trade-off between inflation stabilization and financial stability that conventional Taylor-type rules may inadequately address.

The results carry important implications for monetary policy design and implementation. Central banks face a substantially more challenging environment when financial stress materializes, as the traditional output-inflation trade-off is amplified by credit market impairments and endogenous risk premia. A policy framework that systematically monitors credit conditions, liquidity strains, and corporate balance sheet health can improve inflation forecasts and reduce the risk of misidentifying the source of price pressures. Furthermore, our analysis suggests that macroprudential instruments may serve as complementary tools to mitigate inflation volatility originating from the financial sector, potentially easing the burden on interest rate policy.

Several limitations remain. Our model abstracts from longer-term structural changes in payment technologies, digital currencies, and labor market dynamics that may alter the pass-through of financial conditions to prices. Additionally, empirical identification of financial shocks remains challenging across different institutional and monetary policy regimes. Future research should explore the role of household heterogeneity, state-dependent nonlinearities in the Phillips curve under severe financial stress, and the international dimension of financial spillovers to domestic inflation. Understanding these mechanisms remains essential for designing robust policy responses in an increasingly financially integrated global economy.

title: Prediction of short and long-term droughts using artificial neural networks and hydro-meteorological variables
text: Drought prediction is essential for effective water resources management and disaster risk reduction. This study develops artificial neural network (ANN) models to predict short- and long-term droughts based on key hydro-meteorological variables. Monthly records of precipitation, temperature, evapotranspiration, and soil moisture were employed to forecast standardized drought indices across multiple time scales. Different ANN architectures were systematically trained, validated, and compared to determine optimal predictive configurations. Results indicate that the proposed models successfully capture drought temporal evolution and provide reliable forecasts for both short-term (3–6 months) and long-term (12–24 months) horizons. The integration of multiple hydro-meteorological inputs substantially enhances prediction accuracy relative to univariate approaches. Additionally, long-term projections demonstrate strong stability, offering valuable insights for strategic water planning. This research underscores the effectiveness of ANNs in drought early warning systems and highlights their practical utility for mitigating adverse impacts on agriculture, ecosystems, and socioeconomic sectors.

title: Decentralized Safe Reactive Planning under TWTL Specifications
text: The deployment of multi-robot systems in safety-critical applications, such as warehouse logistics and search-and-rescue operations, demands planning strategies that simultaneously satisfy complex temporal tasks and guarantee operational safety. Temporal logic formalisms, particularly Time-Window Temporal Logic (TWTL), provide expressive semantics for specifying time-bounded missions over finite horizons. However, existing TWTL-based planning approaches predominantly rely on centralized architectures, which suffer from poor scalability, excessive communication overhead, and vulnerability to single-point failures as the team size increases. Although decentralized strategies have been proposed to alleviate these limitations, most either lack reactive replanning capabilities essential for dynamic and partially observable environments, or fail to provide rigorous safety assurances during online execution. To address these challenges, this paper presents a decentralized safe reactive planning framework under TWTL specifications. By exploiting local information exchange and receding-horizon synthesis, each robot independently constructs executable plans that adhere to global TWTL requirements while reactively adjusting to environmental contingencies. The framework leverages finite-state abstractions and local coordination protocols to decouple global constraints into tractable subproblems. Furthermore, a formally guaranteed safety mechanism is integrated to ensure inter-robot collision avoidance and constraint satisfaction without centralized supervision. We establish theoretical guarantees on both mission completion and safety preservation, and validate the proposed approach through comprehensive simulations, demonstrating substantial improvements in scalability, reactivity, and robustness compared to centralized counterparts.

title: Masks and COVID-19: a causal framework for imputing value to public-health interventions
text: The effectiveness of non-pharmaceutical interventions against respiratory pathogens remains a cornerstone of public-health preparedness, yet evaluating their causal impact during emergencies is methodologically fraught. During the COVID-19 pandemic, mask mandates emerged as one of the most widely deployed and politically contested measures, generating observational data plagued by confounding, simultaneity bias, and heterogeneous compliance. We propose a unified causal framework to impute the counterfactual value of mask-related policies when randomized trials are infeasible, natural experiments are imperfect, and policy decisions must be made under uncertainty. Drawing on potential outcomes theory and directed acyclic graphs, we formalize the estimands required to distinguish the biological efficacy of masking from the policy effect of mandates, while explicitly modeling the causal pathways linking individual adoption behavior, community transmission dynamics, and socioeconomic modifiers. Our framework integrates three complementary robust identification strategies: difference-in-differences exploiting staggered mandate rollouts, synthetic control methods for jurisdiction-level comparisons, and negative-outcome control designs to detect unmeasured confounding. We apply this framework to a large-scale harmonized dataset of county-level mask policies, mobility patterns, and epidemiological SARS-CoV-2 surveillance data from the United States (2020–2022). Results indicate that naïve associations substantially overstate mandate effects by conflating endogenous adoption with policy exposure; after adjusting for time-varying confounders and spatial spillovers, mask mandates are associated with a 12–18% reduction in weekly case growth rates during periods of high community transmission, with negligible effects when baseline prevalence is low. Crucially, the causal value of the intervention varies by imputed compliance levels, fabric filtration efficiency, and concurrent ventilation standards, suggesting that policy valuation must be conditional on implementation context and population characteristics. This study demonstrates that explicit causal reasoning—rather than defaulting to raw correlations—enables more rigorous quantification of public-health intervention value under real-world constraints, providing a reusable template for evidence-based policy during future pandemics.

title: Projection methods for solving split equilibrium problems
text:
Equilibrium problems constitute a broad mathematical framework that unifies variational inequalities, convex optimization, and noncooperative games in a single formalism. Because of their wide applicability in economics, engineering, and operations research, equilibrium models have been extensively studied over the past decades. More recently, increasing attention has been devoted to split-type problems, in which the solution satisfies a condition in one space while its image under a given operator satisfies a related condition in another space. The split equilibrium problem, which links equilibrium conditions in distinct domains via a linear or nonlinear operator, generalizes several important problems including the split feasibility problem and the split variational inequality problem.

The inherent complexity of split equilibrium problems, especially when the feasible sets lack simple structure or the bifunctions are merely monotone, poses significant computational challenges. Classical approaches often rely on regularization or proximal point methods that require solving nontrivial auxiliary subproblems at each iteration. Projection methods, by contrast, offer an attractive alternative because they exploit metric projections onto feasible sets and typically demand only modest computational effort per step, provided the projections are computable. Consequently, developing efficient projection-type algorithms that converge reliably under mild assumptions has become an active research direction.

This paper is devoted to projection methods for solving split equilibrium problems. We investigate the convergence properties of iterative schemes that employ projections onto feasible sets and analyze their behavior under standard conditions on the bifunctions and the transforming operator. By establishing weak and strong convergence results without imposing overly restrictive assumptions, we provide a theoretical foundation for these methods.
