title: Causal inference methods for small non-randomized studies: Methods and an application in COVID-19
text:
We applied propensity score matching, inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW), and targeted maximum likelihood estimation (TMLE) to an observational cohort of N=78 hospitalized COVID-19 patients, of whom 31 received early corticosteroids and 47 received standard care. Measured baseline covariates, including age, body-mass index, C-reactive protein, D-dimer, and oxygen saturation, exhibited imbalance before adjustment (standardized mean differences up to 0.48) but were well balanced after propensity score matching (standardized mean differences <0.10 for all covariates).

Using 1:1 nearest-neighbor propensity score matching with a caliper of 0.2, the estimated average treatment effect (ATE) on 28-day mortality was a risk difference of −0.18 (95% confidence interval [CI]: −0.35, −0.02; p=0.031), favoring early corticosteroids. IPTW yielded a similar ATE of −0.16 (95% CI: −0.34, 0.03; p=0.092). TMLE, using a super learner ensemble for the outcome and treatment models, produced an ATE of −0.19 (95% CI: −0.36, −0.04; p=0.018), corresponding to a relative risk of 0.62 (95% CI: 0.41, 0.94) and an odds ratio of 0.45 (95% CI: 0.22, 0.91).

Doubly robust augmented IPTW estimated an ATE of −0.17 (95% CI: −0.33, −0.01). In prespecified subgroup analyses, patients aged ≥65 years demonstrated a larger absolute benefit (ATE = −0.28; 95% CI: −0.51, −0.05) than younger patients (ATE = −0.08; 95% CI: −0.29, 0.13), though the interaction was not significant (p=0.14). Sensitivity analyses using E-values indicated that an unmeasured confounder associated with both treatment assignment and mortality by a risk ratio of at least 2.1 could explain away the observed effect, but weaker confounding would not.

Across methods, point estimates consistently indicated reduced mortality with early corticosteroids, yet precision varied markedly with sample size. TMLE achieved the narrowest confidence intervals and lowest p-value, reflecting the efficiency gains of doubly robust estimation combined with data-adaptive machine learning. These findings demonstrate that modern causal inference techniques can produce stable, interpretable effect estimates in small non-randomized COVID-19 studies, though limited statistical power remains an important limitation.

title: Metamorphic Testing for Quality Assurance of Protein Function Prediction Tools
text: Protein function prediction tools are indispensable in modern biological research, yet their quality assurance is severely hampered by the oracle problem, where correct outputs are difficult or impossible to determine a priori. This paper has demonstrated that metamorphic testing provides an effective, systematic solution for validating such tools without requiring explicit oracles. By defining a comprehensive set of metamorphic relations tailored to the biological domain and the algorithmic properties of protein function predictors, we were able to automatically detect inconsistencies and potential faults in widely used software. Our experimental results confirm that metamorphic testing not only reveals subtle bugs that conventional testing methods frequently miss, but also offers a scalable and automated framework for continuous quality assurance in rapidly evolving bioinformatics pipelines. As protein prediction algorithms grow increasingly complex and are integrated into critical downstream biomedical applications, rigorous validation techniques become essential. We believe that integrating metamorphic testing into standard development and deployment practices will significantly enhance the reliability, robustness, and trustworthiness of computational biology software. Future work will extend our metamorphic relations to encompass multi-functional proteins, explore relations specifically designed for deep learning-based predictors, and generalize this methodology to other oracle-free problems in bioinformatics.

title: The irreducible control property in matrix groups
text: We investigate the irreducible control property for matrix groups acting on finite-dimensional vector spaces. A matrix group has this property if no proper closed subgroup leaves invariant a nontrivial subspace while preserving approximate controllability of the associated bilinear system. We establish Lie-algebraic criteria characterizing this property in terms of generators and their representation-theoretic behavior. For classical groups over algebraically closed fields, we prove that this property is generic among finitely generated subgroups with Zariski-dense orbits. Our approach combines geometric invariant theory, control theory, and the structure theory of linear algebraic groups. The main results yield effective algorithms to test irreducibility of control sets and reveal that any failure of this property is detectable through the existence of a rational invariant subspace. These findings extend classical results on transitive group actions and provide new insights into the geometry and topology of controllable matrix ensembles.

title: Pricing the Information Quantity in Artworks
text: The pricing of artworks has traditionally been examined through established hedonic attributes, including artist reputation, physical dimensions, and provenance. While these factors account for substantial price variation, they often neglect the informational content embedded within the work itself. Art serves fundamentally as a medium for communicating ideas, emotions, and cultural symbols, suggesting that the quantity of information conveyed may represent an underexplored determinant of market value. However, the relationship between information density and transaction prices remains theoretically ambiguous and empirically understudied. This paper addresses this gap by developing a framework to quantify visual and semantic information in artworks and investigating its impact on auction prices. Drawing on information theory and measures of aesthetic complexity, we hypothesize that greater information quantity enhances viewer engagement and perceived value, though potentially at varying marginal effects. Our findings contribute to the cultural economics literature by integrating information-based attributes into hedonic pricing models, offering novel insights into how content complexity shapes valuation in art markets.

title: An AI-powered blood test to detect cancer using nanoDSF
text: Early detection of cancer remains a formidable challenge in clinical oncology, as existing screening approaches are frequently constrained by invasiveness, prohibitive cost, or insufficient sensitivity for early-stage disease, creating an urgent need for minimally invasive population-scale diagnostics. Here, we introduce a transformative liquid biopsy platform that integrates nanoscale differential scanning fluorimetry (nanoDSF) with artificial intelligence (AI) to enable accurate, direct cancer detection from standard peripheral blood draws. Our methodology is grounded in the principle that malignancy induces systemic perturbations throughout the circulating proteome, yielding distinct thermal stability fingerprints and conformational alterations that remain invisible to conventional single-analyte biomarker assays. We performed high-throughput nanoDSF profiling on microliter-scale plasma specimens collected from a large, multi-cohort dataset encompassing healthy controls and patients spanning stage I–IV solid tumors, acquiring complex, high-dimensional thermal denaturation curves without requiring fluorescent labels, capture agents, or amplification steps. These intricate biophysical signatures were decoded by a deep learning pipeline that employed unsupervised feature extraction followed by supervised classification to discern subtle, cancer-associated protein stability patterns from normal physiological variation. The resulting AI-nanoDSF assay demonstrated exceptional diagnostic performance in independent validation cohorts, achieving high sensitivity and specificity for pan-cancer detection while simultaneously enabling accurate classification across diverse malignancies. Notably, the platform identified early-stage cancers with accuracy comparable to—or exceeding—established protein biomarkers, all within a rapid, cost-effective workflow requiring minimal sample preparation. Collectively, these findings establish nanoDSF coupled with machine learning as a powerful, minimally invasive strategy for cancer screening. By exploiting systems-level biophysical changes in blood, this technology lays the groundwork for clinically scalable, next-generation liquid biopsies designed for early detection, longitudinal therapeutic monitoring, and population-wide screening.

title: Few shot domain adaptation for in situ macromolecule structural classification in cryo-electron tomograms
text: Cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) enables the visualization of macromolecular structures within their native cellular environments at near-atomic resolution, yet automated classification of structural states in situ remains hindered by low signal-to-noise ratios, cellular crowding, and the missing wedge artifact. Although supervised deep learning has substantially advanced subtomogram analysis, these models typically demand large, densely annotated training datasets that are impractical to curate for every new specimen or imaging condition. Domain shifts arising from variations in sample preparation, microscope parameters, or reconstruction pipelines frequently degrade classifier performance, necessitating laborious re-annotation. Few-shot domain adaptation offers a compelling solution by transferring knowledge from a labeled source domain to a related target domain using only a handful of annotated examples, thereby bridging disparate experimental contexts without prohibitive data collection costs. In this work, we introduce a few-shot domain adaptation framework specifically designed for in situ macromolecule structural classification in cryo-electron tomograms. By learning domain-invariant feature representations and employing targeted alignment strategies, our method enables robust cross-domain generalization and accurate structural state identification with minimal supervised fine-tuning, accelerating systematic structural discovery in native cellular settings.

title: Coupling Functions in Neuroscience
text: We reconstructed coupling functions from intracranial recordings in 12 subjects during a working-memory task. The mean correlation between inferred and ground-truth phase response curves was 0.87 ± 0.06. Dynamical Bayesian inference yielded a normalized mean-square error of 0.12 ± 0.03, outperforming the Hilbert-transform baseline (0.31 ± 0.05; paired t-test, p < 0.001). Theta-gamma phase-amplitude coupling functions in the hippocampus showed a peak modulation index of 0.42 ± 0.08, significantly exceeding prefrontal values (0.19 ± 0.04; t(22) = 4.3, p = 0.0003). Cross-frequency coupling profiles were markedly asymmetric: the descending gamma phase elicited 34% stronger theta amplitude modulation than the ascending phase. In the sensorimotor network, pairwise coupling strengths ranged from 0.15 to 0.68 across 4–80 Hz, with the strongest directed connection observed from primary motor cortex to dorsal premotor cortex (0.68 ± 0.09). Global synchronization emerged once coupling exceeded a threshold of 0.24, matching the analytically predicted critical value for this network topology. Network-wide coupling entropy reached 2.4 bits, reflecting heterogeneous and non-uniform functional interactions. Pharmacological suppression of GABAergic inhibition via bicuculline infusion reduced mean coupling strength by 41% (from 0.46 ± 0.07 to 0.27 ± 0.05; n = 8 sessions, p = 0.002) and decreased the coupling function curvature by 0.15 rad⁻² across all electrode pairs. Time-resolved analysis further revealed that trial-by-trial coupling variability (CV = 0.18) covaried with reaction time (Pearson r = −0.52, p = 0.008). Surrogate testing confirmed that 94% of channels exhibited significant coupling (p < 0.01), whereas shuffled controls showed chance-level modulation indices of 0.03 ± 0.01. These results indicate that coupling functions capture fine-grained dynamical features—including phase-dependent asymmetries, directionality, and frequency-specific gating—that scalar metrics obscure, thereby offering a mechanistic bridge between synaptic interactions and macroscopic neural oscillations.

title: Heterogeneity Learning for SIRS model: an Application to the COVID-19
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has underscored the limitations of classical compartmental models that rely on homogeneous mixing and uniform epidemiological parameters. In particular, the Susceptible-Infected-Recovered-Susceptible (SIRS) framework, while essential for modeling respiratory diseases with reinfection potential, often fails to capture the pronounced heterogeneity in contact rates, susceptibility, and waning immunity observed across demographic, behavioral, and spatial subpopulations. To bridge this critical gap, we propose a novel heterogeneity learning framework that systematically augments the SIRS model with data-driven subgroup identification and adaptive parameter inference. Our method integrates mechanistic epidemiological principles with modern statistical learning by partitioning the population into latent or observed strata, each characterized by distinct transmission, recovery, and reinfection dynamics. Through regularized optimization techniques and gradient-based learning algorithms, we estimate stratum-specific contact matrices, time-varying recovery rates, and waning immunity parameters directly from high-resolution empirical incidence data, human mobility records, and demographic covariates. Applied to real-world COVID-19 surveillance datasets from multiple regions, the proposed heterogeneous SIRS model markedly improves short- and medium-term forecasting accuracy compared to the homogeneous baseline, successfully capturing asynchronous multi-wave patterns, regional outbreaks, and age-specific reinfection trends. The learned heterogeneity parameters further reveal critical disparities in transmission potential and effective reproduction numbers that remain entirely masked by aggregate models. These findings underscore the necessity of embedding data-driven heterogeneity learning into epidemic modeling frameworks to substantially enhance predictive validity, improve situational awareness, and inform the design of timely precision public health interventions, including targeted booster campaigns and adaptive mobility management strategies.

title: Anchored Causal Inference in the Presence of Measurement Error
text: Causal inference from observational data is fundamental to empirical research across the social, health, and behavioral sciences. Yet, measurement error in covariates, exposures, or outcomes remains a pervasive challenge that threatens the internal validity of causal estimates, often inducing attenuation bias, endogeneity, or spurious associations. Although numerous correction methods have been proposed in the econometrics and biostatistics literature, they typically rely on strong parametric assumptions, replicated measurements, or the availability of gold-standard instruments—requirements that are frequently untenable in real-world observational studies. This paper introduces an anchored causal inference framework that leverages carefully selected auxiliary variables, termed "anchors," to identify and correct for measurement error without imposing restrictive distributional assumptions. By integrating the anchor structure with modern causal identification strategies, we establish nonparametric identification results and develop robust estimators that accommodate both classical and nonclassical measurement errors. The proposed framework not only recovers consistent causal effects when key variables are imperfectly measured but also furnishes transparent diagnostic tools to assess the credibility of the underlying anchor assumptions. Through formal derivation and empirical illustration, we demonstrate that anchored causal inference provides a practical, reliable pathway to trustworthy causal conclusions when data are subject to measurement error.

title: Fixed-Time Nash Equilibrium Seeking in Non-Cooperative Games
text: This paper investigates distributed Nash equilibrium seeking in non-cooperative games with a rigorous emphasis on prespecified convergence guarantees. While existing continuous-time learning algorithms predominantly ensure asymptotic or finite-time convergence, the settling time in finite-time frameworks inherently depends on initial conditions, critically limiting predictability and performance certification in multi-agent systems. To resolve this fundamental limitation, we propose a novel fixed-time Nash equilibrium seeking algorithm that drives all agents' strategies to the unique Nash equilibrium within a uniformly bounded time regardless of their initial states. By integrating fixed-time stability theory with carefully designed nonlinear gradient-based dynamics, we derive tractable sufficient conditions guaranteeing fixed-time convergence for a broad class of strongly monotone games. A rigorous Lyapunov-based analysis establishes an explicit uniform upper bound on the settling time that is strictly independent of initial conditions. Furthermore, the proposed scheme operates in a fully distributed fashion, making it applicable to networked game settings where individual players access only local cost information and exchange data with neighbors over a connected communication graph. Numerical simulations conducted on a representative networked Cournot competition model corroborate the theoretical findings and clearly illustrate the fixed-time convergence properties of the proposed equilibrium seeking strategy.

title: Golden ratio algorithms with new stepsize rules for variational inequalities
text:
Variational inequalities provide a unified framework for problems in optimization, economics, and partial differential equations. Over the past decades, projection-based algorithms have been widely studied for their solution due to their simplicity and low computational cost. Recently, the golden ratio algorithm has emerged as an efficient scheme requiring only one projection per iteration, offering a notable advantage over extragradient-type methods for large-scale problems. By leveraging the golden ratio coefficient to secure convergence, this algorithm has proven effective for pseudomonotone variational inequalities in real Hilbert spaces and has attracted growing interest.

Nevertheless, the practical performance of the golden ratio algorithm is highly sensitive to the stepsize. Existing guarantees predominantly rely on a fixed stepsize bounded by the inverse of the Lipschitz constant, or on diminishing sequences that impair convergence speed. In many applications, however, the Lipschitz constant is unknown or expensive to estimate, severely restricting constant-stepsize implementations. Although adaptive strategies have been developed for other first-order methods, flexible stepsize rules tailored to the golden ratio framework remain scarce. This motivates the investigation of new stepsize mechanisms that enhance robustness without requiring prior knowledge of global Lipschitz constants.

In this work, we introduce self-adaptive stepsize rules for the golden ratio algorithm and establish their convergence for variational inequalities with pseudomonotone and Lipschitz continuous operators. The proposed stepsizes are updated dynamically using local information from previous iterates, allowing the algorithm to adapt automatically to the problem geometry. We prove weak convergence in infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces and demonstrate through numerical experiments that the new strategies significantly accelerate convergence compared with fixed-stepsize counterparts. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 recalls preliminary results. Section 3 presents the algorithm and convergence analysis. Numerical experiments are reported in Section 4, and Section 5 gives concluding remarks.

title: Having a Ball: evaluating scoring streaks and game excitement using in-match trend estimation
text: We applied a LOESS-based in-match trend estimator to 847 professional basketball games. The model identified scoring streaks—defined as sustained deviations from the expected margin—occurring in 68% of matches, with an average streak length of 4.2 minutes and a maximum of 11.3 minutes. Games featuring at least one streak of ≥6 minutes exhibited a 23% higher excitement index (μ = 7.8, σ = 1.2) compared to non-streak contests (μ = 6.3, σ = 1.5; p < 0.01). Trend volatility, quantified as the second derivative of the score-margin function, correlated strongly with viewer retention (r = 0.81). Notably, fourth-quarter streaks generated 34% greater excitement per unit time than first-quarter runs. Additionally, matches with multiple overlapping streaks produced a composite excitement score of 8.9, ranking in the 91st percentile of all observed games. These results suggest that in-match trend estimation effectively captures momentum dynamics and that scoring streaks are reliable predictors of subjective game excitement.

title: A comparative study of convolutional neural network models for wind field downscaling
text: This study presented a systematic comparative evaluation of convolutional neural network architectures for statistical downscaling of wind fields. Multiple CNN variants, including U-Net, ResNet, and super-resolution generative adversarial network generators, were rigorously assessed using high resolution reanalysis and observational validation datasets. Experimental results demonstrated that encoder-decoder architectures with skip connections consistently outperformed standard convolutional networks in capturing fine scale wind variability, topographic forcing, and coastal gradient features, yielding substantially improved structural similarity indices and reduced root mean square error at localized scales. Conversely, generative adversarial approaches produced sharper visual details and enhanced representation of extreme wind speed distributions but introduced occasional spatial artifacts and spectral distortions that may limit physical interpretability. These findings underscore the necessity of careful architectural selection in balancing deterministic accuracy with spatial fidelity for applications in wind resource assessment, turbine micrositing, and numerical weather prediction post processing. Despite these advances, limitations remain regarding generalization across complex terrain, sensitivity to training domain shifts, and computational constraints hindering real time operational deployment. Future research should prioritize hybrid physics informed frameworks, transfer learning across heterogeneous geographic regions, and the integration of temporal dependencies through recurrent or attention based spatiotemporal modules. This comparative framework establishes a reproducible benchmark to guide the selection, optimization, and operational implementation of deep learning strategies for mesoscale to microscale wind field modeling.

title: Model selection for ecological community data using tree shrinkage priors
text: High-dimensional, sparse, and overdispersed species abundance tables, together with complex dependence structures arising from shared evolutionary history, pose substantial statistical challenges in modern community ecology. When modeling how environmental gradients or experimental treatments shape multispecies assemblages, conventional variable selection methods typically treat taxa as independent predictors or responses, thereby ignoring the phylogenetic and functional relationships that govern trait similarity and co-occurrence patterns. This omission not only reduces predictive accuracy but also obscures biologically meaningful aggregation of responses along major lineages. To bridge this gap, we introduce a Bayesian model selection framework that harnesses tree shrinkage priors for ecological community data. Our approach embeds the correlation structure induced by a phylogenetic or taxonomic tree directly into the prior hierarchy, enabling adaptive information borrowing across related taxa while inducing sparsity at multiple resolutions. Specifically, we employ a global–local shrinkage strategy in which species-specific regularization parameters are smoothed along the tree topology via a latent Markov random field or fused-shrinkage mechanism. Consequently, closely related species receive similar penalization and are encouraged to enter the model jointly, whereas distant taxa can be differentially selected. The framework naturally accommodates multivariate abundance responses, variable dispersion, and zero-inflation through appropriate observation models. We develop efficient Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithms for full posterior inference and provide open-source software to facilitate adoption. Through extensive simulations spanning diverse tree shapes and signal sparsity levels, and through re-analysis of published microbiome and macroecological datasets, we demonstrate that the proposed method achieves superior out-of-sample prediction, more stable identification of environment-species associations, and improved power to detect aggregated lineage-level responses compared to standard lasso, ridge, and independent shrinkage priors. By formally integrating tree-structured dependencies into the selection process, this work offers ecologists a principled and computationally feasible tool for disentangling the drivers of community assembly from noisy, high-dimensional observations.

title: DeFi Protocols for Loanable Funds: Interest Rates, Liquidity and Market Efficiency
text: The rapid proliferation of decentralized finance (DeFi) has fundamentally reshaped financial intermediation, with protocols for loanable funds emerging as a critical infrastructure layer within the cryptocurrency ecosystem. Unlike traditional banking systems that rely on centralized credit assessment and discretionary rate-setting, DeFi lending platforms algorithmically determine interest rates through utilization-based models, introducing novel mechanisms for capital allocation and risk pricing without traditional counterparty relationships. Yet, the interplay between these algorithmic rate adjustments, liquidity dynamics, and overall market efficiency remains insufficiently understood, particularly during episodes of market stress, collateral liquidation cascades, and systemic liquidity crunches. This paper examines the structural features of leading DeFi lending protocols to analyze how their interest rate mechanisms influence liquidity provision, collateral stability, and cross-protocol price discovery processes. Leveraging high-frequency on-chain transaction data and drawing upon theoretical frameworks from monetary economics and market microstructure, we empirically investigate whether decentralized credit markets achieve informational efficiency and quantify how idiosyncratic liquidity shocks propagate across interconnected protocol boundaries. Our findings provide novel evidence on the conditions under which algorithmic lending markets enhance or impair financial stability, offering important implications for the design of resilient decentralized financial architectures and the regulation of permissionless credit systems.

title: Clinical connectivity map for drug repurposing: using laboratory tests to bridge drugs and diseases
text: Drug repurposing offers a cost-effective alternative to de novo drug development, yet systematic identification of new therapeutic indications remains challenging. While existing computational strategies predominantly rely on molecular signatures, the clinical manifestations of diseases and pharmacological effects of drugs are routinely captured through laboratory tests, representing an underexploited translational bridge between pathophysiology and pharmacology. Here, we present a clinical connectivity map that systematically links drugs and diseases through laboratory test perturbations. By integrating large-scale clinical laboratory data, drug-induced lab alterations, and disease-associated lab abnormalities, we construct a network where therapeutic candidates are identified as drugs whose lab signatures inversely match disease-specific profiles. We validate this framework by recovering established drug-disease pairs and predicting novel repurposing candidates across diverse therapeutic areas, with supporting evidence from electronic health records and clinical literature. Our results demonstrate that laboratory tests serve as robust intermediate phenotypes connecting drug action to disease mechanism, yielding a highly interpretable approach to computational repurposing. This lab-centric connectivity map not only accelerates the discovery of new indications for existing drugs but also grounds computational predictions in routine clinical measurements, facilitating transparent and seamless translation from bench-side algorithms to bedside applications.

title: Attainment of Herd Immunity: Mathematical Modelling of Survival Rate
text:
Herd immunity represents a fundamental pillar of epidemic control, wherein a sufficient proportion of a population acquires resistance—whether through vaccination or prior infection—to interrupt chains of disease transmission. Mathematical models have long served as indispensable tools for quantifying the thresholds required for herd immunity and for evaluating the impact of public health interventions. These frameworks enable researchers and policymakers to anticipate healthcare demands, allocate resources efficiently, and design targeted strategies during emerging and endemic infectious disease scenarios.

While conventional compartmental models predominantly emphasize transmission rates, contact patterns, and basic reproduction numbers, the role of survival rate in shaping herd immunity trajectories remains comparatively underexplored. Survival rate directly modulates population turnover, the accumulation of immune individuals over time, and the long-term stability of protected communities. Incorporating this demographic parameter into epidemiological models offers a more nuanced understanding of how mortality dynamics and population structure jointly influence the path to community-level protection.

This study develops a novel mathematical framework that explicitly integrates survival rate into herd immunity calculations. By examining the interplay between disease-induced mortality, natural demographic processes, and immunity acquisition, the model elucidates how survival probabilities affect threshold coverage levels and the temporal dynamics of epidemic resolution. The findings provide critical insights for refining public health strategies and intervention timelines aimed at achieving equitable and sustainable herd immunity across diverse demographic contexts.

title: Cryptocurrencies, Mainstream Asset Classes and Risk Factors - A Study of Connectedness
text:
The static total connectedness index (TCI) across the full sample stands at 58.3%, indicating that more than half of the forecast-error variance in the system is attributable to cross-market spillovers. Bond and real estate markets occupy intermediate positions, with total spillover indices of 42.7% and 39.4%, respectively. Cryptocurrencies exhibit pronounced asymmetric linkages with mainstream assets. Bitcoin emerges as a net transmitter of shocks, contributing 12.4% to the variance of global equities while receiving only 8.7% in return. Ethereum displays a similar profile but with lower magnitude, transmitting 9.1% to equity markets and receiving 7.3%. Intra-crypto connectedness is substantially higher: the pairwise spillover between Bitcoin and Ethereum reaches 45.2%, underscoring strong sectoral integration.

Among risk factors, the equity market factor dominates as a net source of systemic risk, with total directional outward spillovers of 34.1% against inward spillovers of 18.2%. The volatility risk factor transmits 22.5% of its forecast-error variance to the cryptocurrency complex, whereas the liquidity factor accounts for 15.3% of Bitcoin’s return variation. The term-premium factor shows a one-way transmission of 11.6% toward Bitcoin, yet receives virtually no feedback, confirming the unidirectional nature of yield-curve stress. Conversely, Bitcoin’s exposure to gold remains muted at 6.8%, challenging the digital-gold diversification narrative. Dynamic analysis reveals significant time-variation: the TCI climbs to 71.5% during the March 2020 liquidity crisis and to 68.9% following the November 2022 FTX collapse, suggesting that connectedness intensifies precisely when diversification benefits are most needed. Panel regressions further indicate that a one-standard-deviation increase in equity-market realized volatility raises crypto-equity pairwise connectedness by 0.38 percentage points (p < 0.01). Taken together, the evidence suggests that cryptocurrencies, while partially segmented during tranquil periods, become deeply intertwined with traditional assets and underlying risk factors during episodes of financial stress, materially eroding their safe-haven properties.

title: Artificial neural networks for disease trajectory prediction in the context of sepsis
text:
In this study, we demonstrated the considerable potential of artificial neural networks to predict disease trajectories in septic patients, offering a robust data-driven framework for anticipating clinical deterioration, therapeutic response, and longitudinal organ function over the course of critical illness. Our findings indicate that deep learning architectures can effectively integrate high-dimensional, longitudinal intensive care data to capture dynamic, non-linear patterns associated with adverse outcomes, thereby outperforming conventional severity scores in both discrimination and calibration. By forecasting individualized patient paths rather than static endpoints alone, these models provide a temporal predictive framework that aligns closely with the heterogeneous and rapidly evolving pathophysiology of sepsis.

The clinical implications of this work are substantial. Early and accurate trajectory prediction may enable timely proactive interventions, optimized resource allocation, and truly personalized treatment strategies, ultimately improving survival rates and reducing the burden of persistent organ dysfunction and long-term morbidity. Nevertheless, important challenges remain. Model interpretability continues to limit widespread clinical adoption, necessitating the integration of explainable artificial intelligence techniques to foster transparency, accountability, and trust among bedside practitioners. Furthermore, the generalizability of our findings across diverse health care systems, treatment protocols, electronic health record infrastructures, and patient populations requires rigorous external validation using large-scale prospective, multicenter cohorts.

Future investigations should focus on incorporating multi-modal data streams—including granular electronic health records, continuous physiological waveforms, laboratory trends, and multi-omics profiles—into unified neural architectures. Combining these methodological advances with seamless real-time deployment pipelines and clinician-in-the-loop interfaces will be critical for translating algorithmic performance into tangible bedside impact. Overall, artificial neural networks represent a transformative paradigm for sepsis trajectory prediction, bridging the gap between complex critical care data and precision medicine, though sustained interdisciplinary collaboration between data scientists, clinicians, and health systems researchers remains essential to fully realize their clinical potential.

title: New Quality Metrics for Dynamic Graph Drawing
text:
Dynamic graph drawing aims to visualize evolving networks by producing readable layouts that preserve users' mental maps across consecutive time steps. Despite significant progress in algorithm design, the quantitative evaluation of dynamic layouts remains hindered by the limited expressiveness of conventional quality metrics. Existing measures, such as average node displacement or stress preservation, primarily focus on absolute coordinate changes of individual nodes, often failing to capture higher-order structural patterns, collective neighborhood behaviors, and the perceptual impact of localized topological changes. Consequently, algorithm developers and practitioners lack reliable tools to comprehensively assess the trade-offs between aesthetic quality and temporal stability.

This paper introduces a novel suite of quality metrics specifically engineered for dynamic graph drawing. We formally define three complementary measures that operate at different levels of abstraction. First, Temporal Edge Crossing Stability (TECS) quantifies the persistence of edge crossing topologies across time slices, addressing a critical yet neglected aspect of visual complexity. Second, Relative Displacement Consistency (RDC) assesses the preservation of geometric relationships and distances among adjacent nodes, capturing local structural fidelity independent of global coordinate frames. Third, Global Shape Preservation (GSP) evaluates the stability of community-level shapes and spatial clustering configurations over time. Integrated together, these metrics establish a multi-resolution evaluation framework that better aligns with cognitive research on mental map preservation.

We validate the proposed metrics through extensive computational experiments on both synthetic benchmarks and real-world dynamic networks, comparing multiple state-of-the-art layout algorithms. The results demonstrate that our metrics possess significantly greater discriminative power than traditional measures, successfully revealing subtle layout trade-offs previously indistinguishable. Additionally, a controlled user study with 40 participants confirms that the new metrics correlate more strongly with human subjective ratings of stability and readability. The metrics are computationally efficient, mathematically rigorous, and implementation-agnostic, providing researchers with practical tools to benchmark algorithms and guiding the development of next-generation dynamic graph visualization techniques.

title: Thunder-cell as Source of Energetic Protons
text: Thunderstorms are among the most powerful natural particle accelerators on Earth. Over the past two decades, compelling evidence has linked thunderstorm cells to intense bursts of gamma-ray radiation, including terrestrial gamma-ray flashes (TGFs) and gamma-ray glows, primarily attributed to relativistic runaway electron avalanches and subsequent bremsstrahlung emission. While electron acceleration has been extensively studied both observationally and theoretically, the capability of thunderstorm electric fields to accelerate ions—particularly protons—to high energies remains poorly constrained. Recent observations of enhanced neutron fluxes and anomalous radiation signatures near active thunderclouds nevertheless suggest that nuclei may undergo significant acceleration within the strong electric fields of thunderstorm cells. In this study, we investigate the hypothesis that thunderstorm convective cells can serve as effective sources of energetic protons. By combining high-resolution observational data with numerical simulations of electric field structures inside thunderstorm cells, we demonstrate that protons can be accelerated to energies exceeding tens of MeV under favorable conditions. These findings challenge the conventional paradigm that thunderstorm acceleration is exclusively electron-dominated and open new avenues for understanding atmospheric ion acceleration, with important implications for atmospheric electricity, aviation radiation hazard assessment, and related space weather phenomena.

title: Processing of body-induced thermal signatures for physical distancing and temperature screening
text: The concurrent need for non-contact physiological monitoring and spatial adherence in high-density environments has motivated the development of integrated thermal sensing systems. This paper presents a unified framework for processing body-induced thermal signatures to simultaneously enforce physical distancing and perform skin temperature screening using passive infrared thermography. We introduce a thermal signature extraction pipeline that segments human regions of interest from cluttered backgrounds, compensates for ambient radiative drift and environmental reflections, and normalizes emissivity variations across skin and clothing boundaries. A calibrated stereo-thermal geometry module reconstructs three-dimensional inter-personal distances, while a sub-pixel radiometric analysis algorithm estimates core body temperature from periorbital and facial keypoints. The proposed method was evaluated on a dataset of 12,500 thermal frames acquired in diverse indoor scenarios, including airports, healthcare facilities, and commercial lobbies under varying ambient conditions. Experimental results demonstrate that the system achieves inter-personal distance estimation with a mean absolute error of 3.2 cm and temperature screening sensitivity of 98.4% at a false positive rate of 2.1%, operating in real time at 30 frames per second. By fusing geometric and radiometric thermal analytics within a single edge-compatible architecture, this work offers a robust, scalable solution for automated public health surveillance without compromising personal privacy.

title: Enterprise Systems Lifecycle-wide Innovation Readiness
text:
Enterprise systems (ES) constitute the digital backbone of modern organizations, integrating core business processes and enabling data-driven decision-making across functional boundaries. As technological turbulence accelerates and competitive pressures mount, firms must not only implement these complex systems but also continuously innovate within and around them. However, the capacity to absorb, adapt, and exploit new technological opportunities—broadly termed innovation readiness—has traditionally been examined through fragmented lenses, often confined to discrete phases of the ES lifecycle such as selection, implementation, or upgrade. This narrow focus risks overlooking how readiness in one stage constrains or enables possibilities in subsequent stages.

Treating innovation readiness as a phase-specific construct obscures the dynamic interdependencies that shape an organization’s ability to sustain value creation from system conception through retirement. Existing research offers limited guidance on how preparatory factors, resource configurations, and organizational capabilities propagate across the entire ES journey. Consequently, practitioners lack holistic diagnostic frameworks to build and maintain the multifaceted competencies required for enduring innovation.

Addressing this gap, the present research conceptualizes Enterprise Systems Lifecycle-wide Innovation Readiness as an integrated phenomenon that transcends individual implementation milestones. By synthesizing insights from information systems, innovation management, and organizational readiness literatures, this paper examines how readiness antecedents, dimensions, and outcomes interconnect across the ES lifecycle. In doing so, it establishes a foundation for understanding how organizations can cultivate resilient innovation capabilities that co-evolve with their enterprise systems over time.

title: Mapping Temporal Trends of Parent-Child Migration from Population-Scale Family Trees
text: Analysis of 4.2 million parent-child dyads spanning 1700–1950 revealed distinct temporal shifts in intergenerational mobility. Prior to 1850, 68% of children settled within 10 km of their birthplace, yielding mean parent-child distances of 8.3 km. This spatial stability declined sharply after 1880: by 1900, only 41% remained within the same radius, and mean distances increased to 34.6 km. Long-distance relocations exceeding 100 km rose from 4% in pre-industrial cohorts to 19% among those born after 1890. Urban hubs absorbed 52% of migrating children post-1870, compared to 23% in earlier periods, with textile and coal regions dominating destination profiles. Notably, maternal proximity persisted longer than paternal bonds, as mother-child dyads consistently showed 15% shorter mean distances than father-child pairs across all cohorts. These trends correlate strongly with railway expansion and industrialization, suggesting that macroeconomic restructuring, rather than isolated household decisions, primarily governed the observed divergence in parent-child spatial relationships.

title: Double-calibration estimators accounting for under-coverage and nonresponse in socio-economic surveys
text: We proposed double-calibration estimators to simultaneously correct for under-coverage and nonresponse in socio-economic surveys. By integrating auxiliary information from multiple sources, the estimators adjust sampling weights through a two-step calibration process that aligns survey totals with reliable population benchmarks while preserving internal consistency. Theoretical results demonstrate that the proposed approach yields approximately unbiased estimates under the assumed models and reduces mean squared error compared to methods that address only a single error source. Empirical investigations based on realistic survey scenarios indicate substantial bias reduction for key socio-economic indicators, even when both coverage errors and nonresponse are nonignorable. The procedure remains computationally tractable and can be implemented using standard calibration software, enhancing its practical appeal for national statistical offices. Future research may extend this framework to longitudinal designs and develop robust variance estimators. Overall, double-calibration offers a flexible and effective strategy for improving the accuracy and reliability of complex household surveys.

title: A general solution to the preferential selection model
text: The preferential selection model, which describes how decision-makers choose among alternatives based on heterogeneous preferences and capacity constraints, is fundamental to strategic behavior in economics, sociology, and operations research. Despite its wide applicability, existing approaches typically address specific institutional settings—such as school choice, labor market matching, or college admissions—through tailored assumptions that limit their generalizability. This paper proposes a general solution framework that unifies these disparate cases by characterizing preferential selection as a constrained optimization over general preference orderings. Our approach employs a dual representation theorem to transform the equilibrium selection problem into a variational inequality, which can be solved efficiently via a modified Newton-Kantorovich algorithm with guaranteed convergence under standard conditions. We establish the existence and uniqueness of the equilibrium selection rule under mild regularity conditions and derive the asymptotic distribution of the estimated preference parameters, enabling valid statistical inference in moderately sized samples. Through extensive Monte Carlo simulations and three empirical applications—analyzing college admissions under affirmative action, priority-based resource allocation in healthcare, and assortative matching in marriage markets—we demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms specialized alternatives in computational efficiency, robustness to misspecification, and predictive accuracy. The proposed framework subsumes classical Gale-Shapley matching models and discrete choice specifications as special cases while flexibly accommodating complex quota constraints, incomplete preference lists, multi-tier priority criteria, and dynamic preference updating. These results provide researchers with a versatile, computationally tractable tool for analyzing preferential selection across diverse institutional environments without requiring setting-specific modifications.

title: Quantitative Cost and Schedule Risk Analysis of Nuclear Waste Storage
text: The safe and efficient management of nuclear waste represents one of the most critical challenges facing the global nuclear energy industry. With the expanding deployment of nuclear power plants worldwide, particularly in rapidly developing nations such as China, the construction of geological disposal repositories and interim storage facilities has become increasingly urgent. These large-scale infrastructure projects are characterized by substantial capital investment, extended construction durations, stringent regulatory requirements, and complex technical uncertainties, rendering them highly susceptible to significant cost overruns and schedule delays. Although previous studies have extensively examined technical safety assessments, site selection criteria, and environmental impacts of nuclear waste disposal, quantitative analyses that systematically integrate both cost and schedule risks throughout the project lifecycle remain notably insufficient. To bridge this gap, this study develops an integrated quantitative risk analysis framework that simultaneously evaluates cost and schedule uncertainties using Monte Carlo simulation combined with correlation and sensitivity analyses. By applying this framework to representative nuclear waste storage projects, we identify critical risk drivers, quantify their interactive effects, and assess the probability distributions of total investment and completion time. The findings offer practical insights for policymakers and project managers to optimize risk mitigation strategies, enhance budget reliability, and improve the overall economic feasibility of nuclear waste management programs.

title: Balancing Taxi Distribution in A City-Scale Dynamic Ridesharing Service: A Hybrid Solution Based on Demand Learning
text: The proliferation of dynamic ridesharing platforms in metropolitan areas has exacerbated spatial imbalances between taxi supply and passenger demand, leading to prolonged waiting times, increased idle cruising, and degraded service reliability across heterogeneous urban zones. Traditional dispatch and repositioning strategies predominantly rely on reactive heuristics or localized matching rules, which struggle to anticipate complex spatio-temporal demand fluctuations and consequently fail to achieve system-wide fleet equilibrium in large-scale operating environments. To address this challenge, we propose a hybrid framework that synergizes deep demand learning with proactive fleet rebalancing for city-scale dynamic ridesharing systems. Our approach first leverages a multi-task spatio-temporal graph neural network to infer fine-grained, short-term passenger demand across urban regions, effectively encoding dynamic contextual dependencies including real-time traffic states, meteorological conditions, and point-of-interest activity patterns. These predictive demand signals are then integrated into a two-stage decision hierarchy: an upper-level mixed-integer programming model generates coarse-grained vehicle relocation directives to align district-level supply–demand ratios, while a lower-level multi-agent reinforcement learning module executes fine-grained, real-time dispatching and routing adjustments in response to stochastic order arrivals and local congestion. By tightly coupling anticipatory demand inference with operational fleet control, our solution balances global spatial efficiency with localized responsiveness without incurring prohibitive computational costs. Comprehensive evaluations on large-scale real-world trajectory and order datasets from a major metropolitan area demonstrate that the proposed method substantially reduces average passenger waiting time, driver vacant mileage, and supply–demand variance compared to both myopic relocation and pure learning-based baselines. Ablation studies further confirm the complementary roles of demand prediction and hybrid optimization in improving overall performance. These findings validate that demand-aware hybrid rebalancing strategies are essential for enhancing system efficiency, driver income equity, and service sustainability in city-wide ridesharing operations.

title: DQI: A Guide to Benchmark Evaluation
text:
Benchmarks have long served as the cornerstone of progress in machine learning and artificial intelligence, providing standardized tasks through which models are trained, compared, and validated. Yet as the field has matured, benchmarks themselves have proliferated to an extent that their quality varies dramatically, while the criteria by which they are judged remain fragmented across subdisciplines. Researchers routinely encounter datasets afflicted by label noise, distributional skew, or inadequate coverage of edge cases, while evaluation protocols often emphasize narrow leaderboard rankings over meaningful generalization. This inconsistency makes it difficult to discern whether reported advances reflect genuine algorithmic improvements or merely exploit idiosyncrasies in benchmark design. Consequently, there is growing recognition that benchmarks must be evaluated with the same rigor applied to the models they test.

To address this gap, we present the Data Quality Index (DQI), a comprehensive framework designed to systematically assess the fitness of benchmarks for their intended purpose. DQI moves beyond single-score summaries by decomposing benchmark quality into interpretable dimensions—including validity, reliability, fairness, robustness, and utility—each accompanied by actionable diagnostic criteria. Rather than treating benchmark evaluation as a post-hoc afterthought, DQI integrates assessment into the design lifecycle, enabling creators to identify vulnerabilities prior to deployment and allowing practitioners to select evaluation suites with documented transparency. By synthesizing best practices from metrology, psychometrics, and machine learning, the framework offers a common vocabulary for articulating what makes a benchmark useful, trustworthy, and durable.

This paper serves as a practical guide to applying DQI in research and development settings. We detail the theoretical underpinnings of each quality dimension, illustrate their measurement through concrete examples drawn from computer vision, natural language processing, and tabular data benchmarks, and provide protocols for reproducible auditing. Our aim is not to prescribe a single universal benchmark, but to equip the community with tools to discriminate between superficially impressive evaluation suites and those that genuinely advance scientific understanding. In doing so, we hope to foster a culture in which benchmark quality is held to the same exacting standards expected of the algorithms they measure.
